doi:10.1001/jama.2026.17403.abstract: One in 5 heart transplant candidates in the US die or are delisted without transplant. Donor hearts are currently allocated by a 6-status therapy-based system criticized for limited risk stratification and susceptibility to gaming. To develop a new heart allocation policy based on an objective medical urgency score that ranks candidates based on the interaction between physiology and mechanical circulatory support. Registry-based observational study using data from the US organ transplant system. All adult (aged ≥18 years) heart transplant candidates from January 2019 to August 2025 were included, split into training (2019-2023), validation (2023-2024), and test (2024-2025) datasets. A marginal structural model of 6-week mortality without transplant was estimated (the US Candidate Risk Score [US-CRS]). Eight models were compared in held-out data by weighted time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and calibration by status. Finally, US-CRS was converted into an allocation policy and a match-run simulation of waitlist reordering was performed compared with the current 6-status system. Adult heart transplant candidates were partitioned into consecutive training (n = 21 859), validation (n = 7897), and test (n = 8256) datasets (mean [SD] age, 53 [13] years; 74% male). The chosen US-CRS model included 5 laboratory values and 4 therapeutic devices (durable left ventricular assist device, intra-aortic balloon pump, microaxial flow pump, and advanced mechanical circulatory support). In test-set cross-sections of candidates actively waiting on the same calendar date, US-CRS had similar or significantly higher time-dependent AUC than the current 6-status system (mean AUC, 0.807 vs 0.693, respectively) and acceptable calibration by status, especially for candidates who received their status by exception. In match-run analysis (n = 45 530 donor hearts), a US-CRS-based system led to 67% of transplant recipients moving down in rank order and increased observed 6-week transplant-censored mortality for the first candidate on the match run from 11.2% (95% CI, 10.1%-12.5%) under the current system to 15.7% (95% CI, 13.9%-17.6%) under the US-CRS-based system. In this registry-based study of US heart transplant candidates, a US-CRS-based allocation system prioritized sicker candidates with higher mortality without transplant compared with the current medical urgency statuses.

doi:10.1001/jama.2026.17622.abstract: Heart failure affects more than 6 million US adults; approximately 4% to 5% progress to advanced disease despite optimal therapy. Heart transplant is a class I guideline-recommended therapy for select individuals with advanced heart failure. Early referral for heart transplant is guided by the "I NEED HELP" mnemonic, a tool that identifies patients with advanced heart failure based on criteria such as use of inotropes, persistent symptoms (New York Heart Association class III or IV), end-organ dysfunction, left ventricular ejection fraction, defibrillator shocks, hospitalizations for heart failure, persistent edema or escalating use of diuretics, and low blood pressure. Each criterion is associated with higher risk of death or first heart failure hospitalization over a median follow-up of 260 days (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.19 [95% CI, 1.11-1.27] for each additional criterion). Typical absolute contraindications to heart transplant include active systemic infection, malignancy with limited life expectancy, severe and irreversible end-organ dysfunction (eg, cirrhosis, severe pulmonary hypertension), active substance use, major untreated psychiatric illness, inadequate social support, and severe frailty. Approximately 4600 heart transplants are performed annually in the US. The mortality rate was 8.5 deaths/100 patient-years for adults on the transplant waiting list in 2023. Leading causes of early death after transplant include primary graft dysfunction (39.5%), multiorgan failure (18.5%), and infection (13.9%). Among adults, contemporary survival rates after heart transplant are 91.5% at 1 year and 80.3% at 5 years. Lifelong maintenance immunosuppression typically combines a calcineurin inhibitor, antiproliferative agents (typically mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine) and corticosteroids, with selective use of induction therapy (intensive immunosuppression immediately after transplant). Acute rejection requiring treatment occurs in 20% to 25% of recipients within a year, and may be treated with high-dose corticosteroids, antithymocyte globulin, and B-cell-targeted therapies (such as rituximab or bortezomib). Rejection surveillance with endomyocardial biopsies of the right ventricular septum is performed 5 to 10 times within the first year after transplant. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (chronic rejection that causes diffuse coronary narrowing) affects 29% of heart transplant recipients within 5 years and 46.8% by 10 years and is the leading cause of late mortality. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy is treated with statins, mechanistic target of rapamycin inhibitors (such as sirolimus or everolimus), and retransplant for severe cases. Infections (62.5% are bacterial, 30.0% are viral, 6.7% are fungal, and 0.8% are parasitic) and malignancy (10.7% within 5 years after heart transplant) are other leading causes of late mortality. Heart transplant is the definitive therapy for carefully selected patients with advanced heart failure despite receiving optimal, guideline-directed therapy. After heart transplant, lifelong multidisciplinary care is necessary to manage immunosuppression, prevent and treat rejection and cardiac allograft vasculopathy, and monitor for infection and malignancy.

doi:10.1001/jama.2026.18471.abstract: Rigorous evidence for inhaled sedation using isoflurane in mechanically ventilated patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF) is limited. To evaluate whether an inhaled sedation strategy lowers hospital mortality compared with usual care intravenous sedation strategy in mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF. Pragmatic, effectiveness, open-label, superiority, randomized clinical trial in 14 intensive care units (ICUs) in Canada. Adults (≥18 years) receiving sedation for less than 72 hours and receiving mechanical ventilation for AHRF from non-COVID respiratory failure (ratio of partial pressure of arterial oxygen [Pao2] to fraction of inspired oxygen [Fio2] <300 mm Hg) or COVID-19 were enrolled between September 2020 and March 2025 with follow-up through June 2025. Patients were randomized to an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed or to a usual intravenous sedation care strategy. Sedatives were titrated to achieve the desired target sedation score guided by clinical teams and continued until extubation or death. Primary outcome was all-cause hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU- and ventilator-free days at day 30; hospital-free days at day 60; use of refractory hypoxemia adjunctive therapies; delirium- and coma-free days at day 14; and quality-of-life and disability scores at 3 months. Of 786 patients randomized, 780 were included in the primary analysis (mean age, 61.1 years; 34.0% female; 73.7% non-COVID AHRF, mean Pao2:Fio2 ratio, 152.6 mm Hg); 385 in the inhaled sedation and 395 in the intravenous sedation groups. In the inhaled sedation group, 49.9% to 55.4% of patients received concomitant intravenous sedation on any day during the first 14 days after randomization. At hospital discharge, 161 of 379 patients (42.5%) in the inhaled sedation group had died, compared with 171 of 390 patients (43.8%) in the intravenous sedation group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.84 to 1.14]; P = .85). There was no effect modification in prespecified subgroup analyses for age, sex, and COVID-19 status. ICU-, ventilator-, and hospital-free days were similar between groups. The inhaled sedation group received more adjunctive therapies for hypoxemia (239 [63.9%] vs 214 [55.0%]; between-group difference, 8.89% [95% CI, 1.95% to 15.83%]) and had fewer delirium- and coma-free days (between-group difference, -0.95 [95% CI, -1.69 to -0.22]). There was no difference in quality-of-life and disability scores between groups. In mechanically ventilated adults with AHRF, an inhaled sedation strategy using isoflurane with intravenous adjuncts as clinically needed did not reduce hospital mortality compared with an intravenous sedation strategy. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04415060.

doi:10.1001/jama.2026.21291.abstract: Fluid therapy is ubiquitous in the intensive care unit (ICU) but carries risks, especially in mechanically ventilated patients. Contemporary global practice across dose, indication, and type is unknown. To characterize ICU fluid practices in mechanically ventilated adults. International prospective observational cohort study between April 2024 and July 2025, across 206 ICUs in 41 countries on 6 continents. Consecutive adult patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation within 3 days of ICU admission and ventilated 24 hours or more. Exclusion criteria were age younger than 16 years and transfer under mechanical ventilation from another ICU. Fluid volume, indication, and type after intubation. Key measures included (1) total infused volume and daily fluid balance over 7 days after intubation; (2) the indication for fluid therapy over the first 3 days after intubation; (3) the proportion of total administered fluid volume attributable to each fluid type over the first 3 days after intubation. Among 2454 patients analyzed (median age, 63 years [IQR, 49-73 years]; 63.6% [1560] male), median daily fluid input peaked on day 1 at 3.0 L (IQR, 2.2-4.0 L) and declined to 2.6 L (IQR, 1.8-3.5 L) through day 6. Daily fluid balance (median, 0.9 L; IQR, 0.1-1.9 L on day 1) decreased to less than 0.3 L (IQR, -0.5 to 1.2 L) by day 3 and remained near-neutral through day 6. Maintenance and replacement fluids (to meet daily requirements and to correct ongoing losses; 31.9%) and creep fluids (to deliver medications and maintain catheter patency; 30.9%) were the primary indications, whereas resuscitation (to restore circulating blood volume; 16.0%) accounted for a smaller proportion. Isotonic balanced crystalloids (48.9%) and isotonic saline (0.9% sodium chloride) (27.0%) were common; colloids were rare (1.3%). Substantial between-site variation persisted after adjustment for case-mix. In this prospective international cohort study, fluid therapy varied widely among mechanically ventilated critically ill patients, with maintenance and creep fluids-rather than resuscitation fluids-accounting for most total volume.

doi:10.1001/jama.2026.21322.abstract: International guidelines recommend dobutamine for management of septic shock and cardiac dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion in adults based on very low-certainty evidence. Randomized trials are lacking on the effect of intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine on postoperative outcomes in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control. To determine whether intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduces acute kidney injury (AKI) within 7 postoperative days in patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control. This randomized, open-label clinical trial in 39 tertiary hospitals in China enrolled adults with septic shock who were undergoing surgical source control between June 2024 and August 2025. Follow-up ended on November 15, 2025. Intraoperative, intravenous infusion of dobutamine (up to 5 µg/kg/min) combined with norepinephrine vs norepinephrine alone. The primary outcome was new-onset AKI or worsening of preoperative AKI within 7 days after surgery, defined using Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria. The 11 secondary outcomes included Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score on postoperative day 1 and urine output 1 hour post intervention. Among 584 patients (median [IQR] age, 67.5 [55.0-76.0] years; 192 [32.9%] females), new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days occurred in 22.8% (66/290) randomized to receive dobutamine plus norepinephrine vs 34.7% (102/294) randomized to receive norepinephrine alone (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 0.64 [95% CI, 0.49-0.83]). No significant differences were observed in 9 of the 11 secondary outcomes. SOFA scores on postoperative day 1 (adjusted difference, -0.53 [95% CI, -0.98 to -0.07]) were lower and urine output 1 hour post intervention (adjusted difference, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.03 to 1.07] mL/kg/h) was higher in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group. Stage 2 and 3 AKI were lower in the dobutamine plus norepinephrine group compared with the norepinephrine alone group (stage 2: 4.8% vs 9.9%; ARR, 0.48 [95% CI, 0.26-0.88]; stage 3: 7.9% vs 13.6%; ARR, 0.56 [95% CI, 0.35-0.91]). Tachycardia (heart rate >100/min) occurred more frequently in patients receiving dobutamine and norepinephrine than norepinephrine alone. Among adult patients with septic shock undergoing surgical source control, intraoperative dobutamine combined with norepinephrine reduced the incidence of new-onset or worsening AKI within 7 postoperative days compared with norepinephrine. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06462313.

doi:10.1001/jama.2026.21333.abstract: The optimal vasopressor dose at which to initiate a second vasopressor in patients with septic shock is uncertain. To compare the effects of hospital-level strategies initiating vasopressin infusion at a lower threshold vs a higher threshold on outcomes in patients with septic shock. Cluster-randomized, cluster-crossover, pragmatic clinical strategy trial including adult patients receiving vasopressors for septic shock at 13 hospitals in Idaho and Utah from February 1, 2024, to July 31, 2025. The last day of follow-up for the primary outcome was February 17, 2026. Hospital-level implementation of septic shock management strategies recommending fixed-dose vasopressin initiation when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.1 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (lower-threshold strategy) or when the total dose of other vasopressors reached 0.4 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent (higher-threshold strategy). Hospitals were randomized for the first month to an initial strategy (6 hospitals to the lower threshold vs 7 hospitals to the higher threshold) and then crossed over to the alternate strategy monthly thereafter. The primary outcome of 28-day mortality and the key secondary outcome of kidney replacement therapy-free days through day 28 were analyzed using multivariable generalized linear mixed-effects models, accounting for trial site and baseline patient characteristics. There were 3959 unique patients with septic shock (median age, 68 [IQR, 57 to 77] years; 1903 [48%] were female). Of the patients more likely to experience differential management under the tested hospital-level vasopressin dose strategies (maximum vasopressor dose ≥0.07 µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent), 1034 of 1521 (68.0%) cared for under the lower-threshold strategy received vasopressin compared with 651 of 1526 (42.7%) cared for under the higher-threshold strategy. In the hospital-level strategy recommending a lower-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation, the maximum vasopressor dose received prior to vasopressin initiation was a median of 0.14 (IQR, 0.10 to 0.22) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent vs 0.34 (IQR, 0.16 to 0.42) µg/kg/min of norepinephrine or equivalent in the hospital-level strategy recommending a higher-dose threshold for vasopressin initiation. Mortality at 28 days occurred in 628 of 1975 patients (31.8%) treated with the hospital-level strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower-dose threshold of other vasopressors vs 655 of 1984 patients (33.0%) treated with the higher-threshold strategy (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.87 to 1.06], P = .62; adjusted risk difference, -0.4 [95% CI, -2.7 to 1.3] percentage points). Patients in both strategies for vasopressin initiation had a median of 29 (IQR, -1 to 29) kidney replacement therapy-free days (adjusted marginal odds ratio, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.91 to 1.14]). In this large, pragmatic clinical trial comparing the effectiveness of 2 hospital-level strategies for second-line vasopressor management in septic shock, a strategy recommending initiation of vasopressin at a lower dose of other vasopressors did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with a strategy recommending vasopressin initiation at a higher dose of other vasopressors. ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT06217562.

doi:10.1002/1878-0261.13752.abstract: Lipid metabolism is altered in rapidly proliferating cancer cells, where fatty acids (FAs) are utilized in the synthesis of sphingolipids and glycerophospholipids to produce cell membranes and signaling molecules. Receptor for activated C‐kinase 1 (RACK1; also known as small ribosomal subunit protein) is an intracellular scaffolding protein involved in signaling pathways. Whether such lipid metabolism is regulated by RACK1 is unknown. Here, integrated spatially resolved metabolomics and spatial transcriptomics revealed that accumulation of lipids in cervical cancer (CC) samples correlated with overexpression of RACK1 , and RACK1 promoted lipid synthesis in CC cells. Chromatin immunoprecipitation verified binding of sterol regulatory element‐binding protein 1 (SREBP1) to acetyl‐CoA carboxylase (ACC) and fatty acid synthase (FASN) promoters. RACK1 enhanced de novo FA synthesis by upregulating expression of sterol regulatory element binding transcription factor 1 ( SREBP1 ) and lipogenic genes FASN and ACC1 . Co‐immunoprecipitation and western blotting revealed that RACK1 interacted with protein kinase B (AKT) to activate the AKT/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR)/SREBP1 signaling pathway to promote FA synthesis. Cell proliferation and apoptosis experiments suggested that RACK1‐regulated FA synthesis is key in the progression of CC. Thus, RACK1 enhanced lipid synthesis through the AKT/mTOR/SREBP1 signaling pathway to promote the growth of CC cells. RACK1 may become a therapeutic target for CC.

doi:10.1002/1878-0261.13786.abstract: Glioblastoma cells rely on connexin 43 (Cx43)‐based gap junctions (GJs) for intercellular communication, enabling them to integrate into a widely branched malignant network. Although there are promising prospects for new targeted therapies, the lack of clinically feasible GJ inhibitors has impeded their adoption in clinical practice. In the present study, we investigated tonabersat (TO), a blood–brain‐barrier‐penetrating drug with GJ‐inhibitory properties, in regard to its potential to disassemble intercellular connectivity in glioblastoma networks. Fluorescence‐guided measurements of calcein cell‐to‐cell transfer were used to study functional intercellular connectivity. Specific DNA fragmentation rates of propidium iodide‐stained nuclei were measured as a surrogate readout for cell death using flow cytometry. CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated gene editing of Cx43 served as a validation tool of cellular effects related to Cx43 GJ inhibition. 3′ mRNA sequencing was performed for molecular downstream analysis. We found that TO reduced intercellular GJ‐mediated cytosolic traffic and yielded a significant reduction of tumor microtube (TM) length. TO‐mediated inhibition of cellular tumor networks was accompanied by a synergistic effect for temozolomide‐induced cell death. CRISPR/Cas9 Cx43 ‐knockout revealed similar results, indicating that TO‐mediated inhibitory effects rely on the inhibition of Cx43‐based GJs. Gene set enrichment analyses found that GJ‐mediated synergistic cytotoxic effects were linked to a significant upregulation of cell death signaling pathways. In conclusion, TO disrupts TM‐based network connectivity via GJ inhibition and renders glioblastoma cells more susceptible to cytotoxic therapy. Given its previous use in clinical trials for migraine therapy, TO might harbor the potential of bridging the idea of a GJ‐targeted therapeutic approach from bench to bedside.

doi:10.1002/1878-0261.70310.abstract: Cancer develops inside organized tissue environments wherein cellular behavior is heavily influenced by local interactions and spatially restricted regulatory programs. While bulk and single‐cell sequencing technologies have fundamentally revolutionized our understanding of tumor biology, these techniques often disrupt tissue architecture and therefore fail to capture the spatial context in which molecular processes occur. Spatial transcriptomics has provided important insights into tumor heterogeneity, microenvironmental organization, and cell‐to‐cell communication. However, gene expression alone offers only an indirect view of the regulatory mechanisms governing cellular states. The emergence of spatial epigenomic technologies now enables the investigation of chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and DNA methylation while preserving tissue structure. Here, we discuss the current landscape of spatial epigenomics, including spatial ATAC‐seq, spatial CUT&Tag, emerging spatial CUT&RUN approaches, spatial DNA methylation profiling, and multimodal strategies integrating epigenetic, transcriptional, and proteomic information within the same tissue context. Despite remaining technical and computational challenges, continued advances are expected to establish spatial epigenomics as a powerful tool for studying cancer pathways and their regulation within intact tissues.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72243.abstract: ABSTRACT The CD40 gene, a key immune regulatory molecule, has been implicated in tumorigenesis, and its functional polymorphism rs1883832 located in the Kozak sequence, may modulate cancer susceptibility by influencing CD40 expression. To clarify inconsistent epidemiological findings, a comprehensive meta‐analysis was conducted to evaluate the association between the CD40 rs1883832 polymorphism and overall cancer risk. Eligible case–control studies were systematically identified from PubMed, Web of Science and Cochrane Library up to August 15, 2025, and pooled odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated under five genetic models. Eight studies encompassing 3858 cancer cases and 4699 controls met the inclusion criteria. The results revealed a significant association between the rs1883832 T allele and elevated cancer risk in 4 multiple models, including the allele (T vs. C: OR = 1.26, 95% CI: 1.09–1.47, p < 0.01), homozygous (TT vs. CC: OR = 1.58, 95% CI: 1.16–2.16, p < 0.01), recessive (TT vs. TC + CC: OR = 1.43, 95% CI: 1.18–1.82, p < 0.01), and dominant (TT + TC vs. CC: OR = 1.29, 95% CI: 1.03–1.62, p = 0.03) models. Subgroup analyses revealed suggestive patterns of associations in lung cancer and Asian populations. Sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings, and no substantial publication bias was detected. In conclusion, this meta‐analysis provides compelling evidence that the CD40 rs1883832 T allele may confer increased susceptibility to cancer, thereby underscoring the potential influence of immune gene polymorphisms in carcinogenesis and their relevance for genetic risk assessment in oncology. Trial Registration: PROSPERO number: CRD420251130223

doi:10.1002/cam4.72283.abstract: ABSTRACT Aim Previous studies have discussed the effectiveness of the Karnofsky Performance Scale (KPS), Palliative Performance Scale (PPS), Palliative Prognostic Index (PPI), and Delirium‐Palliative Prognostic Score (D‐PaP) in predicting the survival of patients with terminal‐stage tumors, but their effectiveness in the Chinese terminal‐stage tumor population still needs to be explored. Therefore, we conducted this prospective cohort study to investigate the applicability of KPS, PPS, PPI, and D‐PaP in predicting survival in Chinese patients with terminal‐stage tumors. Methods This is a prospective cohort study that collected data from 449 terminal‐stage tumor patients across four medical institutions in China from January to December 2024. The feasibility of using KPS, PPS, PPI, and D‐PaP to predict the 7‐day and 30‐day survival of terminal‐stage tumor patients was discussed through ROC curves. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were used to examine the survival differences of terminal‐stage tumor patients using four survival prediction tools with new cut‐off values. Results The study ultimately included 449 patients with terminal‐stage tumors. For the prediction of 30‐day survival, the area under the ROC curve of KPS, PPI, PPS, and D‐PaP was 0.842, 0.749, 0.778, and 0.898, respectively. In our study cohort, the optimal cut‐off values were 25, 3, 35, and 9.25. Their corresponding sensitivity was 86.3%, 92.3%, 77.7%, and 76.0%, while their specificity was 69.7%, 44.4%, 67.7%, and 93.9%, respectively. Conclusion The results of this multicenter cohort analysis reveal that in terminal‐stage tumor patients in China, KPS, PPS, PPI, and D‐PaP are all effective for predicting survival. Specifically, D‐PaP is more applicable for predicting 30‐day survival. Although D‐PaP showed the most significant predictive power, its accuracy in predicting 7‐day and 30‐day survival outcomes was not significantly superior to that of experienced palliative care professionals. Therefore, future research still needs to develop or update scoring tools with better predictive performance.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72312.abstract: ABSTRACT Background This cross‐sectional study aimed to identify symptom profiles and their associated factors in Chinese patients with multiple myeloma, thereby providing an evidence‐based foundation for developing targeted symptom management strategies. Methods Patients with multiple myeloma were recruited via convenience sampling from the hematology departments of three tertiary general hospitals in Zhejiang Province, China, between January and March 2024. Data collection utilized a sociodemographic and clinical characteristics questionnaire and the Chinese version of the M.D. Anderson Symptom Inventory‐Multiple Myeloma Module (MDASI‐MM) scale. The research conducted a latent profile analysis of symptom characteristics, followed by univariate analysis and multivariable multinomial logistic regression to examine factors associated with profile membership. Results The study included 265 Chinese patients with multiple myeloma. Latent profile analysis identified three distinct symptom profiles: “Low Symptom Burden with Walking Distress” (46.7%), “Moderate Physical Symptoms with Daily Life Interference” (37.9%), and “High Global Symptom Burden” (15.4%). Multinomial logistic regression analysis demonstrated that age, marital status, combination chemotherapy status, and Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status were significantly associated with symptom profile membership ( p < 0.05). Specifically, patients of advanced age and those with higher ECOG scores were more likely to belong to the higher burden profiles, while patients receiving combination chemotherapy and those who were unmarried/divorced/widowed were more likely to belong to the low‐burden profile. Conclusions Patients with multiple myeloma exhibit heterogeneous symptom experiences, classifiable into three latent profiles. Our findings suggest that age, marital status, combination chemotherapy, and ECOG performance status may help identify patients at risk for higher symptom burden. Future longitudinal research is needed to evaluate whether profile‐based interventions reduce symptom burden and improve quality of life.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72335.abstract: Immunotherapy has transformed the treatment landscape for advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet resistance mediated by the tumor microenvironment (TME) limits its efficacy in most patients. This review aims to synthesize the current understanding of the TME as an integrated network driving immunotherapy resistance and to evaluate emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at overcoming it. We conducted a comprehensive narrative review of key literature in the field, sourced from PubMed and major conference proceedings. The focus was on mechanistic studies elucidating immunosuppressive cell circuits, metabolic reprogramming, epigenetic regulation, spatial heterogeneity, and microbiome interactions within the lung cancer TME. Preclinical and clinical evidence for TME-targeted combination therapies and biomarker development was also critically analyzed. The TME orchestrates resistance through highly interconnected axes: (1) cellular circuits including myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), regulatory T cells (Tregs), and M2-polarized tumor-associated macrophages (M2-TAMs), (2) metabolic barriers (lactate acidosis, nutrient depletion), (3) epigenetic reprogramming, and (4) systemic communication via exosomes and the microbiome. Spatial transcriptomics reveals that driver mutations (e.g., EGFR, KRAS) shape distinct immune-excluded architectures. To disrupt this network, rational combination strategies-such as immune checkpoint inhibitors with metabolic modulators (LDHAi), epigenetic drugs, targeted agents (METi), or microbiome interventions-show synergistic potential in early-phase trials. Furthermore, a tiered biomarker system integrating spatial, metabolic, and microbial features is proposed to guide patient stratification. Overcoming immunotherapy resistance requires a paradigm shift from single-target to network-targeted therapy. This review provides an integrated framework for understanding TME-mediated resistance and translates these insights into a roadmap for clinical translation. Future efforts must prioritize biomarker-validated, rationally designed combination therapies to improve outcomes for patients with resistant NSCLC.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72356.abstract: Patients with chemotherapy- and androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI)-naïve metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) have generally shown worse overall survival (OS) with abiraterone versus enzalutamide in claims database studies. Given limitations of claims data, analysis using detailed electronic health records (EHRs) is needed to confirm this finding. This EHR-based analysis (2014-2023) of the Flatiron Health database included patients with chemotherapy- and ARPI-naïve mCRPC who initiated first-line ARPI (abiraterone or enzalutamide). OS, treatment duration, and time to subsequent therapy were assessed. A subgroup analysis evaluated patients who received first-line ARPI only with no subsequent treatments. Kaplan-Meier method and Cox proportional hazards models evaluated time-to-event outcomes. Stabilized inverse probability treatment weighting (sIPTW) adjusted for baseline differences. Among 2731 patients, 1316 received first-line abiraterone and 1415 enzalutamide (median follow-up: 21.8 and 23.2 months, respectively). sIPTW-adjusted median OS (24.6 vs. 25.8 months; hazard ratio [HR] 1.13; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.03-1.23), treatment duration (7.9 vs. 9.5 months; HR 1.21; 95% CI, 1.11-1.31), and time to subsequent therapy (14.7 vs. 17.9 months; HR 1.20; 95% CI, 1.08-1.32) were shorter with abiraterone versus enzalutamide. Among the 40% with no subsequent treatment (n = 1102), sIPTW-adjusted median OS (14.0 vs. 17.7 months; HR 1.32; 95% CI, 1.14-1.53), and treatment duration (7.5 vs. 10.6 months; HR 1.30; 95% CI, 1.12-1.50) were also shorter with abiraterone versus enzalutamide. Using more detailed data abstraction, these results confirm prior claims-based analyses showing that despite early use of subsequent therapy, first-line abiraterone is associated with shorter OS versus enzalutamide in ARPI- and chemotherapy-naïve mCRPC. Clinical Trial ID: NCT05968599.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72366.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Platinum‐doublet concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT) for locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC) is frequently complicated by severe neutropenia. This Phase II trial investigated whether combining active bone marrow‐sparing (ABMS) radiotherapy with prophylactic pegylated recombinant human granulocyte colony‐stimulating factor (PEG‐rhG‐CSF) could reduce the incidence of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia below a prespecified historical benchmark of 30%. Methods Patients with FIGO 2018 stage IIA2–IVA LACC received SPECT‐guided ABMS radiotherapy (45 Gy external beam plus 30 Gy brachytherapy) concurrent with paclitaxel/carboplatin every 21 days for 4 cycles followed by prophylactic PEG‐rhG‐CSF. Using Simon's two‐stage design ( α = 0.05, β = 0.20), we tested whether grade ≥ 3 neutropenia could be reduced from a historical benchmark of 30% to ≤ 15%. The primary endpoint was grade ≥ 3 neutropenia incidence; secondary endpoints included other cytopenias, treatment completion, and survival outcomes. Results Fifty‐four patients were enrolled. Grade ≥ 3 neutropenia occurred in 13.0% (7/54; 95% CI: 5.4%–24.9%), meeting the prespecified success criterion (one‐sided exact binomial test, p = 0.003 versus the 30% benchmark). Other grade ≥ 3 toxicities included leukopenia (18.5%), anemia (3.7%), thrombocytopenia (5.6%), and febrile neutropenia (1.9%). Overall, 85.2% of patients completed all 4 planned chemotherapy cycles, and all completed radiotherapy within 8 weeks (median overall treatment time: 50 days). At a median follow‐up of 40 months, the 3‐year progression‐free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) rates were 88.8% and 88.9%, respectively (6 events each); the study was not powered for survival efficacy. Conclusions The combination of ABMS radiotherapy and prophylactic PEG‐rhG‐CSF was associated with a grade ≥ 3 neutropenia rate of 13.0% and a chemotherapy completion rate of 85.2% during platinum‐doublet CCRT for LACC. Because the single‐arm design and reliance on historical controls preclude causal inference, these findings are hypothesis‐generating and primarily establish the operational feasibility of this dual hematoprotection approach. Formal evaluation of safety and efficacy requires the ongoing randomized trial (ChiCTR2400087321). Trial Registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2100046911. Registered May 30, 2021

doi:10.1002/cam4.72369.abstract: Spatial heterogeneity in the colorectal cancer (CRC) tumor microenvironment (TME) is closely related to stromal organization and may influence treatment-related features. In this study, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic data from CRC tissues to examine cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF)-dominant spatial domains. GPC1 and CHPF were enriched in stromal regions and showed higher expression in CRC tissues than in normal tissues. In the analyzed cohorts, higher GPC1 and CHPF expression was associated with advanced clinicopathological features and poorer survival outcomes in univariate analyses. Single-cell analyses showed that GPC1 and CHPF were mainly expressed in fibroblasts and were enriched in an ADAM12-associated fibroblast subset with myofibroblast-like features, extracellular matrix-related genes, and hypoxia/glycolysis-related signatures. Cell-cell communication analysis suggested that this fibroblast subset was linked to higher inferred WNT signaling. Drug-response and immunotherapy-related analyses further showed that GPC1 and CHPF expression was associated with transcriptomic patterns related to treatment response. In mucinous adenocarcinoma (MA), the ADAM12-associated fibroblast program showed stronger inferred MIF-related signaling and was associated with macrophage M2-like features. Spatial mapping and multiplex immunofluorescence supported partial colocalization of GPC1, CHPF, and ADAM12 in CAF-rich stromal regions. In CAFs, GPC1 or CHPF knockdown reduced ADAM12, CAF activation markers, and WNT/MIF-related proteins, while ADAM12 knockdown weakened macrophage M2-like marker expression in a co-culture model. These findings suggest that GPC1 and CHPF mark an ADAM12-associated CAF program linked to stromal remodeling and immune-related features in CRC, especially in MA, but further studies are needed to define its functional role.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72371.abstract: Healthcare services and data ecosystems remain fragmented, inequitable and misaligned with patient, clinician and public health needs. Three pathways to patient-centred Artificial Intelligence (AI) have emerged to address this: data collaboration, Whole System Approaches and digital inclusion. Each has advanced the field. However, none delivers the continuous, participatory and outcome-grounded learning that equitable AI demands. The populations whose data drives AI learning must also be the populations who benefit from it. This principle has not been structurally embedded in any existing pathway. This narrative review defines a framework for operationalising Adaptive Machine Learning (AML) as a fourth, integrative pathway to patient-centred AI. AML is defined as continuous learning from real-world individual-level data to generate personalised, population-level insights returning direct benefit to the communities who produce them. A narrative review of PubMed and Google Scholar (2018-2025) was conducted across five thematic domains: AI and machine learning in healthcare; real-world data and evidence; patient-centred care and digital health; data governance and AI regulation; and adaptive clinical trial design. Search terms covered healthcare AI applications and adaptive, continuously learning systems, emphasising prediction-oriented rather than static diagnostic approaches. Eligibility was determined through iterative thematic analysis. Eight systemic barriers to patient-centred AI are identified and the three existing pathways critically examined for limitations in addressing bias, validation and equitable implementation. AML is proposed as the mechanism that closes this gap, connecting systems medicine, personalised medicine and precision medicine through continuous, outcome-based learning, identifying three original conceptual contributions as enablers: Integrative Data Governance (IDG), Adaptive Clinical Trial (ACT) designs and Evidence Sandbox Facilities (ESFs). Progress requires globally standardised Healthcare Data Recycling frameworks, adaptive evaluation methodologies and ESFs enabling multi-stakeholder validation. Future research should address federated AML validation, collective consent mechanisms and alignment of regulatory frameworks with international AI governance standards.

doi:10.1002/cam4.72386.abstract: TP53 mutations are linked to poor prognoses in B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL), indicating that specific p53 target genes may contribute to drug resistance. Although the impact of specific genetic alterations on drug sensitivity has been reported in BCP-ALL, the effects of TP53 mutations on sensitivity to individual agents remain poorly defined in the clinical setting because of the use of combination chemotherapy regimens. In the present study, we addressed this issue through two complementary analyses using a large panel of BCP-ALL cell lines. Initially, 30 cell lines harboring TP53 mutations demonstrated significantly greater resistance to daunorubicin (DNR), mafosfamide (MAF; an active analog of cyclophosphamide), 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), and prednisolone compared to 46 cell lines without mutations. Second, 11 CRISPR/Cas9-mediated TP53-knockout sublines derived from cell lines with wild-type TP53 recapitulated resistance to DNR, MAF, and 6-MP, as well as to vincristine (VCR) and cytarabine (Ara-C). Consistent with these findings, re-evaluation of genome-wide CRISPR screening datasets revealed significant enrichment of TP53 gRNAs in cells treated with DNR, MAF, 6-MP, Ara-C, and VCR. Furthermore, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of p53 target genes in the two cell line models, along with re-evaluation of genome-wide CRISPR screening datasets, identified BAX, BBC3, and FDXR as key p53 target genes associated with multidrug resistance. These results highlight the potential value of targeting these p53 downstream pathways to improve outcomes in TP53-mutated BCP-ALL cases.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70852.abstract: Thoracic radiotherapy can cause delayed cardiac fibrosis, but the immune mechanisms linking radiation injury to fibroblast activation remain unclear. We investigated whether CCR2+ monocytes contribute to radiation-induced cardiac fibrosis and whether AXL regulates their fibroblast-activating activity. C57BL/6 mice received 20 Gy whole-thorax irradiation, and remodelling was assessed from IR_D0 to IR_D60. Bulk RNA sequencing was integrated with single-cell datasets and CIBERSORTx deconvolution, lineage tracing, and tissue staining. CCR2+ monocyte function was examined by CCR2 neutralisation, and circulating CCR2+Ly6Cʰi monocytes were quantified by flow cytometry. AXL was investigated using inducible myeloid Axl deletion and bemcentinib (R428). MAPK signalling was assessed by transcriptomic analysis and immunoblotting of sorted CCR2+Ly6Cʰi monocytes. Conditioned medium from sorted monocytes after Axl deletion, AXL inhibition with R428, or MEK1/2 inhibition with U0126 was applied to cardiac fibroblasts. Cardiac fibrosis was established by IR_D30, while leukocyte infiltration and apoptotic signals remained above baseline. Transcriptomic analyses and lineage tracing showed increased cardiac accumulation of CCR2+ monocytes. CCR2 neutralisation reduced circulating CCR2+Ly6Cʰi monocytes and attenuated interstitial collagen deposition and fibrotic marker expression. Axl was enriched in the CCR2+ monocyte compartment. Myeloid Axl deletion and R428 reduced cardiac fibrosis. Axl deletion suppressed MAPK-related transcriptional programs, whereas genetic or pharmacological AXL targeting reduced MEK and ERK phosphorylation in sorted monocytes. Conditioned medium from IR_D30 monocytes induced COL1A1 and α-SMA expression in fibroblasts, and this effect was reduced by Axl deletion, R428, or U0126 treatment of donor monocytes. AXL signalling contributes to the fibroblast-activating paracrine activity of cardiac CCR2+ monocytes after irradiation, at least in part through MEK/ERK signalling. Radiation exposure induces cardiac fibrosis through immunestromal interactions. CCR2+ monocytes promote fibroblast activation during radiation-induced cardiac fibrosis. AXL regulates monocyte-mediated fibroblast activation through MEK/ERK signaling. Targeting the AXL-MEK/ERK pathway may provide a potential strategy for preventing radiation-induced cardiac fibrosis.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70854.abstract: Allergic rhinitis (AR) remains a global health challenge. However, the transcriptional and epigenetic features associated with seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR) and perennial allergic rhinitis (PAR) relative to non-allergic rhinitis (NAR) remain poorly characterised at single-cell resolution. We performed integrated single-cell transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of nasal mucosal tissues from 22 patients, including NAR (n = 8), SAR (n = 6), and PAR (n = 8), to characterise transcriptional and epigenetic patterns associated with immune cell heterogeneity. We identified eight major immune cell types and 29 immune cell subsets across the nasal mucosa. Comparisons with NAR revealed distinct transcriptional and epigenetic features in SAR and PAR across both myeloid and T-cell compartments. In Macro_CCL3 cells, SAR showed enrichment of inflammation-associated programs, whereas PAR showed greater enrichment of antigen-presentation-related features. CD4_Tcm cells exhibited subtype-associated epigenetic differences, with IL-1β/IL-17-related features enriched in SAR and eosinophil- and Th2-associated programs enriched in PAR. CD8_Trm cells in both AR groups showed cytotoxicity-related features, including increased accessibility near GZMB and PRF1, while distinct inferred regulatory patterns were observed across the two AR groups. In addition, T-cell co-expression modules identified by hdWGCNA showed distinct associations with NAR, SAR, and PAR. sLDSC analysis revealed significant enrichment of pollinosis-associated heritability in CD8 T-cell open chromatin regions. Our study characterises distinct immune regulatory features associated with SAR and PAR relative to NAR across innate and adaptive immune compartments, providing a multi-omic framework for characterising AR heterogeneity and identifying subtype-associated molecular features for further investigation.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70857.abstract: Mitochondrial transplantation is built on a simple idea: failing cells might be rescued by healthy mitochondria. The approach has entered early clinical testing, and encapsulation and cell-type targeting have improved uptake in selected systems. Better delivery, however, does not explain the therapy. Internalised donor mitochondria encounter an established network, quality-control machinery and sensors for mitochondrial material. Donor material may remain in the endolysosomal system or reach the cytosol. Cytosolic fates include network integration, clearance and a candidate functional contribution without fusion. Intracellular processing may also generate bioactive cargo. These fates imply different mechanisms and evidence requirements. This Review examines how recipient cells shape the contribution of internalised mitochondria, while recognising extracellular routes to benefit. We distinguish direct transplantation evidence from mechanistic support drawn from endogenous mitochondrial biology and natural intercellular transfer. The required donor fate and duration depend on the therapeutic task. Transient rescue may rely on short-term donor function or productive processing in specific models; sustained support may depend on continued donor function, recipient adaptation or redosing. Durable mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) correction requires donor-mtDNA retention and replication. Linking these tasks to product design, safety assessment and clinical endpoints shifts the question from how many mitochondria enter cells to what they accomplish after arrival. Recipient-cell handling shapes what transplanted mitochondria do after uptake. Uptake, structural integration and donor mitochondrial DNA retention require distinct evidence. Transient rescue, sustained support and durable mitochondrial DNA correction impose different requirements. Therapeutic goals should guide donor selection, product testing and clinical endpoints.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70863.abstract: Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 (TREM2) is a pivotal lipid-sensing receptor that governs the functional plasticity and metabolic fitness of mononuclear phagocytes, including microglia, osteoclasts, dendritic cells and tissue-resident macrophages. While originally identified as a genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD), TREM2 functions as a context-dependent immunometabolic checkpoint rather than a uniform phenotypic driver, exerting divergent biological outputs dictated by distinct tissue microenvironments and ligand repertoires. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of TREM2 immunobiology, detailing how ligand engagement-including cell-surface phospholipids and apolipoprotein E (ApoE)-activates the DAP12/DAP10-SYK-PI3K-mTOR signalling axis. This coordinated intracellular cascade instructively drives myeloid adaptation towards metabolically competent disease-associated microglia (DAM) and lipid-associated macrophage (LAM) states, sustaining bioenergetics and debris clearance under pathological stress. Across neurodegenerative proteinopathies and acute cerebral ischemia, TREM2 signalling is predominantly neuroprotective by promoting aggregate compaction and mitigating secondary excitotoxicity, although chronic dysregulated activation may drive stage-dependent neuroinflammation. In peripheral inflammatory pathologies such as rheumatoid arthritis and sepsis, TREM2 fine-tunes macrophage efferocytosis and systemic metabolic thresholds. In oncology, TREM2 displays a complex, microenvironment-dependent divergence: in central nervous system malignancies such as glioblastoma (GBM), TREM2 exerts controversial, stage-dependent effects, spanning microglial tumour containment in early stages versus pro-tumoural myelin recycling and immunosuppression by monocyte-derived macrophages in post-treatment recurrence; conversely, in peripheral solid tumours, monocyte-derived TREM2+ tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) predominantly orchestrate an immunosuppressive, nutrient-deprived niche that impairs cytotoxic T-cell function. Furthermore, we synthesise emerging paradigms along the bidirectional microbiome-gut-brain-tumour axis, elucidating how commensal and intra-tumoural microbial cues dynamically calibrate myeloid signalling tone and therapeutic susceptibility. We address translation bottlenecks-including blood-brain barrier (BBB) shuttles, human trial scarcity and soluble TREM2 (sTREM2) biomarker harmonisation-outlining a biomarker-guided, context-tailored precision therapeutic framework for targeting the TREM2 axis.

doi:10.1002/ctm2.70864.abstract: Pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA) remains one of potentially curative options for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). The operation can remove proximal thromboembolic materials and their secondary branches. However, the cellular landscape and pathological features across different anatomical regions remain limited understood. Ten patients with CTEPH undergoing PEA surgery and six reference distal pulmonary arteries were conducted single-cell transcriptomics to profile the cellular composition of the main and its bifurcate portion. Pronounced muscularised and fibrotic thrombi organisation were presented in the main portion, and the proportion of mononuclear phagocytes was significantly increased. Inflammatory response and pro-inflammatory activity were attributed to CD8+ effector T cells and nature killer cells subsets and a M1-like (high IL1B and TNF, minimal IL6) phenotypic macrophage subcluster. The colander-like lesions were dominant in the bifurcate portion, and the percentage of plasma cells was markedly increased. Immune dysregulation was induced from CD4 naïve T cells, and a downregulation of M2-like macrophage infiltration into the vascular wall. The expression of plasminogen activator, urokinase receptor, urokinase receptor (PLAUR; plasminogen activator) were observed in M2-like (high MRC1 and CD163, virtually no IL1B or TNF) macrophage in bifurcate portion. Notably, one of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) subclusters in the bifurcate portion gained more significantly myofibroblast markers than those in the main portion, and other subclusters remained the function of SMCs. The regions with colander-like lesions changes had more obviously T cell and macrophages driving immune-inflammatory response and SMCs differentiation, suggesting that combining therapeutic interventions after surgical removal of accessible thrombus may be beneficial. This study reveals the comprehensive cellular composition in main/lobar and bifurcate pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA) specimens at the single-cell level. The bifurcate regions with colander had more obviously T cell and macrophages driving immune-inflammatory response and smooth muscle cells (SMCs) differentiation, however, the remodelling of distal or micro-vessels still remained.

doi:10.1002/hon.3153.abstract: Abstract CD19‐targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T‐cells have revolutionized the treatment of lymphoid malignancies, including large B cell lymphoma (LBCL). Following seminal early phase multicenter clinical trials published between 2017 and 2020, three CD19‐CAR T‐cell products received FDA and EMA approval designations in lymphoma in the third‐line setting, paving the way for follow‐up studies in the second‐line. Meanwhile, investigations into the applications of CAR T‐cell therapy have further broadened to treating high‐risk patients even prior to completion of first‐line conventional chemo‐immunotherapy. Furthermore, as early trials excluded patients with central nervous system involvement with lymphoma, several studies have recently shown promising efficacy of CD19‐CAR T‐cells in primary and secondary CNS lymphoma. Here we provide a detailed overview on clinical data supporting the use of CAR T‐cells in patients with LBCL.

doi:10.1002/hon.70253.abstract: ABSTRACT In recent years the addition of the oral BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax to hypomethylating agents (HMAs) has emerged as the standard‐of‐care for patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) who are not fit for intensive chemotherapy, significantly improving survival and quality‐of‐life. Venetoclax is metabolized mainly by cytochrome P450 3A4 enzymes and serves as a P‐glycoprotein substrate, which make it largely affected by interactions with drugs. Dose reductions are needed to allow mold active antifungal prophylaxis, but there is no consensus on the exact venetoclax target dose concomitantly with posaconazole. We report on efficacy and safety of venetoclax combinations in 38 first‐line (FL) and 51 relapsed‐refractory (R/R) AML patients. Although complete remission (CR) rate was lower in R/R than in FL (49% vs. 68%; p = 0.08), achievement of this status was associated with comparable median overall survival (OS) in R/R and FL (13.67 vs. 13.72 months). Eighteen (20%) patients underwent allogenic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) with a 2‐year OS probability of 66.7%. Although antifungal prophylaxis was associated with a lower rate of grade 3–4 fungal infections (6% vs. 24%, p 0.044), patients treated with venetoclax daily dose of 50 mg with posaconazole had significantly shorter mOS in multivariate analysis (16.5 vs. 4.5 months; p 0.011). We conclude that AML patients in remission with venetoclax combinations may still be consolidated, and potentially cured, by HSCT, even after failure of intensive chemotherapy. Posaconazole prophylaxis effectively reduces risk of severe fungal infections, but a concomitant venetoclax dose of 50 mg may be sub‐optimal.

doi:10.1002/ijc.70774.abstract: While current colorectal cancer (CRC) screening guidelines consider family history to determine starting age for screening, they inadequately incorporate other important unmodifiable risk factors, including polygenic risk score (PRS) and biological sex. In 353,118 average-risk UK Biobank participants, we used family history-stratified Cox models to estimate associations of sex and PRS with CRC incidence, metastasis, and CRC-specific mortality. We translated risk differences into risk-adapted initiation screening ages using both risk advancement period (RAP) and absolute 10-year cumulative risk. Men had a higher risk of CRC compared to women, with HRs of 1.41 (95% CI, 1.33-1.50) for those without family history and 1.42 (95% CI, 1.26-1.61) for those with family history. For each one-standard deviation (SD) increase in PRS, the risk was 1.49 times higher (95% CI, 1.45-1.53) in participants without a family history and 1.42 times higher (95% CI, 1.34-1.51) in those with a family history. The increase in PRS was associated with elevated risks of both metastatic CRC at diagnosis and CRC-specific mortality, indicating delayed diagnosis in high-PRS individuals and highlighting the potential benefit of earlier screening. Consequently, risk-adapted initiation ages ranged from before 40 years for men with a family history in the high-PRS group to after 60 years for women without a family history in the low-PRS group. Our findings demonstrate that the integration of PRS, biological sex, and family history identifies substantial heterogeneity in CRC risk and risk-adapted screening initiation ages.

doi:10.1002/ijc.70779.abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, including esophageal (EC), gastric (GC), and colorectal cancer (CRC), impose a substantial global burden, with early detection remaining crucial for improving patient outcomes. The oral and gut microbiota are increasingly implicated in cancer development and hold promise as sources of non-invasive biomarkers. However, current evidence on microbiome-based diagnostics remains fragmented, and a systematic comparison of the diagnostic accuracy between oral and fecal sampling across multiple GI cancer types is lacking. To address this gap, a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus up to December 31, 2025, identified 43 case-control studies (59 cohorts) comprising 4452 cancer patients and 5809 controls. The pooled area under the curve (AUC) was 0.846 (95% CI: 0.824-0.867), though with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 86.5%). By cancer type, pooled AUCs were 0.746 for EC (5 cohorts), 0.886 for GC (8 cohorts), and 0.850 for CRC (46 cohorts). A bivariate analysis of 20 cohorts comparing sample types found no statistically significant difference in diagnostic performance between oral (sAUC = 0.863) and fecal sampling (sAUC = 0.820; p = 0.369). While these exploratory findings suggest that oral and fecal microbial biomarkers may offer comparable diagnostic accuracy for GI cancers, with oral sampling presenting a more practical option for screening, the results are preliminary. Significant heterogeneity, a limited number of oral cohorts, and the absence of clinical control groups highlight the need for large-scale prospective studies with direct comparisons and real-world validation to validate these biomarkers for clinical translation.

doi:10.1002/ijc.70781.abstract: Available epidemiological evidence shows that many cancers share familial risks, and this is increasingly confirmed by data on shared pathogenic germline gene variants between cancers. We decided to harness the world's largest resource on familial cancer to assess discordant familial risks for female breast (BC), prostate (PC), colorectal (CRC), and lung (LC) cancers with any of 22 different cancers in first-degree relatives (proband cancers). Familial relative risk was calculated as standardized incidence ratio (SIR) when either one proband or 2 or more (2+) probands were found in a family to distinguish low- and high-risk associations. Discordant familial associations of BC were significant for 12 1-proband and 5 2+ proband cancers. For PC, the numbers were 11 and 4; for CRC, they were 8 and 4; and for LC, they were 15 and 5. The results with large case numbers showed that BC, CRC, and LC associated with each other, but the familial association between PC and LC was negative. Many known or novel associations with possible genetic causes were found, including lobular BC with stomach cancer, PC with kidney cancer, CRC with squamous cell skin and thyroid cancers, and LC with gallbladder and endocrine tumors, the most common of which were parathyroid adenomas. Also, LC associations with esophageal and cervical cancers were unlikely to be due to smoking alone and require additional explanations. In conclusion, 2/3 of discordant associations could suggest low-risk genetic and environmental causation and 1/3 high-risk genetic causation, both waiting for experimental proof.

doi:10.1002/ijc.70785.abstract: Rising incidence of endometrial cancer among young women has increased the demand for fertility-sparing treatment (FST) in patients with endometrial atypical hyperplasia (EAH) and endometrioid endometrial cancer (EEC). However, approximately 20%-30% of patients exhibit progesterone resistance, and reliable predictive biomarkers remain inadequately defined. Therefore, we aimed to identify biomarkers associated with treatment response and prognosis in patients undergoing FST. In this retrospective study, we analyzed 161 patients undergoing mainly progestin-based FST, including 125 with EAH and 36 with G1 EEC. Molecular classification, pretreatment pathological morphology, hormone receptor expression, oncological outcomes, recurrence, and reproductive outcomes were evaluated. According to molecular classification, the cohort included POLEmut (n = 2), NSMP (n = 143), MMRd (n = 11), and p53abn (n = 5). Over a median treatment duration of 7 months, molecular classification significantly stratified complete response (CR) rates (p = 0.027), with distinct cumulative CR curves (p = 0.034). Patients with EEC showed lower CR rates than those with EAH (p < 0.001). Reduced CR was associated with extensive lesions, larger lesion diameter, proliferative endometrial background, papillary structure, and squamous metaplasia, whereas morular metaplasia and high estrogen receptor (ER)/progesterone receptor (PR) expression predicted higher CR rates. Multivariate analysis identified MMRd and squamous metaplasia as independent predictors of recurrence. Within the NSMP subgroup, pathological morphology and PR expression further refined risk stratification. Pregnancy outcomes were comparable across molecular subtypes. These findings suggested that integrating molecular classification with clinicopathological characteristics can improve prognostic assessment and support individualized management for patients undergoing FST.

doi:10.1002/ijc.70789.abstract: Neoadjuvant therapy has recently become an integral component of multimodal treatment for resectable lung cancer. However, real-world data on perioperative morbidity and treatment adherence remain limited. This study aimed to assess the feasibility and safety of different neoadjuvant treatment approaches applied within daily clinical routine. We retrospectively analyzed patients with resectable stage II-III non-small cell lung cancer undergoing either neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy or chemotherapy/chemoradiotherapy followed by curative surgical resection. Treatment groups were compared with respect to perioperative outcomes, radiologic and pathologic downstaging, and pathologic response. A total of 143 patients met the inclusion criteria, of whom 46 (32.2%) received chemoimmunotherapy and 97 (67.8%) were treated with chemotherapy prior to surgery. Adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation occurred in only two patients in the chemoimmunotherapy group and four patients in the chemotherapy group. Chemoimmunotherapy was associated with significantly higher rates of pathologic complete response (37.0% vs. 4.1%) and more pronounced nodal downstaging, with a higher proportion of patients achieving ypN0 status (76.1% vs. 34.0%). High tumoral PD-L1 expression (≥ 50%) and squamous cell carcinoma histology were independently associated with pathologic complete response. Real-world treatment with neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy was feasible and resulted in improved response rates compared with chemotherapy, without increasing perioperative morbidity. Histology and high PD-L1 expression may serve as predictors for complete pathologic response, although the predictive value of PD-L1 requires confirmation in larger cohorts with more complete biomarker data.

doi:10.1002/ijc.70790.abstract: Lynch syndrome, a prevalent hereditary cancer predisposition, is frequently caused by pathogenic variants in the MutL homolog 1 (MLH1) mismatch repair gene. However, a significant proportion of MLH1 missense variants remain classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS), creating clinical ambiguity. Functional validation assays in vertebrate models are crucial to assess the pathogenicity of these VUS. We previously reported the rare MLH1 NM_000249.4:c.335A>G (p.His112Arg) variant in individuals with cancer histories within the Qatar Genome Program. To assess its functional impact, we established the MLH1 p.His112Arg variant in the human colorectal cancer cell line, COLO205, using CRISPR-Cas9 technology. Isogenic wild-type (WT) and variant-carrying cells were xenotransplanted into the zebrafish. Tumor growth was quantified via fluorescence microscopy at 24 and 72 h post-injection. Zebrafish xenografted with MLH1 p.His112Arg cells exhibited a significant increase in tumor area compared to WT. This accelerated growth was associated with a significant upregulation of the proliferation marker MKI67 in variant-carrying tumors, while cyclin D1 (CCND1) and proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) (key regulators of cell cycle progression and DNA replication, respectively) expression remained unchanged, despite a tendency for increased expression. Furthermore, our functional characterization of the MLH1 p.His112Arg variant in COLO205 cells showed an enhanced proliferation capacity compared to the WT cell line, as well as increased cell viability and decreased apoptotic susceptibility when subjected to methylation-induced DNA damage. The MLH1 p.His112Arg variant confers a tumor-promoting phenotype in an in vivo zebrafish model, providing functional evidence that supports its reclassification from VUS to likely pathogenic.

doi:10.1002/jso.70391.abstract: The PRODIGE 24/CCTG PA.6- trial has shown an overall survival (OS) up to 55 months in patients treated with (modified) 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, irinotecan and oxaliplatin ((m)FOLFIRINOX) chemotherapy after resection of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). The applicability of these results to a real-world patient population is, however, unknown. This study aimed to assess the efficacy of (m)FOLFIRINOX compared to other adjuvant chemotherapy regimens in a real-world cohort. We performed a post-hoc analysis in a prospectively maintained cohort of patients undergoing PDAC resection in the Regional Academic Cancer Centre Utrecht, the Netherlands, from 2016 to 2020. Median OS was evaluated using Kaplan-Meier curves, primarily stratified by adjuvant chemotherapy regimen and secondarily by eligibility for the PRODIGE 24/CCTG PA.6- trial. Multivariable Cox regression was used to assess the association between chemotherapy regimen and OS, presented as hazard ratio's (HR) with 95% confidence interval (95%CI). A total of 161 patients with a median follow-up of 51 months (interquartile range (IQR) 43-61) were included. With (m)FOLFIRINOX (n = 30), OS was 29 months (IQR 22-42; [HR 0.26, 95%CI 0.14-0.47, p < 0.01]). Comparing (m)FOLFIRINOX with gemcitabine monotherapy yielded a HR of 0.62 (95%CI 0.33-1.17, p = 0.14), while (m)FOLFIRINOX versus gemcitabine combination therapy had a HR of 0.66 (95% CI 0.35-1.24 p = 0.20). Patients without adjuvant therapy (n = 71) had a median OS of 13 months (IQR 11-23, reference group). In patients receiving gemcitabine monotherapy (n = 31), median OS was 21 months (IQR 15-31; [HR 0.41 95%CI 0.25-0.69, p < 0.01]); for gemcitabine combination therapy (n = 29), OS was 28 months (IQR 23-43; [HR 0.39, 95%CI 0.23-0.66, p < 0.01]) In patients who received (m)FOLFIRINOX and who did or did not meet trial eligibility criteria, OS was 27 months (IQR 12-NR), compared to 30 months (IQR 21-NR) (p = 0.16), respectively. The survival benefit of (m)FOLFIRINOX observed in the clinical trial setting was not observed in our real-world cohort, not even in the selected subset of patients who would have deemed eligible for inclusion in the PRODIGE 24/CCTG PA.6- trial. Survival was not different for patients treated with (m)FOLFIRINOX and gemcitabine combination therapy.

doi:10.1002/jso.70419.abstract: Among patient with early-stage breast cancer, breast conservation surgery (BCS) is the most performed surgery, utilized in approximately two-thirds of patients. While 5-year overall-survival rates are strong-typically above 90%-additional re-excisions can occur in up to 25% of patients who undergo index BCS and some patients will require subsequent surgery for new breast cancer or recurrences. As such, these additional procedures can complicate patients' pathway to survivorship, negatively impact quality of life, and lead to excess healthcare costs. This retrospective cohort study used linked claims and an electronic healthcare record database to (1) characterize patients at higher risk for additional breast oncologic surgery (aBOS) following BCS, and (2) quantify the long-term financial impact of aBOS after BCS. In total, 87,190 patients with breast cancer, who had an index BCS between January 1, 2012, to March 31, 2023, were followed for up to 5-years post-operatively. Patients with and without aBOS were analyzed, comparing demographics, tumor characteristics, healthcare utilization, and per-person-per-month (PPPM) costs. Twenty-three percent (n = 20,212) of patients underwent aBOS. These patients were younger, had higher tumor grades and larger tumor sizes, and incurred greater healthcare costs compared to patients who did not undergo a secondary surgery. This study highlights significant factors influencing BCS outcomes and healthcare utilization, underscoring the need for tailored therapeutic strategies for patients with breast cancer.

doi:10.1002/jso.70422.abstract: Upper extremity soft tissue sarcomas (UE STS) present unique management challenges; existing prognostic nomograms were developed from mixed anatomic cohorts. This study develops anatomically specific machine learning (ML) models to predict UE-STS outcomes and benchmarks them against established tools. Time-to-event models for local recurrence (LR), distant metastasis (DM), and overall survival (OS) were developed in 188 patients treated at a single sarcoma center, treating death as a competing risk. Five survival algorithms were compared within a nested cross-validation framework. Discrimination was benchmarked against the Sarculator, PERSARC, and MSKCC nomograms. Five-year event rates were 24% (LR), 20% (DM), and 13% (death) over a median follow-up of 3.9 years. Best-performing models achieved competing-risks concordance indices of 0.79 (LR), 0.67 (DM), and 0.75 (OS). Parsimonious models performed comparably. Discrimination was similar to Sarculator and PERSARC and higher than the MSKCC nomogram for LR (C-index 0.90 vs. 0.68). Predicted-risk groups separated clearly on cumulative-incidence and survival curves (p < 0.001). These results demonstrate the feasibility and potential value of anatomy-specific, time-to-event risk modeling in UE STS, achieving discrimination comparable to established nomograms despite a smaller cohort. Multicenter cohorts and multidimensional data may strengthen future efforts. External validation is warranted.

doi:10.1002/jso.70423.abstract: Timely medical intervention is critical to achieve optimal outcomes in gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, yet numerous patients experience delayed or forgone (D/F) medical care. This study aimed to evaluate the national impact of D/F care on emergency surgical interventions and associated healthcare expenditures among patients with GI cancers. Adults with a self-reported history of GI cancer were identified from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, 2007-2017. Multivariable regression analyzes was performed to assess associations between D/F medical care, ED-associated GI surgery, inpatient utilization, and related healthcare expenditures after adjusting for demographic and socioeconomic variables. Among a weighted sample of 6 517 883 patients with GI cancers, 8.5% (n = 552 751) reported D/F medical care. Patients with D/F care were older (76 years [IQR: 69-82] vs. 68 years [IQR: 58-76]), more frequently male (57.3% vs. 50.6%) and frequently had family income below the poverty line (40.2% vs. 11.3%) (all p < 0.001). Furthermore, individuals reporting D/F care were more likely to have emergency department visits (44.2% vs. 27.4%), hospitalizations (64.6% vs. 34.5%) (both p < 0.05), or undergo ED-associated GI surgery (41.0% vs. 19.1%; p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, after adjusting for relevant factors, D/F care was associated with markedly greater odds of ED-associated GI surgery (OR 2.70, 95%CI 1.47-4.95) and higher annual inpatient healthcare costs (β +$31,410, 95% CI $23,592-$39,227) compared with individuals who did not report D/F care. Self-reported D/F medical care was associated with greater acute healthcare utilization, higher odds of ED-associated GI surgery, and greater healthcare expenditures. These findings highlight the importance of understanding barriers to healthcare access among adults with a history of GI cancer.

doi:10.1002/path.70127.abstract: Pretreatment prediction of neoadjuvant response remains an unresolved challenge in locally advanced rectal cancer, where management is moving towards risk-adapted and response-oriented treatment strategies. Prediction remains difficult because response reflects interacting tumour-intrinsic, immune, stromal, and spatial processes that are incompletely captured by standard clinical and radiological assessment. From a technology-centred perspective, in this Review we assess how molecular, spatial, image-based, and artificial intelligence-enabled approaches are being used to study and predict response to neoadjuvant treatment from pretreatment biopsies and how readily they may be translated into clinical workflows. Genomic profiling has its clearest current clinical role in identifying hypermutated immune-responsive subgroups, whereas broader genomic, epigenomic, and immune-repertoire markers remain largely investigational. Bulk transcriptomics has generated multiple response signatures with variable reproducibility but has consistently highlighted immune activation, interferon signalling, stromal remodelling, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition as recurrent response-associated programmes; its most feasible clinical route is likely through targeted expression panels rather than open-ended transcriptome profiling. Higher-resolution approaches such as spatial transcriptomic and proteomic platforms refine these observations by localising signals to tumour, immune, and stromal compartments and capturing therapy-induced tissue reorganisation, but they are currently best positioned for deepening biological understanding and nominating rational treatment combinations for future testing. Established platforms such as digital pathology are closer to routine deployment as they build on clinically embedded workflows, although response-prediction algorithms still require robust external validation, calibration, and regulatory-grade implementation. Patient-derived models provide functional systems for testing candidate biomarkers and resistance mechanisms. Multimodal artificial intelligence may support response prediction by identifying complementary signals across data types and distilling complex signatures into parsimonious models suitable for clinical translation. Progress will depend on harmonised, longitudinal, multi-centre studies that couple biological depth with assay standardisation, model reduction, and prospective evidence that response predictors improve patient management. © 2026 The Author(s). doi:10.1002/path.70136.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) with anaplastic features is a rare and highly aggressive subtype with an extremely poor prognosis. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying anaplastic transformation remain poorly understood. To characterize the anaplastic transformation molecular landscape, we analyzed genomic alterations in 5,997 conventional PDAC and 41 anaplastic carcinoma cases from the Memorial Sloan Kettering-Integrated Mutation Profiling of Actionable Cancer Targets (MSK-IMPACT) cohort. Additionally, four PDAC samples from the Kyorin cohort with both tubular and anaplastic components were subjected to spatial transcriptomics using the Visium platform. Differential gene expression and pathway enrichment analyses were performed to identify key molecular drivers. Genomic analysis revealed higher KRAS (90 versus 75%), TP53 (85 versus 60%), and CDKN2A (50 versus 30%) mutation frequencies, but notably fewer SMAD4 mutations (5 versus 20%; p = 0.022), in anaplastic carcinoma than in conventional PDAC. Spatial transcriptomics identified distinct molecular signatures, with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) pathways significantly enriched in anaplastic regions. Levels of ELF3, an epithelial transcription factor, were consistently downregulated in all anaplastic components. Importantly, we detected a strong inverse correlation between SMAD4 and ELF3 expression in both the bulk RNA sequencing cohort and spatial transcriptomic data. Functional validation using the KC-shSmad4 mouse model demonstrated that increased Smad4 suppressed Elf3 expression and promoted mesenchymal reprogramming. Our findings suggest a novel SMAD4-ELF3 regulatory axis that may contribute to anaplastic transformation in PDAC. The retention of SMAD4 functions coupled with ELF3 downregulation may promote EMT and contribute to tumor dedifferentiation. This SMAD4-ELF3 regulatory axis may provide a framework for identifying therapeutic vulnerabilities in this aggressive PDAC variant and further highlight the utility of spatial transcriptomics for understanding tumor heterogeneity. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

doi:10.1007/s00262-026-04585-8.abstract: Abstract Background Relapsed B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) after allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), particularly with extramedullary disease (EMD), has a dismal prognosis. The efficacy and durability of allogeneic chimeric antigen receptor T cell (allo-CAR-T) therapy in this setting remain unclear. Methods Fourteen patients with post-transplant relapsed B-ALL received allogeneic anti-CD19 CAR-T cells, including eight with EMD. Clinical responses, survival, CAR-T kinetics, and toxicities were evaluated. Results With a median follow-up of 13.8 months (range, 4.4–52.9 months), the overall complete remission (CR) rate was 92.9% (13/14), with a median duration of remission (DOR) of 12.7 months (range, 3.5–50.3 months). Among patients with EMD, 87.5% (7/8) achieved CR, with a median DOR of 14.7 months (range, 3.5–50.3 months). Of the eight patients with EMD, four were Philadelphia chromosome-positive and received maintenance therapy with tyrosine kinase inhibitors after allo-CAR-T, including dasatinib ( n =1), ponatinib ( n =2), and olverembatinib ( n =1). Median overall survival and event-free survival were not reached in either the overall cohort or EMD subgroup. CAR-T cells persisted in vivo for a median of 5.9 months (range, 1.2–51.6 months). One patient experienced grade 3 cytokine release syndrome and grade 4 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome. One patient developed acute gastrointestinal graft-versus-host disease, followed by chronic graft-versus-host disease involving the skin and lungs. Conclusion Allo-CAR-T therapy induces sustained remissions in patients with post-transplant relapsed B-ALL, including patients with EMD, and may serve as an effective backbone for tailored combination strategies.
