doi:10.1007/s00262-026-04592-9.abstract: Abstract High-dose vitamin C (HDVC) exhibits antitumor and immunomodulatory properties and may enhance the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs); however, its ability to reprogram the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) in pancreatic cancer, particularly through modulating tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) polarization, remains unclear. In this study, the antitumor activity of HDVC was evaluated in a subcutaneous KPC mouse model, while in vitro models utilizing lipopolysaccharide (LPS) + IFN-γ-stimulated mouse and human macrophages were employed to investigate polarization. Mechanisms were probed by RNA sequencing, western blotting, flow cytometry, pharmacological inhibition, and siRNA-mediated JAK2 knockdown. Macrophage involvement was confirmed in vivo via clodronate liposome-mediated depletion, and the combinatory effect of HDVC with anti-PD-1 therapy was assessed. The results showed that HDVC significantly inhibited pancreatic tumor growth and prolonged survival in vivo. Mechanistically, HDVC enhanced LPS + IFN-γ-induced M1 macrophage polarization, at least in part through activation of the JAK2-STAT1 signaling pathway, without markedly increasing M2-associated features. The antitumor efficacy of HDVC was markedly attenuated upon macrophage depletion, supporting the involvement of macrophage-dependent immune modulation. Furthermore, HDVC enhanced the efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy, accompanied by increased M1-like macrophages and CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration in the TME. These findings identify HDVC as a potential immunomodulator that remodels the immunosuppressive TME of pancreatic cancer through macrophage-centered immune remodeling, providing a rationale for further investigating HDVC-based combination strategies with ICIs in pancreatic cancer.

doi:10.1007/s00262-026-04594-7.abstract: Abstract Despite growing enthusiasm for immunotherapy in cancer treatment, only a few colorectal cancer (CRC) patients experience lasting therapeutic effect. This limited efficacy is likely driven by different tumor-intrinsic resistance mechanisms, including loss or downregulation of HLA-I molecules, which may impair antigen presentation and cytotoxic T cell recognition. Interestingly, the downregulation of HLA-I can augment tumor susceptibility to natural killer (NK) cell attack. However, NK cell activity may be inhibited by immunosuppressive signals within the tumor microenvironment. This study describes two patients with metastatic CRC and microsatellite instability who showed durable responses to pembrolizumab despite unfavorable prognostic factors (tumor recurrence, BRAF V600E mutation and markedly reduced HLA-I on tumor cells). Tumor samples obtained at surgical resection also revealed PD-L1 expression on tumor cells and a substantial fraction of tumor-infiltrating PD-1 + NK cells. These findings raise the hypothesis that PD-1/PD-L1 blockade may have contributed to NK-cell-mediated antitumor activity in the context of markedly reduced HLA-I expression. Furthermore, assessing PD-L1 and HLA-I expression on tumor cells at diagnosis could help identify patients who could benefit most from pembrolizumab treatment, alone or combined with inhibitors of HLA-I-specific inhibitory NK receptors. These observations provide a rationale for further investigation in larger and multicenter patient cohorts.

doi:10.1007/s00262-026-04595-6.abstract: Abstract Effective therapies remain limited for neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)- and schwannomatosis (SWN)-related nerve sheath tumors, particularly for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNSTs). Although tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy induces durable responses in multiple solid tumors, its feasibility and optimized manufacturing workflows have not been established for these hereditary neoplasms. Herein, we evaluated T cell infiltration in 109 clinical specimens and detected moderate-to-high CD3⁺ T cell infiltration in most neurofibromas (84.0%), schwannomas (98.3%), and MPNSTs (75.0%), supporting the biological prerequisite for TIL intervention in this disease. We established OM-400, a pre-rapid expansion (pre-REP) protocol utilizing CD3/CD28-bead co-stimulation plus low-dose IL-2 (400 IU/mL) for NF1/SWN-related nerve sheath tumor-derived TILs. Compared with the traditional high-dose-IL-2 method, OM-400 achieved 100% expansion success, shortened culture duration, enriched CD8⁺ effector T cells, showed preliminary evidence of better preservation of original TCR repertoires based on analysis of one representative specimen, and enhanced autologous tumor-reactive cytotoxicity and IFN-γ secretion. Exploratory subgroup analysis across 15 independent patient samples covering NF1, SWN, and NF1-related MPNST revealed no statistically significant differences in TIL performance among subtypes. However, the study was not powered to establish equivalence, and larger cohorts are needed to definitively assess the impact of tumor subtype. Using autologous MPNST patient-derived xenograft models, we confirmed that OM-400-expanded TILs infiltrated tumor tissue and significantly suppressed in vivo tumor growth. In summary, this work provides first preclinical proof of concept for TIL-based immunotherapy against NF1/SWN-related nerve sheath tumors and establishes a reproducible manufacturing platform to facilitate future clinical translation.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05774-2.abstract: Outcome prediction in neuro-oncology remains challenging due to heterogeneity in tumor biology, imaging characteristics, treatment response, and patient-specific clinical factors. Although molecular databases have advanced understanding of brain tumor biology, many datasets lack broader data necessary for generalizable predictive modeling. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly being explored to integrate these heterogeneous data sources and support precision neuro-oncology. A narrative review was performed using PubMed and Embase to identify studies evaluating oncology databases, ML models, multimodal data integration, and AI applications relevant to neuro-oncology. Studies published between 2020 and 2026 were preferentially reviewed, with additional landmark studies included when relevant. Traditional ML approaches including regression-based models, random forests, support vector machines, and gradient boosting algorithms have been applied to survival prediction, recurrence classification, treatment response estimation, and molecular biomarker prediction using clinical, imaging, molecular, and population-level datasets. More advanced architectures including natural language processing, large language models, vision transformers, geometric deep learning, and graph neural networks have expanded the ability to analyze unstructured and multimodal data sources including radiology reports, histopathology slides, MRI volumes, molecular datasets, and electronic health records. Multimodal AI systems integrating imaging, molecular, histopathologic, clinical, and socioeconomic data frequently demonstrated improved predictive performance compared with single-modality models. However, widespread clinical implementation remains limited by dataset heterogeneity, limited external validation, interpretability concerns, and inconsistent representation across patient populations. AI and ML approaches are increasingly capable of integrating complex neuro-oncology datasets in ways that more closely reflect real-world clinical decision-making. Although most current models remain investigational, multimodal AI frameworks may ultimately improve prognostic assessment, treatment stratification, and precision neuro-oncology care. Continued progress will require larger representative datasets, improved data harmonization, external validation, and clinically interpretable models.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05821-y.abstract: MGMT promoter methylation (MGMTpm) is a well-established molecular biomarker in neuro-oncology. We review current practices, challenges, and future directions for MGMTpm as a biomarker in central nervous system (CNS) tumors. The literature on MGMT function, and MGMTpm clinical significance and testing in CNS tumors was reviewed. We discuss the biological role of MGMT in DNA repair and the mechanisms by which MGMTpm leads to increased tumor sensitivity to alkylating agents. We summarize the clinical significance of MGMTpm in glioblastoma and its emerging relevance in other CNS tumors. Testing practices using methylation-specific PCR, pyrosequencing, and genome-wide methylation array-based approaches are discussed, along with challenges related to testing variability and "gray-zone" methylation, and emerging technologies such as nanopore sequencing. Despite ongoing technical and interpretative challenges, MGMTpm remains a robust and clinically valuable biomarker in neuro-oncology.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05822-x.abstract: To characterize the weekly trajectory of hippocampal diffusion during fractionated partial-brain radiation therapy (RT) for high-grade glioma and determine whether the magnitude of change is associated with planned hippocampal dose. Forty-five adults enrolled in a prospective observational imaging study and treated with 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concurrent temozolomide underwent diffusion MRI before RT and weekly during treatment. Relative bilateral hippocampal apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) change and fractional anisotropy (FA) were evaluated longitudinally. Linear mixed-effects models included treatment week and planned mean bilateral hippocampal dose as fixed main effects. A secondary laterally-specific analysis evaluated baseline-to-Week-6 ADC change separately in the hippocampi ipsilateral and contralateral to the tumor. Hippocampal ADC increased progressively from a median relative change of 0.5% at Week 1 to 12% (IQR, 6%-18%) at Week 6. The ADC time coefficient was + 2.2% points per week (95% CI, 1.8-2.5; P < 0.001). After accounting for week, higher planned mean bilateral hippocampal dose was associated with greater ADC change (+ 0.81% points/Gy; 95% CI, 0.76-0.93; P < 0.001). In the secondary laterally-specific analysis, higher dose was associated with greater Week-6 ADC change in both the ipsilateral hippocampus (β = 0.83% points/Gy; 95% CI, 0.52-1.26; P = 0.013) and the contralateral hippocampus (β = 0.36% points/Gy; 95% CI, 0.05-0.712; P = 0.046). FA remained stable through Week 3 and declined during Weeks 4-6. Weekly diffusion MRI demonstrates a progressive, dose-associated hippocampal response during fractionated RT. The laterality-specific findings further support an association between local radiation exposure and ADC change and support hippocampal ADC as a candidate treatment-phase imaging phenotype for prospective validation.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05828-5.abstract: Despite significant advances in glioma surgery, early postoperative neuroimaging frequently reveals signs of surgical brain injury (SBI). This prospective observational study aimed to investigate the incidence, radiological characteristics, neurological outcomes and risk factors of SBI following glioma resection. Patients with newly diagnosed supratentorial gliomas who undergo tumor resection were prospectively enrolled. Serial MRI examinations were administrated early postoperative (≤ 72 h) and on postoperative days 7, 14 and 28 to assess the characteristics of infarction, edema and microhemorrhage. Neurological outcomes were evaluated using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at postoperative day 28. A total of 64 patients was included. Postoperative infarction was identified in 14 patients (21.9%), with all anatomically localized to the basal ganglia, thalamus, or insular regions. Intraoperative blood loss ≥ 300 mL was independently associated with postoperative infarction (Odd Ratio [OR]: 4.62, p = 0.035). Microhemorrhage was observed in 53.8% of patients. Peritumoral edema occurred in all cases and exhibited two distinct patterns: residual tumor-associated edema (n = 42) and de novo surgery-induced edema (n = 22). The average volume of tumor-associated edema decreased, whereas that of surgery-induced edema increased over time. Among the 53 patients who completed neurological outcome assessments, 13 developed disability (mRS ≥ 2). Risk factors were higher intraoperative blood loss (OR: 8.88, p = 0.013) and postoperative infarction (OR: 6.33, p = 0.031). SBI, including infarction and edema, is common following glioma surgery and associated with adverse neurological outcomes. Meticulous intraoperative hemostatic management is essential to prevent postoperative infarction and even disability outcome.

doi:10.1007/s11060-026-05830-x.abstract: Routine blood counts may capture treatment-related host immune perturbation in glioblastoma, but most studies rely on static pretreatment values. We investigated whether the intra-individual preservation of circulating monocytes during chemoradiotherapy provides prognostic information beyond established clinical factors and other hematologic trajectories. We retrospectively analyzed adults with histologically confirmed IDH-wildtype glioblastoma treated with radiotherapy and concurrent temozolomide. Absolute monocyte counts obtained before and at the end of chemoradiotherapy were used to define monocytic resilience as log2(post-treatment/pre-treatment monocyte ratio). Overall survival (OS) was the primary endpoint. Cox models adjusted for MGMT promoter methylation, gross total resection, Karnofsky Performance Status, and age. The ratio was analyzed continuously for primary inference. A post/pre ratio of 0.75 was additionally evaluated as an exploratory, clinically interpretable threshold for two-group Kaplan-Meier visualization and sensitivity analysis. Among 127 patients, 115 had complete monocyte trajectories and OS data. The primary adjusted model included 102 patients and 86 deaths. The continuous monocyte post/pre ratio was independently associated with OS (HR 0.53 per doubling, 95% CI 0.37-0.76; p = 0.00051). Using the exploratory 0.75 threshold, 52 patients had low resilience (< 0.75) and 63 had preserved resilience (≥ 0.75), with median OS of 10.2 and 17.3 months, respectively (log-rank p = 0.00064). Preserved resilience was associated with lower mortality in univariable Cox analysis (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.34-0.75; p = 0.00080). Bootstrap resampling showed that outcome-optimized cut-points clustered around this region (median 0.74; IQR 0.70-0.81), although the threshold remains exploratory and requires external validation. Preservation or recovery of circulating monocytes during chemoradiotherapy was associated with a favorable host-response phenotype in IDH-wildtype glioblastoma. This dynamic signal remained associated with survival after adjustment for established clinical factors, baseline monocyte burden, lymphocyte change, systemic inflammatory imbalance, and measured corticosteroid exposure. External prospective validation, medication-level confounder assessment, and immune phenotyping are required before clinical use.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103250.abstract: Cancer incidence is rising among young adults in several high-income countries, yet comprehensive data from Southern Europe, particularly Portugal, remain limited. We characterized temporal trends in cancer incidence among young adults (20-49 years) in Portugal between 2001 and 2022, comparing them with older adults (≥50 years). This nationwide population-based cohort study included 1,102,774 incident cancer cases recorded by the Portuguese National Cancer Registry. Age-standardized incidence rates (ASIR) per 100,000 inhabitants were calculated using the European Standard Population. Temporal trends were analysed using joinpoint regression, estimating annual percentage changes (APC) and average annual percentage changes (AAPC) by sex, age group, and cancer type. Cancer cases increased from 36,604 in 2001 to 60,926 in 2022. Young adults accounted for 13.0% of all cases. Among young women, ASIR increased by 31.6% (from 156.2 to 205.6; AAPC: +1.48%), driven largely by breast cancer (+50.0%), thyroid (+94.1%), melanoma (+84.1%), and lung cancer (+78.7%). In contrast, young men showed stable overall ASIR (AAPC: -0.05%), with a biphasic pattern of increase (2001-2010) followed by decline (2010-2022). However, young men experienced substantial rises in colorectal (+56.6%), thyroid (+185.1%), and melanoma (+70.1%) incidence, alongside declines in stomach (-67.0%), oesophageal (-56.8%), and lung (-45.8%) cancers. Older adults demonstrated significant ASIR increases driven by trends before 2011, with subsequent stabilization or decline. Cancer incidence among young Portuguese adults is increasing, particularly among women, with sex-specific and site-specific patterns. While declines in tobacco-related cancers reflect successful prevention efforts, rising rates of breast, colorectal, thyroid, and melanoma in young adults signal the need for enhanced targeted prevention strategies and continued etiological research.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103251.abstract: The five-year relative survival (RS) for cervical cancer in Puerto Rico and the United States (US) is less than 70%. To assess survival trends in the past decades, we compared the five-year RS of cervical cancer in Puerto Rico and in the US. Data was obtained from the Puerto Rico Central Cancer Registry and the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results Program. We included microscopically confirmed cases of cervical carcinoma between 2000 and 2021. The five-year RS trends were analyzed with Joinpoint regression models using the JPSurv software, which estimated the Average Absolute Change in Survival (AAC_S). Puerto Rico showed a lower five-year RS than US overall across the study period. In the US, the AAC_S was -0.78 for patients diagnosed between 2000 and 2003 (95%CI: -1.32 to -0.23), -0.22 for 2003-2013 (95%CI: -0.36 to -0.08), and 0.25 for 2013-2021 (95%CI: 0.01-0.49). In Puerto Rico, the AAC_S was -0.03 for 2000-2011 (95%CI: -0.56-0.51), 1.71 for 2011-2016 (95%CI: 0.60-2.83), and -1.10 for 2016-2021 (95%CI: -3.12-0.92). Puerto Rico shows poorer cervical cancer five-year RS than the US. Increased five-year RS was observed in the US overall population after 2013. In Puerto Rico, improvements in five-year RS were observed after 2011, but these were halted after 2016. This finding may suggest that barriers to accessing care during periods of extreme events, such as the convergence of the 2017 hurricanes and the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic challenges, likely affected survival trends from 2016 to 2021. Future research should further characterize barriers to improve cervical cancer survival.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103252.abstract: The burden of second primary cancers (SPCs) is rising, partly because patients with a first cancer now survive longer. Two metrics coexist to quantify SPC risk: cumulative incidence, whose dependence on survival is well recognised, and the standardized incidence ratio (SIR), widely treated as survival-robust because it accounts for person-years at risk. Calendar-era SIR trends are increasingly reported and interpreted as real changes in risk, yet whether such trends could instead arise artefactually from concurrent gains in index-cancer survival has never been tested. We combined a calibrated simulation with an empirical analysis of SEER 17 (2000-2023). The simulation generated cohorts with strictly constant, stage-specific SPC risk, allowing only index-cancer 12-month survival to vary according to SEER-measured values, and applied a 12-month latency exclusion reproducing the SEER*Stat multiple-primary SIR procedure. Empirically, across 27 site × stage strata spanning wide survival-gain gradients, we related the observed 12-month survival gain (2004-09 vs 2015-18) to the calendar-year slope of the SPC SIR (Poisson regression), with six sensitivity analyses and a power calculation. At constant stage-specific risk, the simulated SIR drifted with survival, but across 200 Monte-Carlo replications the median bias-attributable slope was more than an order of magnitude smaller than the observed SIR slope (0.28 vs 7.9 × 10⁻³ per year), despite per-stage SIRs differing enough for the mechanism to act. Empirically, survival gain and SIR slope were unrelated (Pearson r = -0.00, p = 0.99), robust across all sensitivity analyses; power was adequate to detect r ≥ 0.50. Survivor-recomposition bias in the SPC SIR exists in principle but was small on average in the sites and calendar period studied. Unlike cumulative incidence, the SIR can generally be interpreted across calendar eras without major survival correction, although weak, site-specific, or longer-term effects cannot be excluded.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103253.abstract: Breast cancer treatment, commonly involving chemo- and/or radiotherapy, is associated with adverse cardiac effects, including cardiac dysfunction. While most research focuses on adverse effects during treatment, breast cancer survivors may also be at risk of developing cardiac dysfunction ≥ 5 years post-treatment. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of cardiac dysfunction in long-term female breast cancer survivors. CINAHL, Embase, and MEDLINE were systematically searched for articles that included breast cancer survivors treated with chemo- and/or radiotherapy and measured left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) ≥ 5 years post-diagnosis. The pooled prevalence of cardiac dysfunction, defined as LVEF ≤ 54% or a decline in LVEF of > 10% compared to baseline, was calculated and presented in a forest plot. Subgroup analyses based on treatment modality were performed, along with additional explorative forest plots to explore heterogeneity. Twenty-three studies encompassing 7309 patients were included with a median follow-up time since diagnosis of 5-30 years; Four studies included patients all treated with radiotherapy, of which two studies with radiotherapy as monotherapy and twenty studies included patients all treated with chemotherapy in combination with other therapies. Prevalence of cardiac dysfunction varied from 0% to 30%,. The pooled prevalence was estimated to be 10.8%, with significant heterogeneity (I² = 92.4%). Visual exploration of stratified analysis did not indicate explanations for this heterogeneity. Prevalence of cardiac dysfunction appears to be higher among long-term breast cancer survivors compared to the general population. Long-term breast cancer survivors remain at risk of cardiac dysfunction years after treatment, supporting the integration of cardiovascular risk assessment into survivorship care.

doi:10.1016/j.canep.2026.103254.abstract: Experimental studies suggest that thyroid hormones may influence tumor development through endocrine and cellular signaling pathways. Although malignant melanoma (MM) is primarily associated with ultraviolet radiation exposure, the potential role of thyroid dysfunction in melanoma development remains unclear. We investigated the association between hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism and the rate of MM in a nationwide cohort of Danish women. Our cohort comprised 1,058,939 women born between January 1, 1960, and December 31, 1997, and was followed from 1996 to 2022. Information on thyroid disease, MM diagnoses, covariates and follow-up was obtained from Danish nationwide registries. Cox proportional hazards models with attained age as the underlying scale were used to estimate Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Analyses were stratified by time since diagnosis, menopausal status and histological subtype. Hyperthyroidism was not associated with the rate of overall MM (HR: 0.94; 95% CI: 0.79-1.12). For hypothyroidism, the HR for overall MM was 0.89 (95% CI: 0.77-1.02). Estimates for superficial spreading MM were similar. Among women diagnosed with hypothyroidism within the past 10 years, the HR for superficial spreading MM was 0.80 (95% CI: 0.66-0.98). Stratification by menopausal status did not materially alter the associations. Our findings do not provide clear evidence of an association between thyroid dysfunction and the rate of MM in women. The observed decreased rate of superficial spreading MM among women with hypothyroidism within 10 years of diagnosis should be interpreted cautiously, as it was the only statistically significant finding among multiple subgroup analyses and may represent a chance finding. Further studies incorporating detailed clinical and biochemical measures of thyroid function are warranted.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218859.abstract: Metal ions serve as key regulators of the dynamic equilibrium within the tumor microenvironment (TME). In recent years, the TME has emerged as a central regulatory hub for tumor initiation, progression, and metastasis; its complexity has become both a frontier and a major challenge in oncology research. Current therapies are often constrained by immune tolerance, metabolic heterogeneity, and microenvironment-mediated escape mechanisms, necessitating breakthroughs in novel targets and strategies. Metal ions, functioning as enzyme cofactors, signaling molecules, and redox regulators, profoundly affect tumor progression by modulating redox homeostasis, immune responses, and metabolic reprogramming. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in metal ion-mediated regulation of the TME. It focuses on elucidating the multidimensional mechanisms by which metal ions facilitate immunogenic remodeling and metabolic interactions, and prospectively explores innovative metal-ion-based diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. It further highlights the potential of personalized metal metabolomics to advance precision oncology and facilitate the clinical translation of metal ion-based theranostic strategies.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218861.abstract: Tumor drug resistance is still the core obstacle limiting the long-term benefit of modern anticancer therapy, especially in the context of treatment tolerance, persistence of minimal residual disease (MRD) and recurrence after treatment. Increasing evidence has shown that therapy-associated myeloid niches can involve cell recruitment, enrichment of pre-existing populations, or state reprogramming, together with local relationships among myeloid cells, tumor cells, stroma, vessels, and other immune cells. These niches can support residual tumor-cell survival, immune escape, local regrowth, and distant dissemination through overlapping mechanisms linking fibrotic exclusion and perivascular organization with hypoxic metabolic suppression and myeloid replenishment. The formation of neutrophil extracellular traps, failure of antigen uptake and presentation, impaired T-cell priming, and phagocytic escape can further sustain treatment tolerance. Focusing on the myeloid cell state and common molecular circuits, this article presents an evidence assessment framework that interprets spatial and clinical associations alongside functional and pharmacologic findings without assigning hierarchical ranks. It summarizes lessons from clinical failure, considering potentially limited target contributions, compensatory pathways, inadequate exposure, and toxicity, while distinguishing drug exposure and local pharmacodynamic changes from clinical benefit. Candidate biomarkers, intervention windows, and selective delivery approaches require validation to guide mechanism-matched combinations. In the future, longitudinal tissue analyses, functional validation, and prospective studies should test whether these combinations provide durable benefit with acceptable safety in defined patient populations and treatment settings.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218879.abstract: Prolonged colonic inflammation and ulcerative colitis lead to colon cancer. The rapid growth and treatment-resistant nature of these tumors are primarily influenced by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which is led by tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). However, factors influencing or regulating the immunosuppressive nature of TAMs have not been sufficiently studied. In this manuscript, we use a mouse model of colitis-associated colorectal cancer (CRC) to demonstrate that WNT expression in TAMs regulates their immunosuppressive function by inhibiting Glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3β) within the macrophages, possibly through an autofeedback loop. GSK3β is a positive regulator of PD-1 and PD-L1 expression in macrophages and promotes an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Therefore, GSK-3β inhibition alters the immunosuppressive nature of the immune microenvironment and effectively controls tumor growth. In Csf1r.iCre; Porcnfl/fl mice, the absence of macrophage-derived WNT promotes tumor growth in the model of colitis-associated colon cancer. Absence of macrophage-derived WNT stabilizes GSK-3β in macrophages and promotes an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. We also show that pharmacological inhibition of GSK-3β in a macrophage-specific manner, achieved by systemic delivery of a lipo-GSK3β inhibitor, effectively inhibits tumor growth. Therefore, this manuscript demonstrates for the first time that the macrophage-specific modulation of GSK3β can be a potential target to treat colitis-associated colon cancer.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218884.abstract: Immunotherapy has improved outcomes for patients with breast cancer, yet therapeutic resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Therefore, we integrated single-cell and spatial transcriptomic data from breast cancer cohorts treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors to identify resistance-associated cellular populations and pathways, with validation across eight independent bulk RNA-seq immunotherapy cohorts. Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) were isolated from anti-PD-1-resistant breast tumors for functional studies, including in vitro co-culture and in vivo models. Mitochondrial function and metabolic alterations were assessed by flow cytometry, transmission electron microscopy, ATP and adenosine quantification, and JC-1 staining. Tumor mitochondrial metabolism was markedly upregulated in anti-PD-1 non-responders and consistently associated with poor therapeutic response across validation cohorts. MDK-expressing CAFs were enriched in resistant tumors, exhibited strong interactions with tumor cells, and were negatively associated with intratumoral CD8+ T cell infiltration. Single-cell source contribution and depletion analyses identified CAF-derived MDK as the major paracrine mediator linking stromal signaling to tumor metabolic adaptation and immune suppression. Mechanistically, MDK activated SDC1-dependent PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling in cancer cells, promoting mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming, ATP production, and CD38/CD73-dependent extracellular adenosine accumulation, thereby suppressing CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity. Receptor-depletion experiments further identified SDC1 as the principal functional receptor mediating these effects. Importantly, CAF-specific MDK depletion or pharmacological MDK inhibition enhanced anti-PD-1 efficacy and restored CD8+ T cell effector activity in vivo. Collectively, MDK+ CAFs facilitate anti-PD-1 resistance via mitochondrial rewiring and adenosine-mediated immunosuppression, supporting the MDK-SDC1 axis as a potential therapeutic target for overcoming resistance and improving immunotherapy efficacy in breast cancer.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218889.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is driven by cancer stemness and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, which collectively contribute to therapeutic resistance. While the RNA-binding protein HNRNPC has been implicated in tumor progression, it has primarily been characterized as a downstream effector, and its autonomous regulatory functions, particularly in governing cancer stemness, remain entirely unexplored. Through multi-omics analyses of HCC cohorts, we identified HNRNPC as a pivotal driver of a high-risk molecular subtype. Mechanistically, HNRNPC expression was transcriptionally activated via WDR5/KMT2A complex-mediated deposition of H3K4me3 at its promoter. Functionally, HNRNPC was essential for maintaining cancer stemness, promoting tumor growth and metastasis, and conferring oxaliplatin resistance. Notably, depletion of HNRNPC reprogrammed the immunosuppressive microenvironment by enhancing CD8+ T cell infiltration, reducing T cell exhaustion, and polarizing macrophages toward an M1-like anti-tumor phenotype. At the molecular level, HNRNPC bound to the m6A-modified 3'UTR of CD24 mRNA in an RNP2 motif-dependent manner, thereby enhancing its stability and elevating CD24 protein expression. Therapeutically, we developed a novel lipid nanoparticle (LNP) encapsulating siRNA against HNRNPC. Systemically administered AP-EG-si potently suppressed tumor growth, attenuated stemness, and synergized with anti-PD-L1 therapy to enhance anti-tumor immunity. Our findings thus unveil the H3K4me3-HNRNPC-CD24 axis as a central epigenetic and post-transcriptional regulatory pathway that coordinately drives HCC stemness and immune evasion, nominating HNRNPC-targeted nanotherapy as a promising strategy for advanced HCC.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218890.abstract: Rising incidence of colorectal cancer (CRC) and limited therapeutic options highlight the urgent need to define the drivers of its progression. The SPP1+ tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) subset identified by single-cell transcriptomics is a functionally dominant population that extends beyond the classical M1/M2 paradigm. Here, we dissected the molecular mechanisms by which SPP1+ TAMs reprogram tumor progression and determined whether the gut microbiota regulates this process in colorectal cancer. Using a multi-platform strategy integrating clinical specimens, murine models and CRC cell lines, we found that SPP1+ TAMs increase progressively during CRC evolution and exhibit crosstalk with malignant epithelial cells, and their abundance is associated with adverse clinical outcome. Integrative analysis reveals a significant positive correlation between SPP1 and ARG2 expression. Further, TAM-derived SPP1 engages CD44 on CRC cells to induce ARG2 expression. Mechanistically, ARG2 facilitates the interaction between USP10 and c-Myc to deubiquitinate and stabilize c-Myc, which transactivates the glycolytic enzyme HK2, driving Warburg metabolism that fuels CRC cell proliferation. Moreover, ARG2 secreted by CRC cells is internalized by TAMs, which reciprocally upregulates SPP1, creating a feed-forward loop that drives a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment. Notably, Bifidobacterium longum downregulates CD44 expression on tumor cells, thereby disrupting the SPP1-ARG2 axis and attenuating CRC progression. These findings identify the SPP1-ARG2 circuit as a therapeutic target and propose B. longum as a microbiome-derived precision adjuvant therapy for CRC suppression.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218891.abstract: Although neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NICT) has improved survival in locally advanced gastric cancer (GC) and gastroesophageal junction cancer (GEJC), lymph node metastasis (LNM) patterns following NICT remain undefined. We aimed to characterize topographical LNM patterns after NICT and evaluate the association between lymphadenectomy extent, surgical approach, and survival outcomes. Data were pooled from 4 prospective clinical trials (NEOSUMMIT-01 - 04), comprising 126 patients with GC (n = 61) or GEJC (n = 65) undergoing curative gastrectomy following NICT. ypN0 was achieved in 71 patients (56%). In GEJC, station No. 3, 7 were high risk; No. 1, 2, 9, and 11 were intermediate risk; and No. 4, 5, 6, 8, 12 were low risk. In GC, station No. 12 was low-risk; D1 stations (No. 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) were high-risk, D1+ stations (No. 8, 9) and No. 11 were intermediate-risk. At a median follow-up of 36.2 months, 24-month EFS and OS rates were 76.4% and 90.5%. Nodal yield (≥ 30 vs. < 30) was not significantly associated with EFS (P = .611) or OS (P = .911). In exploratory comparisons within the GEJC cohort, EFS (P = .219) and OS (P = .290) did not differ significantly between proximal and total gastrectomy. In GEJC, distal perigastric lymph node stations (No. 4, 5, 6, and 12) exhibited low metastasis rates, while exploratory survival outcomes support prospective clinical trials of proximal gastrectomy in appropriately selected patients. Conversely, the broader residual nodal involvement in GC reinforces the continued role of standard D2 lymphadenectomy.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218892.abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is characterized by a highly infiltrated yet immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), in which tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) contribute to disease progression. Here, we identify an extracellular vesicle (EV)-mediated LMP1-NF-κB-LIF signaling axis that promotes macrophage reprogramming and immune suppression in NPC. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis revealed that EV exposure induces transcriptional remodeling across tumor and immune-cell populations, accompanied by an increased proportion of TAMs within the myeloid compartment. NPC-derived EVs were taken up by macrophages, where EV-associated LMP1 induced NF-κB activation, LIF expression, and polarization toward an immunosuppressive phenotype. Loss- and gain-of-function studies, together with structure-function analyses of the LMP1 CTAR1/CTAR2 domains, further supported the requirement of these CTAR domains for efficient NF-κB activation and LIF induction. Functionally, EV-educated macrophages exhibited impaired phagocytic activity and promoted inhibitory T-cell responses. In zebrafish, 3D spheroid, and mouse xenograft models, EV-educated macrophages promoted NPC growth and vascular dissemination, whereas blockade of LIF signaling with soluble LIFR attenuated these effects. Tumor LIF expression positively correlated with CTLA4 expression. In NPC tissues, LIF expression was preferentially associated with stromal macrophages, and elevated stromal LIF expression was associated with metastasis, advanced nodal disease, and advanced clinical stage. Stromal immune-cell LMP1 expression also correlated with LIF expression and was higher in patients who developed metastasis. Collectively, these findings support an EV-associated LMP1-NF-κB-LIF axis that links EBV-positive NPC cells to macrophage-mediated immune suppression and tumor progression and provide a basis for further investigating this pathway as a potential therapeutic target.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218893.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) drive the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), promoting oncogenic progression, metastasis and treatment resistance. While we previously established that intratumoral administration of poly(I:C) and R848 (TLR3 and TLR7/8 agonists) has strong therapeutic efficacy and triggers STAT1-mediated TAM reprogramming superior to monotherapies, this study evaluates the translational potential, systemic tolerability and immunological impact of their combined systemic (intravenous) delivery. Across diverse syngeneic murine models of solid tumors, including lung adenocarcinoma, triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), fibrosarcoma and glioblastoma, systemic poly(I:C)+R848 administration significantly inhibited primary tumor growth and spontaneous lung metastasis. The treatment exhibited good tolerability under the conditions tested, with no body weight loss or histopathological damage to major organs. Treatment triggered a transient trend toward elevation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IFN-γ, CXCL10, CCL5), while anti-inflammatory markers (IL-10, IL-4) remained unchanged. In primary tumors, treatment-induced TAM reprogramming was evidenced by upregulated M1-like markers (Irf7, Ccl5) and decreased M2-like markers (Arg1), accompanied by enhanced Cd8 and Cd4 T cell markers and cytotoxic effectors (Prf-1 and Gzmb). Multispectral immunophenotyping confirmed this shift toward an antitumor macrophage phenotype, characterized by increased CD86 and decreased ARG1 across all primary tumors. Furthermore, treatment significantly prevented lung metastasis and tumor-induced splenomegaly, shifting splenic macrophages toward an elevated M1/M2 ratio in both fibrosarcoma and TNBC models. These findings demonstrate that intravenous administration of the poly(I:C)+R848 combination effectively reprograms TAMs, suppressing tumor progression and preventing metastasis across a variety of preclinical models of difficult-to-treat solid tumors.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218894.abstract: Atovaquone is an approved antimalarial drug which could sensitise tumours to radiation and may modulate tumour immune microenvironment. Here we evaluated the triple combination of radiation with atovaquone plus anti-PD-L1 in HNSCC syngeneic mouse tumour models. We observed significant tumour growth delay induced by the triple combination treatment with differential responses in three different mouse models. There was complete tumour eradication in 6 of 12 mice in the MOCL1 model but not in the other two murine models. The triple combination was associated with increased populations of CD8+-T Granzyme B+ cells as well as decreased populations of Tregs, CD11b+Gr1+ granulocytic MDSCs and CD11b+ Ly.6G+ neutrophils. Atovaquone inhibited EGFR and its downstream signalling as well as reduced PD-L1 expression. The differential antitumour effects of the triple combination may be due to different basal and post-treatment levels of PD-L1, pERK1/2 and pS6, in particular, their levels were reduced by atovaquone +/- RT in MOCL1 models and not in the other two murine models. Radiotherapy plus atovaquone combination increased cell cycle arrest in G2/M phase, which led to inhibition of DNA damage repair by homologous recombination and increased cell death. We also observed increased activation of CD8+-T cells that led to enhanced killing in our HNSCC patient-derived organoid models treated with the triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. Overall, our results suggest that the triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade has the potential to increase the efficacy of radiotherapy and/or immunotherapy. Thus, this may provide a rationale to further validate this triple combination of radiotherapy and atovaquone plus PD-1/PD-L1 blockade in clinical trials to improve treatment outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218895.abstract: Antiapoptotic buffering in solid tumors is generally mediated by both BCLXL and MCL1, so that BH3 mimetic drugs targeting only one have limited efficacy. To identify agents that may sensitize tumors to BH3 mimetics targeting BCLXL, we screened prostate cancer cells against a panel of mitochondria-targeted drugs in combination with navitoclax, a BH3 mimetic targeting BCL2 and BCLXL. Homoharringtonine (HHT) in combination with navitoclax and as a single agent emerged as a potent inducer of apoptosis. HHT has been identified as an inhibitor of protein translation, and proteomic analysis showed broad suppression of translation-related pathways, while immunoblotting demonstrated rapid decreases in short-lived proteins, including MCL1. HHT dose response and time course studies showed marked declines in MCL1 within 2 hours that were associated with apoptosis in response to BCLXL inhibition with navitoclax or A1331852. Further cell viability assays showed synergy between HHT and BCLXL inhibitors in multiple prostate, lung, and colorectal cancer cell lines. HHT monotherapy in vivo caused tumor regression in two prostate cancer xenograft models. Analysis of tumor tissue taken at 4 hours after dosing showed decreases in MCL1 and MYC, indicating that HHT levels obtainable in vivo are adequate to deplete short-lived proteins and potentially sensitize to BH3 mimetics targeting BCLXL. These findings support further exploration of HHT as a single agent in solid tumors and establish a rationale for investigating safer, tumor-selective approaches to combine HHT-mediated translational inhibition with BCLXL targeting.

doi:10.1016/j.canlet.2026.218896.abstract: Reciprocal interactions between immune and stromal cells are increasingly recognized as major determinants of colorectal cancer (CRC) progression. However, the specific macrophage and fibroblast states cooperating to establish and sustain a tumor-promoting microenvironment remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify a self-reinforcing inflammatory circuit linking monocyte-derived IL-1β+ macrophages with IL1R1+ cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in CRC. Integrated single-cell transcriptomic analyses of human CRC revealed a marked expansion of IL1B-associated inflammatory macrophages and IL1R1+ inflammatory CAFs, with their respective and combined transcriptional signatures associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Pseudotime analysis and Ms4a3 lineage tracing supported a predominantly monocyte-derived origin of IL-1β+ macrophages in the tumor microenvironment. Mechanistically, macrophage-derived IL-1β activated IL1R1 signaling in fibroblasts, promoting the acquisition and expansion of an inflammatory CAF state. Myeloid Il1b deletion or fibroblast-lineage Il1r1 deletion disrupted this interaction and suppressed tumor growth in vivo. In turn, IL1R1+ CAFs produced abundant CCL2, which recruited CCR2+ monocytes and replenished the IL-1β+ macrophage population. Fibroblast-lineage Ccl2 deletion, myeloid Ccr2 deletion, and CCL2 rescue experiments established the functional requirement of the CCL2-CCR2 axis for closure of this reciprocal circuit. Acquisition of the IL-1β+ inflammatory macrophage program was further supported by coordinated NF-κB and AP-1 activity, with RELA and JUN/FOS contributing to IL1B transcriptional regulation. Finally, therapeutic blockade of either IL-1β or CCL2 disrupted the macrophage-CAF circuit, increased intratumoral CD8+ T-cell responses, and enhanced the antitumor efficacy of anti-PD-1 therapy. Collectively, our findings establish the IL-1β-IL1R1-CCL2-CCR2 axis as a self-amplifying immune-stromal circuit that sustains a tumor-promoting and immunosuppressive microenvironment in CRC. By demonstrating that disruption of this circuit restores antitumor immune activity and sensitizes tumors to PD-1 blockade, our study provides a mechanistic and preclinical rationale for targeting IL-1β-CCL2-mediated macrophage-CAF crosstalk as a combination strategy to improve immunotherapy responses in CRC.

doi:10.1016/j.ccell.2026.09.005.abstract: With seven products approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for 15 indications and more than 2,600 active clinical trials, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy is firmly established as an effective therapeutic modality for cancer treatment, and promising early data demonstrate its potential in autoimmune diseases. Key challenges facing the field include extending efficacy to solid tumors and reducing the cost and complexity of manufacturing to improve patient access. In this review, we summarize the clinical lessons learned from the now substantial experience with commercial CAR T cells and clinical trials and discuss three waves shaping next-generation development: multi-engineered and logic-gated CAR T cells, rational combination strategies, and in vivo CAR T cell generation. By integrating clinical experience with emerging strategies, we highlight where CAR T cell therapy has succeeded, where current approaches remain insufficient, and how next-generation cell therapies may be designed to overcome these barriers.

doi:10.1016/j.cell.2026.08.053.abstract: Human centromeres are highly variable but remain among the least characterized regions of the genome because their repetitive structure has hindered conventional analysis of population diversity and disease relevance. Here, we show that rare k-mers in centromeric regions capture lineage-specific variation, defining discrete haplogroups with distinct structural features. We developed ascairn to infer these haplogroups from short-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data. Applying this framework to >3,300 genomes reveals extensive global diversity in centromere haplogroups and signatures of population history. Analyzing short-read WGS data from 142 oligodendroglioma cases with 1p/19q co-deletion, we mapped breakpoints to the centromere regions of chromosomes 1 and 19, revealing a clear positional relationship to kinetochore attachment sites and a link between centromere haplotype structure and rearrangement susceptibility. Rare k-mers thus open centromeres to population-scale analysis, linking centromere structural diversity to human evolutionary history and disease-associated genomic instability.

doi:10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.016.abstract: Trehalose-6-phosphate (T6P) is a central metabolic signal linking sugar availability to plant growth, carbon utilization, and productivity, yet its sensing and signaling mechanisms remain elusive. Using chemical biology and functional approaches, we identify the noncatalytic pseudoenzyme Class-II T6P synthase (TPS-II) as a T6P sensor in Arabidopsis. In the apo state, TPS-II dimerizes to form an autoinhibitory inter-subunit interaction. T6P binding to the N-terminal TPS-like domain triggers a conformational change that releases the C-terminal domain, enabling interaction with the central metabolic integrator SNF1-related protein kinase 1 (SnRK1) to repress its kinase activity. Loss of TPS-II genes activates catabolic and stress-responsive programs while suppressing anabolic gene expression, consistent with constitutive SnRK1 activity. Conservation of this T6P-TPS-II-SnRK1 signaling axis throughout the plant kingdom highlights its fundamental role in coupling carbon availability to metabolic homeostasis. These findings resolve a long-standing question in sugar signaling and provide a framework for improving crop carbon-use efficiency.

doi:10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.026.abstract: Tetanus neurotoxin (TeNT) invades the central nervous system (CNS) via retrograde transport through motoneurons. Whether a host factor is needed to mediate TeNT trafficking has remained unknown. Here, using pull-down and mass spectrometry analysis, and by developing a luciferase-based in vivo transport assay, we identify receptor protein tyrosine phosphatase sigma (PTPRS; PTPσ) as the retrograde transport receptor for TeNT. Global or motoneuron-specific PTPRS knockout (KO) abolishes TeNT entry into the CNS in mouse models. PTPRS-TeNT interactions occur in endosomes, prevent toxin translocation, and direct TeNT trafficking in neurons. Structural studies establish that the TeNT light chain and belt region bind to the immunoglobulin domain of PTPRS. Disrupting TeNT-PTPRS interactions blocks TeNT trafficking into the spinal cord; consistently, a PTPRS-binding-deficient TeNT mutant induces botulism-like flaccid paralysis. Thus, PTPRS is the host factor mediating TeNT trafficking into the CNS, revealing a targetable pathway for post-entry intervention and drug delivery into the CNS.

doi:10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.028.abstract: Distal enhancers activate genes over vast genomic distances, but how this communication occurs and what signals are transmitted are poorly understood. Using real-time single-gene nanoscopy and targeted perturbations, we define physical parameters and mechanisms of enhancer-promoter communication. We find that productive interactions are dynamic, occur at a proximity of ≲100 nm, and are coordinated with transcriptional bursts. Enhancers and promoters find one another not only through passive diffusion; we often directly observe them being actively brought together by cohesin-mediated loop extrusion, which is a key determinant of transcriptional burst frequency. We also discover that specific general transcription factors (GTFs) of RNA polymerase II machinery are key to initiating transcriptional bursts, and enhancer-promoter interactions activate bursting by embedding the promoter within GTF clusters that form at the enhancers. Our results resolve the molecular and biochemical signals involved in long-range gene activation and elucidate the biophysical mechanisms for their transmission from the enhancer to the promoter.

doi:10.1016/j.cell.2026.09.029.abstract: Elucidating the neural computations underlying natural, complex movement remains a fundamental challenge in neuroscience. Bat flight presents a formidable motor control challenge, requiring hand-like wings whose many degrees of freedom must be precisely coordinated to enable rapid three-dimensional (3D) maneuvers. Here, we performed large-scale wireless recordings from the wing motor cortex of freely flying bats, combined with 3D tracking of wing kinematics. Despite the complexity of flight control, bats repeatedly executed accurate flights through precise adjustments of individual wingbeats. Surprisingly, motor cortical activity was not dominated by the wingbeat cycle. Instead, neurons were sparsely active, exhibiting mixed selectivity for flight kinematics and variable entrainment to the wingbeat phase reaching millisecond-scale precision. This yielded a high-dimensional population code driven by successive wingbeats occupying distinct neural states. These findings reveal a mode of motor cortical population dynamics expressed during natural dexterous movement that is not well captured by prevailing views derived from constrained paradigms.

doi:10.1016/j.cels.2026.101716.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has transformed treatment of resistant cancers, yet it faces major limitations such as variable patient responses, relapse, and safety issues. Optimizing CAR T cell treatment regimens and genetic design could offer solutions to some of these problems, but the resulting design space is often too large to explore experimentally alone. Mathematical modeling-spanning ordinary differential equation (ODE), agent-based, statistical, and machine learning methods-provides a framework to link mechanistic understanding of CAR T cells to predictive design and clinical decision-making. Here, we present a perspective that organizes modeling approaches around key translational challenges in CAR T therapy, evaluating the strengths, limitations, and data gaps of current approaches. We outline a roadmap for clinicians and modelers alike, highlighting advances in machine learning, multiscale modeling, control theory, and alternative cell types as emerging opportunities in model-guided design of next-generation cell therapies.

doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2026.09.016.abstract: Loss of skeletal muscle mass is a major driver of frailty and disability, yet how systemic metabolic cues protect muscle integrity remains unclear. We identify Serpina3n, an adipose-derived adipokine, as a key mediator of the protective effects of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) supplementation against muscle atrophy. Elevation of NAD+ in adipose tissue activates signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT)1-dependent transcription of Serpina3n, leading to its systemic release and muscle protection across models of aging, disuse, and cancer cachexia. In muscle, Serpina3n preserves pyruvate carboxylase protein level, promoting anaplerosis, oxidative metabolism, and protein synthesis. These findings define an NAD+-responsive adipose-to-muscle signaling axis that links metabolic status to tissue preservation, defining a systemic mechanism by which inter-organ communication maintains muscle integrity and suggesting potential strategies to counteract muscle degeneration.

doi:10.1016/j.ctrv.2026.103219.abstract: Pathological response (pR) has increasingly been used as a surrogate marker of neoadjuvant treatment efficacy in soft tissue sarcoma (STS), yet evidence linking it to improved survival remains inconsistent. This review evaluates the prognostic value of pR in neoadjuvant-treated STS. A systematic literature review identified clinical trials, observational studies, and retrospective studies assessing survival outcomes associated with pR, defined by residual viable tumour cells (RVT), necrosis, or fibrosis/hyalinization, in STS treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or chemoradiotherapy. Results were reported narratively given substantial heterogeneity between studies. Twenty-seven studies comprising 3961 patients (median 112, range 50-496) were included. Twenty-five reported RVT, eight necrosis, and seven fibrosis/hyalinization. Considerable variability was observed in the prognostic value of pR across studies. Low RVT predicted improved survival in 36% (9/25), high necrosis predicted decreased survival in 75% (6/8), and fibrosis/hyalinization was inconsistent (43% favourable, 29% unfavourable). Cut-off values, histological parameters and definitions, and patient and treatment characteristics varied widely. Analyses were predominantly unadjusted for confounders, including tumour grade, histological subtype, and resection margin. Current evidence is insufficient to support pR as a reliable prognostic predictor. The prognostic value of RVT, necrosis, and fibrosis/hyalinization varies substantially across studies, likely reflecting differences in histological subtype, tumour biology, treatment heterogeneity, and methodological inconsistencies in pR assessment. Standardisation of histological parameters assessed, their definitions, and pR categorisation criteria is required to determine the prognostic relevance of pR in STS. The proposed CHIRE framework provides a practical foundation for harmonising pR assessment and reporting in future STS studies.

doi:10.1016/j.ctrv.2026.103223.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into pharmaceutical discovery, yet the extent to which AI-enabled assets have translated into clinical-stage programs remains incompletely characterized. We performed a cross-sectional descriptive analysis of therapeutic assets discovered or developed using AI approaches that had entered at least one interventional human clinical trial through March 1, 2026. We identified 129 AI-enabled therapeutic assets across 69 companies. Oncology was the dominant therapeutic area (74 assets, 57.3%), and small molecules accounted for the majority of the pipeline (103 assets, 79.8%). Among these assets, 72 (55.8%) had completed Phase 1 and 24 (18.9%) had completed Phase 2; only five had entered or completed Phase 3. The observed probability of success was 77.8% for Phase 1 and 19.5% for Phase 2. Forty-eight assets (37.2%) were classified as targeting a novel biological target. Among companies with available data, the median time from founding to Phase 1 entry was 6.5 years (IQR 4.0-9.2), median total funding raised was $186.7 million (IQR $48.1-$595.0 million), and the median employee count at clinical entry was 73 (IQR 32-129), with a median operational intensity of $2.72 million per employee. AI-enabled therapeutics are entering clinical testing at increasing scale, but most programs remain early in development, with few having advanced beyond Phase 2. This dataset provides a baseline for future evaluation of whether AI-enabled discovery ultimately improves regulatory approval rates and clinical outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.ctrv.2026.103225.abstract: Hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (HDGC) caused by germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in CDH1 remains a difficult hereditary cancer syndrome to manage. Prophylactic total gastrectomy has long been considered the most definitive preventive strategy, but recent penetrance estimates, expert endoscopic surveillance cohorts, and better characterization of early signet-ring cell lesions have challenged a uniform approach for all carriers. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on CDH1-associated gastric cancer risk, testing criteria, mechanisms of carcinogenesis, prophylactic gastrectomy, endoscopic surveillance, and emerging biomarkers for risk stratification. The available data support a more individualized discussion that integrates family history, age, comorbidity, sex-specific cancer risks, patient preferences, and access to expert surveillance. However, current biomarkers remain investigational, and no blood-, stool-, gastric-fluid-, or tissue-based assay is validated to replace surgery or endoscopic surveillance in routine care. At present, personalized management is best understood as structured shared decision-making within specialist centers, rather than fully biomarker-driven prevention. Future progress will require prospective registries, standardized surveillance protocols, molecular endpoints linked to clinical progression, and careful evaluation of quality of life after both surveillance and gastrectomy.

doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106502.abstract: Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (AAV) is a complex autoimmune disease with distinct clinical and serological subtypes. Previous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified several susceptibility loci, particularly within the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), but the broader genetic architecture and causal variants underlying AAV remain incompletely defined. We conducted a genome-wide association study including 2068 individuals with AAV and 3258 controls of European ancestry. The discovery cohort comprised a previously published GWAS dataset supplemented with newly recruited cases. Analyses were stratified by clinical (granulomatosis with polyangiitis [GPA] and microscopic polyangiitis [MPA]) and serological (proteinase 3-ANCA [PR3] and myeloperoxidase-ANCA [MPO]) subtypes. Findings were evaluated in an independent case cohort of 465 individuals. We performed conditional and joint analyses of the HLA region, functional fine-mapping, linkage disequilibrium score regression, and integrative multi-omics analyses to prioritise candidate causal variants and assess genetic correlations. We identified eight previously unreported loci and replicated four known loci associated with AAV at genome-wide significance. Within the HLA region, HLA-DPB1∗04 showed the strongest association with AAV, GPA, and PR3 subtypes, whereas HLA-DRB1∗04 was most strongly associated with MPO and MPA. Conditional analyses identified additional independent effects, including amino acid variation in HLA-DQA1. SNP-based heritability estimates indicated a substantial genetic contribution to AAV (h2 = 0·40). Genetic correlation analyses revealed shared heritability with multiple traits, including celiac disease and hypothyroidism. Integrative analyses highlighted candidate genes, including HCG9 and PRTN3, and implicated protein interaction networks involving genes related to neutrophil biology. Protein-protein interaction analysis identified networks involving genes implicated in AAV risk, including PRTN3, AZU1, ELANE, and SERPINA1. These findings expand the genetic landscape of AAV and support a complex and heterogeneous genetic architecture involving both MHC and non-MHC loci. The integration of genetic association, functional annotation, and network analyses suggests that disease susceptibility is mediated through multiple biological pathways, including immune regulation and neutrophil function. These insights may inform future mechanistic studies, improved disease stratification, and the development of targeted therapeutic strategies. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106506.abstract: Canopy FGF signalling regulator 3 (CNPY3) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident chaperone essential for toll-like receptor (TLR) folding, trafficking and inflammasome activation. In rare paediatric cases, biallelic CNPY3 variants have been associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), but available data remain sparse. 50 individuals from 38 unrelated families with biallelic CNPY3 variants and DEE were evaluated for exome and genome findings, standardised clinical phenotype descriptions, EEG results, and neuroimaging data. A selection of variants underwent functional analysis focussing on protein stability and localisation, TLR2 function, NLPR3 inflammasome activation, and structural conformation. Disease onset occurred in early infancy (median age at onset 68 days), with a clinical phenotype comprising global developmental delay (100%) and intractable epilepsy (86%), accompanied by microcephaly (70%), spasticity (77%), growth faltering (63%), stridor (48%), and early mortality (38%). Epileptic spasms and tonic seizures (46% each) were the most frequent seizure types, and EEG findings included suppression-burst (37%) and hypsarrhythmia (28%). Phenotypic severity varied substantially, with most patients being severely affected (median score 16, range 2-20). Most variants occurred in the homozygous state (95%), including 13 missense changes and 7 truncating alleles. Variants were classified as of uncertain significance (71%), followed by likely pathogenic (23%) and pathogenic (6%) according to ACMG/AMP criteria. Genotype-phenotype correlation showed that individuals with truncating variants were, on average, more severely affected than those with non-truncating variants (median score 18 vs 14.5). Protein modelling predicted conformational effects for most missense variants. In cells, frameshift alleles abolished CNPY3 protein expression, whereas nonsense alleles markedly reduced protein levels. ER localisation of CNPY3 remained preserved across tested genotypes; however, capacity to support TLR2 maturation and processing varied substantially. Remarkably, some missense variants permitted TLR2 surface expression but impaired downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, uncoupling trafficking from signal transduction. CNPY3-associated DEE is a severe early-onset disorder with genotype-dependent phenotypic severity, accompanied by allele-specific disruption of innate immune pathways. Our findings reveal separable effects on TLR trafficking, downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, identifying CNPY3 as a key regulator of multiple cellular pathways involved in inflammatory responses and neurodevelopment. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106508.abstract: Although antigenemia is associated with poor outcomes in respiratory viral infections, the underlying mechanisms driving viral bloodstream dissemination remain not fully understood. Herein, we aimed to characterise SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N)-antigenemia kinetics in patients with severe COVID-19. We also sought to identify host and viral determinants associated with viral dissemination through a multiparametric integrated analysis and assess the associated risk of death. This observational study included hospitalised patients with severe COVID-19 across three independent cohorts (discovery, n = 66; confirmation, n = 137; validation, n = 27), used respectively for identification, replication, and validation of findings, along with patients with mild COVID-19 and with severe influenza infection, as a disease severity and non-COVID-19 control group. From blood and nasal samples, N-antigenemia levels were analysed in relation to 45 host/viral parameters. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to assess the association with in-hospital mortality. Single-cell RNA sequencing was used to identify host determinants, and in vitro primary human airway epithelial models were used to assess epithelial barrier integrity and viral translocation. Across cohorts, we observed a significantly higher detection rate and concentration of N-antigenemia in patients with severe COVID-19 at admission compared to those with mild COVID-19 or controls (fold change [FC] >54.7, p < 0.001 [Kruskal-Wallis, Dunn post-hoc]). Type-I interferon (IFN-I) activity was the strongest correlate of N-antigenemia (ρ = 0.72, p.adj < 0.001 [Spearman, Benjamini-Hochberg]), and longitudinal analyses revealed a strong positive sigmoidal relationship (p < 0.001 [approximate Wald test]). Patients with severe COVID-19 with neutralising autoantibodies against IFN-I lacked detectable N-antigenemia, further supporting a link between systemic viral dissemination and IFN-I activity. Single-cell RNA sequencing showed higher expression of interferon-stimulated genes in monocytes and dendritic cells in patients with a high N-antigenemia level. Furthermore, high N-antigenemia at hospital admission was independently associated with an increased risk of death (aOR 2.6, 95% CI 1.0-6.7; p = 0.042 [Wald test]). Finally, we demonstrated that prolonged IFN-I exposure in vitro appears to impair epithelial barrier integrity. These findings suggest that sustained IFN-I activity is associated with systemic viral dissemination and epithelial barrier dysfunction in patient with severe COVID-19. The concordance between clinical observations and in vitro data supports a potential link between prolonged IFN-I responses and these processes, although causality remains to be established. These results highlight the potential importance of the timing and duration of IFN-I immunity and warrant further investigation of its clinical relevance. doi:10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106512.abstract: Disease features in resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTHβ), caused by THRB mutations, arise from insensitivity to thyroid hormone in tissues expressing thyroid hormone receptor (TR)β and from lifelong thyrotoxic effects in TRα1-expressing tissues, posing substantial cardiovascular morbidity/mortality. The T3-analogue triiodothyroacetic acid (Triac) holds potential as an effective treatment. Systematic data on Triac therapy in RTHβ are lacking, and the mechanisms through which Triac acts are unclear. This study aims to elucidate these knowledge gaps. Clinical and biochemical data were obtained through an, international retrospective cohort study in patients with RTHβ. Transcriptional activity of all TRβ mutants, on the background of the pituitary-expressed β2 receptor isoform and positively (DR+4-TRE) or negatively (TSHα-TRE) regulated reporter genes plus T3 or Triac, was studied. Thyroid function and TSH responses to T3 and Triac were tested in zebrafish expressing TRβ mutants. We collected data from 28 patients with RTHβ (range: 0.4-73.1 years) with 18 unique mutations treated with Triac in 6 centres. Triac reduced TSH (by 43%) and FT4 (by 37%) concentrations in all heterozygous patients, supported by consistent findings in zebrafish. Our functional studies showed that TRβ2 mutants exhibited reduced (all) or absent (G432del) T3-dependent transcriptional activity, with similar EC50 and IC50 values for T3 and Triac, except for R316H, which showed a 5-times lower EC50/IC50 value for Triac compared to T3. In this international, multicentre study we have documented that Triac lowers elevated FT4 concentrations in patients with RTHβ effectively. Integrating our clinical and molecular observations we suggest that Triac can act via different modes of action, with activation of the wild-type receptor being a relevant mechanism. Our study may inform clinical management and could shape future interventional studies in patients with RTHβ. doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108584.abstract: We conducted a randomized phase II trial to evaluate whether adding erlotinib to platinum/docetaxel improves clinical outcomes in the first-line treatment of recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous-cell carcinomas, building on our previous single-arm phase II trial. This was a placebo-controlled, double-blind, single-center phase II study. Patients (N = 120) were randomly assigned (1 : 1) to receive platinum (carboplatin area under the curve 6 or cisplatin 75 mg/m2 every 21 days for six cycles) plus docetaxel (75 mg/m2 every 21 days for six cycles) with either erlotinib (150 mg/day orally until progression) or placebo. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary endpoints included overall survival, response rates, duration of response, and correlations of erlotinib-induced rash/biomarkers with outcomes. Median PFS was 6.1 months with erlotinib versus 4.4 months with placebo [hazard ratio (HR) 0.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.42-0.95, P = 0.026]. Median overall survival was 17.0 months in the erlotinib arm compared with 13.7 months in the control arm (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.43-1.04, P = 0.0718), meeting the prespecified type I error threshold. Subgroup analyses demonstrated numerically favorable PFS HRs across most clinical subgroups, with a more pronounced benefit observed in patients with oropharyngeal and human papillomavirus-related tumors. Development of grade ≥2 rash during the first cycle of erlotinib was associated with significantly improved overall survival (HR 0.40, 95% CI 0.19-0.87, P = 0.021). The addition of erlotinib increased the incidence of grade 2-4 adverse events, particularly gastrointestinal toxicity, rash, fatigue, and dehydration but no unexpected safety signals were observed. The study met its primary endpoint, supporting the continued relevance of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibition in this disease. Although contemporary immunotherapy-based standards limit direct adoption of this regimen, these results provide clinically meaningful insight into EGFR biology and support further development of modernized, tyrosine kinase inhibitor-based EGFR strategies, including rational combinations and biomarker-driven approaches, to improve outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.esmoop.2026.108596.abstract: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) are associated with poor outcomes, with many patients never receiving any cancer-directed treatment. Population-based registries from England, France, Italy and Spain share a similar picture: emergency presentation, rather than planned referral, accounts for roughly half of diagnoses, and >50% of patients with cholangiocarcinoma in England received neither surgery, systemic therapy nor stenting. This attrition is not exclusive to real-world settings: in PROOF-301 and FIGHT-302, a considerable proportion of eligible or randomly assigned patients never started their allocated treatment. BTC is also no longer a disease confined to older adults, with ∼7% of cases diagnosed in individuals <50 years of age. On top of this, access to reimbursed therapies, molecular profiling and expert multidisciplinary discussion remains markedly uneven across Europe. "Our patients deserve better" and closing these gaps in diagnosis, access to treatment and care delivery is as urgent as developing new drugs for this disease.

doi:10.1016/j.eururo.2026.09.005.abstract: The phase 2 randomized LUNAR trial previously demonstrated that neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 before stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with oligorecurrent hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (orHSPC). We report updated efficacy and safety outcomes with extended follow-up. Patients with prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-detected orHSPC and one to five metastatic lesions amenable to SBRT were randomized 1:1 to SBRT alone or two cycles of neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 followed by SBRT. The primary end point was PFS, defined as new lesions on PSMA PET/CT, initiation of salvage hormonal therapy, or death. Secondary end points included hormonal therapy-free survival (HT-FS) and 24-mo progression-free status. Exploratory end points included polymetastatic PFS (poly-PFS), castration-resistant disease-free survival (CRFS), and conventional imaging progression-free survival (CT-PFS). Between September 2022 and November 2023, 92 patients were randomized to SBRT alone (n = 47) or 177Lu-PNT2002 plus SBRT (n = 45). At a median follow-up of 31.9 mo, 177Lu-PNT2002 significantly improved PFS (median 17.6 vs 7.4 mo; hazard ratio [HR] 0.38, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 0.23-0.61; p < 0.001) and HT-FS (HR 0.57, 95% CI = 0.34-0.95; p = 0.03). Exploratory analyses demonstrated improved poly-PFS (HR 0.28, 95% CI = 0.08-1.03; p = 0.04), CRFS (HR 0.13, 95% CI = 0.02-1.10; p = 0.03), and CT-PFS (HR 0.46, 95% CI = 0.19-1.09; p = 0.07). No new safety signals were observed. With extended follow-up, neoadjuvant 177Lu-PNT2002 before SBRT produced durable improvements in PFS and HT-FS. While poly-PFS, CRFS, and CT-PFS were exploratory end points, their improvement provides hypothesis-generating evidence that the addition of radioligand therapy to SBRT may alter disease trajectory beyond delaying PSMA PET/CT-detected recurrence.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.09.018.abstract: To compare proton dynamic arc therapy (DynamicArc) with conventional intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) for breast/chest wall irradiation across diverse clinical anatomies. Forty patients were analyzed (10/cohort): tissue expanders, permanent implants, no reconstruction, and bilateral disease. DynamicArc plans used coplanar partial arcs (150-160°) with arc retracing; paired IMPT plans used 2-4 static fields. RayStation 2023BDTK-generated plans shared contours and prescriptions (50.4 Gy[RBE]/28; subset bilateral 42.56 Gy[RBE]/16) and were robustly optimized/evaluated (±5 mm setup,±3.5% range) with Monte Carlo dose calculation (0.5%uncertainty,40000ions/spot) and a 7.5cm range shifter. Target coverage and OAR endpoints were compared using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with FDR correction. Additionally, robustness pass rates, LETd metrics, and estimated treatment times were compared. DynamicArc achieved target coverage comparable to IMPT and improved robustness pass rates for selected targets. In the expander cohort, DynamicArc improved coverage posterior to the expander port and increased coverage of the chest wall evaluation volume and nodal targets. Improved D95% was accompanied by increased target V105% in several targets. DynamicArc increased thyroid mean dose and skin V95% in multiple cohorts, although skin D2cc and skin V100% remained low. Focal hotspot metrics for the esophagus, heart, and LAD were largely unchanged, with LAD D0.03cc numerically lower though not statistically significant in the expander cohort. Ipsilateral lung V20 was generally similar, with a reduction in implant cases. Several unadjusted significant findings did not remain significant after FDR correction. High-dose CTV LETd was broadly comparable between techniques with changes in the tails of the distribution. DynamicArc increased spots, energy layers, and beam-on time, but estimated total treatment time was comparable after accounting for IMPT room entry and imaging. DynamicArc achieved comparable target coverage with improved robustness in challenging anatomies, at the cost of increased V105%, thyroid mean dose, and skin V95% while maintaining comparable treatment times.
