doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.09.019.abstract: While accelerated hypofractionated radiotherapy has increasingly been adopted in the multidisciplinary management of locally-advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ineligible for concurrent chemotherapy, there is a paucity of randomized prospective evidence guiding utilization. Given the marked heterogeneity in the presentations of locally-advanced NSCLC, the American Radium Society (ARS) Thoracic Appropriate Use Criteria (AUC) Panel evaluated the appropriateness of accelerated hypofractionation in the context of multidisciplinary management. Five clinical variants representing manifestations of locally-advanced NSCLC were developed by the 15-member multidisciplinary ARS Thoracic AUC panel. The English-language medical literature was formally reviewed from 2010-2025 and scrutinized for prospective clinical trials utilizing accelerated hypofractionation for concurrent chemotherapy ineligible patients. All case variants were evaluated with respect to use of radiation technique, radiation fractionation, and utilization of programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy with Modified Delphi methodology. Consensus recommendations were reviewed and approved by the ARS Executive Committee and subject to public comment. The literature review identified 228 articles, of which there were 14 prospective trials/registries including nine Phase I-II trials, four prospective registries, and one randomized Phase III trial. There was consensus that it is appropriate to utilize intensity modulated radiation therapy and proton therapy across presentations of locally-advanced NSCLC, with the aim of constraining the lung V20Gy<30% and heart V40Gy<20% with accelerated hypofractionation. When utilizing 15-fraction accelerated hypofractionation for disease abutting the esophagus or brachial plexus, there was consensus that it is inappropriate to exceed doses of 45-55 Gy. With respect to PD-L1 immunotherapy, there was consensus that consolidative immunotherapy after definitive radiation therapy is appropriate, but that concurrent immunotherapy is inappropriate. There was panel consensus that it may be appropriate to utilize induction PD-L1 immunotherapy prior to radiation therapy in cases of bulky or N3 disease to test disease biology. Across variants, there was consensus that conventionally fractionated radiotherapy to 60 Gy in 30 fractions remains appropriate. The ARS Thoracic AUC Panel has provided consensus case-based guidelines on the multidisciplinary management of locally-advanced NSCLC ineligible for concurrent chemotherapy reflecting the heterogeneity of disease presentation in this population. In absence of randomized prospective data demonstrating superiority of accelerated hypofractionation, conventionally fractionated radiotherapy remains an appropriate option.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.09.021.abstract: High-dose hyper-fractionated radiotherapy has been recently included in NCCN guidelines for limited-stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC), which clinical outcomes are dependent on actually delivered biologically effective dose (BED). However, most tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models rely on planed physical dose without considering inter-fractional deviations and BED of fractionization. This study aims to develop TCP and NTCP models for LS-SCLC incorporating CBCT-based inter-fractional anatomies and hyper-fractional radiobiological dose. Inter-fractional dose was accumulated based on deformable image registration between CBCT and planning CT (pCT). Both TCP and NTCP were formulated within a BED-based framework, using dose-volume parameters calculated from planned dose and CBCT-based accumulated dose for comparison. The LQ model with "4R" effects and Gompertzian tumor growth (LQRG) and Lyman-Kutcher-Burman (LKB) models were used for TCP and NTCP modeling. Based on the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), negative log-likelihood (NLL), and Akaike information criterion (AIC), model performances were assessed for local progression-free survival (LPFS), radiation pneumonitis and radiation esophagitis. Compared with pCT dose, CBCT dose showed superior discrimination of normal tissue toxicity. For grade ≥2 radiation pneumonitis, the CBCT-based NTCP model achieved significantly higher AUC (0.67 vs. 0.59) and lower NLL (62.39 vs. 66.13) than that of the pCT-based mode. Superiority of CBCT-based NTCP model was also observed for grade ≥3 radiation esophagitis, i.e., AUC (0.62 vs. 0.58) and NLL (55.55 vs. 56.64). Using the observed LPFS as reference, marginally improved TCP modeling was observed using CBCT dose than that of pCT, where the AUC values were 0.80 vs. 0.79 (GTV 45 Gy) and 0.77 vs. 0.75 (GTV 54 Gy). By incorporating inter-fractional deviation and biological effectiveness, the improved accuracy of TCP and NTCP models provides preliminary evidence supporting the treatment planning and toxicity management for LS-SCLC patients treated with the hyper-fractionated radiotherapy, which needs further clinical validation.

doi:10.1016/j.ijrobp.2026.09.023.abstract: Radiotherapy confers a later risk of secondary malignancies, including radiation-associated breast cancer. Distinctive molecular profiles emerge in tumors from pre-irradiated tumor beds, but effects on therapeutic options remain understudied. We developed a murine model of radiation-associated breast cancer by transplanting p53-mutant mammary HC11 epithelial cells that had been previously exposed to radiation (HC11RT) into mammary fat pads (MFP) that had been previously irradiated. Tumor incidence from HC11RT cells increased two-fold when grown in irradiated MFP. Compared to tumors grown in sham-irradiated MFP, tumors from irradiated MFP had elevated TGFβ in both tumor and CD8+ T cells and elevated PD-L1 on CD4+ T cells, resulting in improved response to immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI). This study provides evidence that prior irradiation potentiates tumorigenesis and immune evasion through both tumor cell autonomous and non-autonomous mechanisms. As a result, radiation-associated cancers may exhibit greater response to ICI than tumors of the same histology that are not associated with prior radiotherapy.

doi:10.1016/j.immuni.2026.09.010.abstract: CD4+ tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells are crucial for relapse in allergic skin conditions. However, the mechanisms underlying their maintenance and pathogenic potential remain poorly defined. Here, across multiple models of allergic dermatitis, we identified a C-X-C chemokine receptor 6 (CXCR6+) subpopulation within CD4+ TRM cells as a distinct pathogenic subset that rapidly induces relapse. This subset is supported by C-X-C chemokine ligand 16 (CXCL16)-dependent interactions with CD301b+ conventional type 2 dendritic cells (cDC2s) for in situ maintenance. Functional blockade of the CXCL16-CXCR6 signaling pathway impaired proliferation and maintenance of CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM cells. In human atopic dermatitis (AD), CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM cells co-localized with CD301+ cDC2s in perivascular clusters even after successful anti-IL-13 therapy. These findings point to CXCR6+ CD4+ TRM cells as a pathogenic reservoir sustaining chronic and recurrent inflammation and suggest the CXCL16-CXCR6 axis as a therapeutic target to prevent relapse in allergic skin diseases.

doi:10.1016/j.immuni.2026.09.021.abstract: Inflammation can have lasting effects, but the mechanisms that drive these effects remain unclear. Adir and colleagues1 reveal that intestinal inflammation leaves a durable imprint in the extracellular matrix. This modified matrix redirects stem-cell fate, sustains wound-associated epithelial programs and promotes persistent immune activation, establishing extracellular matrix memory as a mechanism linking resolved injury to chronic inflammatory disease.

doi:10.1016/j.jhep.2026.09.024.abstract: Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy (CCM), a clinically consequential comorbidity of cirrhosis, remains undefined and underappreciated in children. This study aimed to characterize myocardial structural, functional, morphometric, and histopathologic features in pediatric cirrhosis and objectively derive a reliable echocardiographic (2DE) metric to predict perioperative adverse events, including mortality. 2DE, morphometry, histopathology, and vasoactive-inotropic score (VIS) were compared between children with (n=226) and without (n=160) cirrhosis listed for liver transplantation (LT) over 2011-2021. Discriminatory performance of left ventricular mass index (height)2.7(LVMI g/m2.7) for predicting waitlist decompensation, composite serious adverse events post liver transplant and mortality was assessed using ROC analysis, with AUCs and optimal thresholds compared against PELD-Cr/MELD scores. LV mass was significantly higher in children with cirrhosis on 2DE and necropsy specimens compared to non-cirrhotic controls, with ∼25% demonstrating LV hypertrophy, with OR of 6.9 [CI 3,16], p< 0.0001. In the cirrhotic cohort, LVMI correlated with vasoactive needs under stress of LT (p <0.001) and was significantly higher in patients with WLD, CSAE, and non-survivors. In cirrhosis, LVMI values ≥ 88 g/m2.7, ≥ 91 g/m2.7, and ≥ 95 g/m2.7 were independently associated with WLD, CSAE, and mortality, when adjusting for PELD-Cr/MELD, bilirubin, and INR (p <0.01). Combining LVMI + PELD-Cr/MELD significantly outperformed PELD-Cr/MELD in discriminating both WLD and CSAE, whereas LVMI alone significantly outperformed PELD-Cr/MELD for CSAE and was comparable for WLD. All three models performed comparably in discriminating death. LVMI is a strong predictor of morbidity and mortality, serving as a prognostic marker in children with cirrhosis. Incorporating LVMI into PELD-Cr/MELD may enhance risk stratification and organ allocation.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103063.abstract: Cisplatin resistance remains a major obstacle in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), yet the contribution of the vascular microenvironment and its variation across HPV statuses remains unclear. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and bioinformatics analyses to characterize cisplatin resistance-associated cellular states in HNSCC. Cisplatin resistance scoring, pseudotime analysis, transcriptional regulatory network analysis, and cell-cell communication analysis were used to identify resistant subpopulations. Spatial localization, survival analysis, immune infiltration assessment, and drug sensitivity prediction were further performed to evaluate key candidate genes. Cisplatin resistance signals were preferentially enriched in tumor endothelial cells and were stronger in HPV-negative HNSCC. Endothelial cells with high resistance scores exhibited enhanced angiogenesis, extracellular matrix remodeling, hypoxia, and inflammatory programs. Multidimensional screening identified SERPINE1 as a key resistance-associated endothelial gene, showing significant upregulation and positive correlation with resistance scores. Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses consistently demonstrated vascular-associated enrichment of SERPINE1, particularly in HPV-negative tumors. High SERPINE1 expression was associated with poor survival and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Drug sensitivity prediction suggested increased sensitivity of SERPINE1-high tumors to EGFR/SRC- and MAPK-pathway inhibitors, whereas no significant differences were observed for conventional cytotoxic agents. SERPINE1 defines a tumor endothelial state associated with cisplatin resistance in HNSCC and may contribute to HPV-related differences in the vascular microenvironment, providing a potential basis for therapeutic stratification.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103064.abstract: Renal cystic conditions are heterogeneous. We used a broad renal cyst-associated disease-gene framework to identify molecular programs shared with clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), without modeling a specific cystic disorder or direct cyst-to-cancer progression. We identified 237 shared genes between renal cyst disease and ccRCC (TCGA-KIRC), performed functional enrichment, Mendelian randomization, and built a random survival forest (RSF) risk score benchmarked against published signatures and immunotherapy cohorts. Single-cell (Scissor, SCENIC, scTenifoldKnk virtual FOXM1 knockout) and spatial transcriptomics (RCTD, CellChat) were integrated with fibroblast subclustering and oncoPredict drug screening. Candidate FOXM1 inhibitors were prioritized by docking and 100-ns molecular dynamics, with isovitexin validated functionally. The shared program was enriched for epithelial development and ECM remodeling. Two direction-specific Mendelian randomization analyses supported associations between genetic liability to kidney cancer and related renal cystic phenotypes. The RSF score showed robust prognostic discrimination across cohorts and separated immunotherapy outcomes. High-risk tumors were enriched for Tregs, B cells, and fibroblasts. FOXM1+ malignant epithelium represented the high-risk state, with elevated CNV burden and regulon activity; virtual FOXM1 knockout identified COL6A1 and CD44 among 129 significant non-target perturbation hits. Convergent single-cell and spatial analyses nominated a COL6A1-CD44 communication axis associated with fibroblast remodeling, with F5_SFRP2+ fibroblasts as the most plausible receiving state. These fibroblasts showed ECM-remodeling, adverse prognosis, and pathway activation. Isovitexin emerged as a lead FOXM1-targeting compound, significantly suppressing ccRCC proliferation, migration, and invasion. These findings support a testable communication model involving FOXM1+ epithelium, COL6A1-CD44 and F5_SFRP2+ fibroblasts. The in vitro results also support further evaluation of isovitexin in ccRCC.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103065.abstract: Gastric cancer (GC) poses a distinct modeling challenge. The disease varies by region, histology, metastatic site, and treatment history. It also develops within a gastric niche shaped by acid, mucus, polarity, microbes, and stroma. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) can preserve tumor-linked epithelial states and support living biobanks. They also enable genotype-phenotype studies and functional testing of therapeutic vulnerabilities. Their clinical value depends on representation, not model complexity alone. The assay must also return clear results within a useful clinical window. This review evaluates GC PDOs as functional companion models for precision oncology rather than stand-alone treatment decision tools. We discuss four barriers that limit clinical readiness. Establishment bias reduces representation of diffuse-type, scirrhous, and signet-ring cell carcinomas. Standard organoid lumens do not reproduce gastric acidity, stratified mucus, or Helicobacter pylori-driven polarity loss. Long-term expansion can select culture-adapted clones and weaken clinical representativeness. PDO drug screening also remains difficult to align with urgent treatment timelines. Fresh-sample assays may shorten turnaround time but reduce scale and depth. We further highlight biological insights gained from GC organoids. These include niche independence, epigenetic dependencies, ARID1A-linked vulnerabilities, and chemotherapy resistance. We propose a readiness framework based on six criteria: tumor authenticity, subtype coverage, niche fidelity, turnaround time, assay standards, and outcome validation. This framework may help define where GC PDOs can support clinical reasoning.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103067.abstract: Chemotherapy non-response remains a major challenge in bladder cancer, yet the endothelial states and intercellular communication programs associated with treatment failure remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, bulk transcriptomic data, computational analyses, and in vitro experiments to characterize endothelial programs associated with chemotherapy response. A non-response-related transcriptional program was preferentially enriched in endothelial cells and was most prominent in the TipEC_2 tip-like endothelial subset. Integrative analyses identified DLL4 as a key feature of this endothelial state. Spatial and ligand-receptor analyses further supported a DLL4-associated tip-like endothelial niche and inferred DLL4-NOTCH3-related communication between endothelial and malignant compartments, together with RBPJ-associated transcriptional activity in DLL4-positive TipEC_2 cells. Consistently, cisplatin-resistant bladder cancer cells showed increased expression of NOTCH3 and downstream transcriptional targets, whereas pharmacological Notch inhibition suppressed downstream HES1 and HEY1 expression and partially restored cisplatin sensitivity. Elevated DLL4 expression was associated with chemotherapy non-response and unfavorable survival. In a separate prognostic analysis, a DLL4-positive TipEC_2-associated risk model stratified patients by overall survival in TCGA-BLCA and GSE13507. Collectively, these findings identify a DLL4-associated tip-like endothelial niche linked to chemotherapy non-response and suggest DLL4-NOTCH3 signaling as a potential molecular link between vascular remodeling and treatment resistance in bladder cancer.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103068.abstract: Antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) activity and target-dependent on-target/off-tumor toxicity depends in part on which cells express the target antigen, a feature that bulk assays cannot resolve. We analyzed a publicly available whole-transcriptome CosMx breast tumor dataset including 154,816 cells and 18,934 genes. Eleven clinically relevant ADC targets were profiled across seven annotated lineages. Findings were contextualized using TCGA-BRCA bulk transcriptomes (1,097 tumors and 114 normal tissues) and assessed in two public Xenium breast cancer specimens. HER2 (ERBB2), TROP2 (TACSTD2), HER3 (ERBB3), NECTIN4 and MUC1 were enriched in tumor epithelium. B7-H3 (CD276) was highest in endothelial and myoepithelial cells, with similar mean expression in stromal and tumor cells. PSMA (FOLH1) was enriched in endothelium. TCGA-BRCA tumor-normal differences did not identify these cellular sources. No overall-survival association remained after multiple-testing correction or covariate adjustment. HER2 and TROP2 tumor enrichment recurred in both Xenium specimens, whereas EGFR was not tumor restricted. Cell-resolved spatial profiling separated ADC targets enriched in tumor epithelium from those expressed in vascular and stromal compartments. B7-H3 and PSMA localization was consistent with prior immunohistochemical reports and is confirmatory. These RNA-level results do not establish surface-protein abundance, ADC response, or clinical toxicity. Low-abundance microenvironmental findings remain based on a single discovery specimen and require protein-level validation. Protein-level confirmation, and correlation with ADC efficacy and toxicity, are required before these maps can inform clinical decisions.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103071.abstract: Acquired resistance to programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitors presents a major clinical challenge in the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). This study aims to elucidate the epigenetic mechanisms underlying PD-1 inhibitor resistance, with a specific focus on the expression profiles of PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) and their associated signaling networks. High-throughput RNA sequencing was performed on matched pre- and post-resistance plasma samples from three NSCLC patients to identify differentially expressed piRNAs. The top five candidate piRNAs were selected for subsequent verification. Plasma piRNA levels and comprehensive clinical data from an independent cohort of 50 NSCLC patients (evaluated at both pre- and post-resistance stages) were analyzed. Downstream target genes of the candidate piRNAs were predicted using TargetScan and miRanda algorithms, followed by Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) functional enrichment analyses. Target gene expression was experimentally validated via quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). Spearman's rank correlation was utilized to assess the relationship between piRNA expression and systemic inflammatory indices. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. Five candidate piRNAs (Hsap_2765751, Hsap_249, Hsap_1847317, Hsap_681799, and Hsap_857420) exhibited significant differential expression. Notably, Hsap_1847317 was robustly upregulated following the development of resistance (P < 0.001). Bioinformatic and experimental analyses implicated Hsap_1847317 is implicated in the Wnt signaling pathway, while qRT-PCR demonstrated significantly higher AXIN2 mRNA expression after resistance (P < 0.001). these associative data do not establish direct regulation. Furthermore, the systemic neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) significantly increased during the resistance phase (P < 0.001) and exhibited a positive correlation with Hsap_1847317 expression (r = 0.395, P = 0.005). ROC curve analysis demonstrated excellent predictive efficacy, yielding an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.944 for Hsap_1847317 and 0.720 for NLR in this cohort. Our findings indicate that plasma Hsap_1847317 and NLR are candidate non-invasive biomarkers for monitoring acquired resistance to PD-1 inhibitors in NSCLC. This study association between Hsap_1847317, Wnt-related enrichment, and AXIN2 mRNA provides a hypothesis for further mechanistic testing rather than evidence of a causal Hsap_1847317/Wnt/AXIN2 axis.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103072.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive subtype of breast cancer characterized by high molecular heterogeneity and a lack of effective targeted therapies. Increasing evidence indicates that metabolic reprogramming and redox homeostasis are critical determinants of TNBC progression; however, the transcriptional mechanisms linking these processes to mitochondrial function remain incompletely understood. In this study, integrative bioinformatics analyses identified nuclear receptor subfamily 3 group C member 2 (NR3C2) as a potential regulatory factor in TNBC. NR3C2 expression was significantly decreased in TNBC and was associated with patient prognosis. Functional assays demonstrated that NR3C2 overexpression markedly inhibited cell proliferation and migration in vitro and suppressed tumor growth and dissemination in zebrafish xenograft models. Mechanistically, RNA sequencing identified NDUFB3, an accessory subunit of mitochondrial complex I, as a downstream target of NR3C2. Dual-luciferase reporter assays further confirmed that NR3C2 directly regulates NDUFB3 transcription. Functional analyses revealed that NR3C2 modulates mitochondrial activity, as evidenced by increased mitochondrial membrane potential and complex I activity, accompanied by reduced ATP production and elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. Notably, NR3C2-induced ROS accumulation promoted apoptosis, whereas these effects were partially reversed by NDUFB3 knockdown or treatment with the ROS scavenger N-acetylcysteine (NAC). Consistently, in vivo experiments demonstrated that NR3C2 suppresses tumor growth and metastasis in a ROS-dependent manner. Collectively, these findings indicate that NR3C2 inhibits TNBC progression by regulating mitochondrial function and ROS homeostasis, at least in part through NDUFB3. This study provides new insights into the interplay between transcriptional regulation and mitochondrial redox balance and highlights NR3C2 as a potential therapeutic target for TNBC.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103074.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) lacks reliable biomarkers for early detection and remains a highly aggressive disease. Ephrin type-A receptor 2 (EphA2), a receptor tyrosine kinase frequently overexpressed in advanced cancers, undergoes MMP14-mediated cleavage that releases soluble N-terminal fragments. Here, we investigated the diagnostic and functional significance of this fragment in TNBC. Immunohistochemical analysis of clinical specimens revealed elevated EphA2 expression in TNBC tissues, with a trend toward higher levels in tumors of advanced stage and grade. To enable non-invasive detection, we established a dual-epitope sandwich ELISA targeting spatially distinct regions of the EphA2 extracellular domain. The assay showed concentration-dependent detection of recombinant EphA2 (EC₅₀, 48 ng/mL) and detected soluble EphA2 in TNBC cell-conditioned media. Serum analysis showed significantly higher EphA2 levels in TNBC patients compared with healthy controls (median 93.3 vs 25.6 ng/mL). In this exploratory cohort, ROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.912 (95% CI, 0.862-0.962), with a sensitivity of 95.0% (95% CI, 86.3-98.6%) and a specificity of 78.3% (95% CI, 66.4-86.9%), and higher levels were associated with lymph node metastasis and higher histological grade. Functionally, recombinant EphA2-P328 promoted TNBC-cell migration and induced cell context-dependent changes in EMT-associated markers in vitro. Collectively, these findings support the soluble N-terminal EphA2 fragment as a candidate serum biomarker and an in vitro modulator of TNBC cell migration, warranting validation in larger independent cohorts and further mechanistic investigation.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103075.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the clinical, pathological, and immune characteristics of macrotrabecular hepatocellular carcinoma (MT-HCC) to identify distinct features, evaluate prognostic significance, and explore potential therapeutic targets for MT-HCC. A total of 83 MT-HCC and 111 CV-HCC patients who underwent liver resection were included. Clinicopathological data were analyzed using statistical methods. Among these cases, immunohistochemical (IHC) staining was performed on 48 cases of massive trabecular hepatocellular carcinoma to evaluate the distribution of immune cells across different tumor regions. The Friedman test, Spearman's correlation analysis, Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, and Cox regression analysis were used to examine the relationships between immune infiltration characteristics and prognosis. MT-HCC exhibited more aggressive features, such as higher serum AFP levels (68% vs. 21%, p < 0.001), larger tumor size (7.65 cm vs. 4.47 cm, p < 0.001), and a higher frequency of vascular invasion (22% vs. 4%, p < 0.001), satellite nodules (41%vs. 16%, p < 0.001), and tumor necrosis (84% vs. 47%, p < 0.001). Survival analysis showed worse overall survival and higher recurrence rates in MT-HCC. The immune microenvironment displayed a typical "immune desert" phenotype, characterized by the spatial distribution of adaptive immune cells: sparse distribution within the tumor, enrichment at tumor margins, and enrichment adjacent to the tumor. In MT‑HCC, PD‑L1 expression was extremely low across all three tumor regions, whereas CTLA‑4 showed specific high expression at the tumor margins. Intratumoral CD8⁺ T cells exhibited a significant positive correlation with PD‑1 and CTLA‑4 (r = 0.701, P < 0.001), suggesting the dual exhaustion state of intratumoral T cells. Multivariate analysis identified cross‑regional FOXP3⁺ Treg infiltration, maximum tumor diameter, and macrovascular invasion as independent risk factors for overall survival. Conversely, peritumoral CD4⁺ T cells served as protective immune markers and were associated with reduced mortality risk in patients. The findings suggest that MT-HCC possesses invasive clinical characteristics and exhibits distinctive spatial immune heterogeneity, where immune cell distribution plays a critical role in prognosis. Targeting specific immune cell populations may offer new therapeutic strategies for MT-HCC and improve patient outcomes.

doi:10.1016/j.tranon.2026.103078.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is molecularly, cellularly and spatially heterogeneous, and current staging systems and biomarkers incompletely explain prognosis and treatment response. This study integrated transcriptomics, machine learning, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics and in vitro experiments to prioritize candidate CRC-associated markers and characterize their potential biological and clinical relevance. GSE44861 and GSE44076 from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and The Cancer Genome Atlas Colon Adenocarcinoma (TCGA-COAD) were used for differential expression, consensus differentially expressed gene (DEG) identification and functional enrichment analyses. Four machine-learning algorithms were applied for feature selection. Candidate genes were prioritized by differential expression, model importance and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) performance. GSE231559 single-cell data and spatial transcriptomics characterized the cellular source, pseudotime dynamics and spatial distribution of the core gene. TCGA-COAD assessed prognosis, pathways and computationally predicted drug sensitivity. Western blotting, Transwell and MTT assays were used for experimental validation, and public immunohistochemistry images from the Human Protein Atlas were used as supplementary protein-expression evidence. We identified 544 consensus DEGs enriched in leukocyte migration, chemotaxis, extracellular matrix organization, cytokine activity and metabolic pathways. Six genes were jointly selected: CLDN1, CDH3, KRT24, MMP7, NEBL and SCGN. CLDN1 was markedly upregulated and showed the highest tumour-versus-normal discrimination among the six candidates in the TCGA-COAD cohort. Single-cell and spatial analyses showed that CLDN1 was mainly expressed in CRC epithelial cells, displayed increasing expression across the inferred pseudotime ordering, and was enriched in malignant and mixed regions. In the TCGA-COAD cohort, high CLDN1 expression was associated with poorer overall survival and pathways involving the cell cycle, proteasome, autophagy, Hippo, ErbB and CRC. CLDN1 manipulation altered CRC-cell invasion and in vitro response to Nutlin-3a (-). These findings support CLDN1 as a candidate CRC-associated marker linked to malignant epithelial-cell states, tumour-associated spatial heterogeneity, invasive phenotype and Nutlin-3a (-) response. Further independent and prospective validation is required to determine its clinical diagnostic, prognostic and treatment-response relevance.

doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2026.103111.abstract: Immunotherapy for colorectal cancer (CRC) remains limited due to the inherently low tumor immunogenicity and the profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Herein, capitalizing on the metabolic traits and anatomical accessibility of CRC, we propose a broadly applicable oral strategy based on metabolically engineered bacteria (EcN-HlpA-CGL [EHC]) for CRC immunotherapy. Mechanistically, cystathionine γ-lyase expressed by EHC disrupts redox homeostasis, triggering ferroptosis in CRC cells and thereby enhancing tumor immunogenicity. Concurrently, the intrinsic adjuvant activity of the bacteria amplifies the cancer-immunity cycle driven by immunogenic cell death and remodels the immunosuppressive TME. In vivo studies demonstrate that this orally delivered engineered bacterial platform not only suppresses the growth of orthotopic CRC tumors but also inhibits metastatic progression, indicating the induction of a potent systemic immune response. Immune profiling confirms robust systemic and gut mucosal immune activation following oral administration. Collectively, this oral metabolically engineered bacterial platform is precisely tailored to the features of CRC and offers a safe and effective immunotherapeutic strategy for this malignancy.

doi:10.1016/j.xgen.2026.101391.abstract: The importance of gene-environment interactions (G × E) for complex human traits is heavily debated. Recently, biobank-based genome-wide association studies (GWASs) have revealed many statistically significant G × E signals, though most lack clear evidence of biological significance. Here, we partly explain this discrepancy by showing that many G × E signals simplify to additive effects on a different phenotype scale, a classical concern that is currently underappreciated. Our results clearly distinguish G × sex effects on height, which vanish on the log scale, from G × sex effects on testosterone, where the log scale uncovers biologically meaningful female-specific effects. Across 32 phenotypes in UK Biobank, we find that scaling by a power transformation can explain 45% of polygenic score (PGS) × sex interactions and that simple log transformation can explain 23%, with similar results for other environments. We also show that the phenotype scale can substantially impact GWAS discovery and the construction and evaluation of polygenic scores. Finally, we provide a set of guidelines to consider and choose phenotype scales in modern genetic studies.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.004.abstract: Metformin is a potential anticancer agent; however, evidence of benefit in endometrial neoplasia is limited. We evaluated whether adding metformin improved the outcomes of progestin-based fertility-sparing treatment. In this multicenter, open-label, randomized, phase IIb trial using blinded central adjudication, women aged 18-42years with an institutional diagnosis of atypical endometrial hyperplasia (AEH) or presumed stage IA grade 1 endometrioid carcinoma were assigned (1:1:1) to medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) alone, MPA plus metformin 750mg/day, or MPA plus metformin 1500mg/day. Central pathological review reclassified baseline specimens according to the 2020 World Health Organization criteria and adjudicated remission and recurrence. The primary endpoint was the 3-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) rate from treatment initiation. Secondary endpoints included remission, pregnancy outcomes, and safety. Analysis included 154 patients. Median body mass index was 24.3 (range, 15.6-57.1) kg/m2. The Kaplan-Meier estimates of the 3-year RFS rate were 44.7% with MPA alone and 44.5% with the pooled metformin groups. The prespecified log-rank test showed no significant difference (P=0.825). Remission rates were 54.0%, 58.8%, and 50.9% in the MPA-alone, metformin 750mg, and metformin 1500mg groups, respectively. Among the 57 women who attempted to conceive, pregnancy occurred in 36.8%, 57.9%, and 42.1%, and live birth in 31.6%, 52.6%, and 31.6%, respectively. Metformin increased gastrointestinal adverse events and was associated with less MPA-associated weight gain; no new safety signals emerged. Adding metformin to MPA did not improve RFS or remission rates, suggesting limited benefit in fertility-sparing treatment of endometrial neoplasia.

doi:10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.10.005.abstract: As immunotherapy (IO) is increasingly utilized for treatment of endometrial cancer (EC) and cervical cancer (CC), optimal treatment strategies after IO remains poorly defined. We evaluated clinical outcomes, treatment patterns, toxicity, and survival among patients with recurrent EC and CC who received IO after prior IO. An Institutional Review Board approved, single-institution retrospective cohort study was conducted among patients with recurrent EC or CC treated with subsequent IO between January 1, 2017, and January 1, 2025. Patients were included if they received at least one dose of IO after prior IO. Clinical characteristics, immune-related adverse events, response, progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) were abstracted from the electronic medical record. Of fifty eligible patients, 36 had EC and 14 had CC. Pembrolizumab was the most common first IO agent in both cohorts. Second IO regimens differed by disease site, with pembrolizumab plus lenvatinib most common in EC and pembrolizumab alone most common in CC. Following second IO exposure, objective response rate was 27.8% for EC and 14.3% for CC, while disease control rate was 55.6% and 64.3%, respectively. Median PFS with second IO exposure was 8.1 months in EC and 9.7 months in CC. Grade 3/4 immune-related adverse events occurred in 20.0% during second IO. IO retreatment demonstrated clinical activity in selected patients with recurrent EC and CC after prior IO, with disease control achieved in more than half of patients. Prospective studies are needed to define optimal patient selection and post-IO treatments.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03159-y.abstract: Abstract CD24 is highly expressed in aggressive B-cell malignancies and represents a novel immunologic vulnerability to overcome resistance to CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. We developed a CD24 × CD3 bispecific antibody (CD24 BsAb) and CXCR3-armed CD24 CAR-T cells, both exhibiting potent antitumor activity in lymphoma and leukemia models. CD24 BsAb and CD24 CAR-T overcome CD19 CAR-T resistance driven by antigen loss and apoptosis defects in vitro and in vivo. Beyond direct cytotoxicity, CD24-targeted T cells reprogram macrophages toward an M1-like phenotype and enhance phagocytic clearance. We further engineered a dual-specific, dual-functional CD19 CAR-T that secretes a CD24 bispecific T-cell engager (CD24 BiTE), enabling simultaneous targeting of CD19 and CD24 to address tumor heterogeneity and achieve superior efficacy. Collectively, our study demonstrates that CD24-directed adoptive T-cell therapies are warranted for B-cell malignancies through robust induction of both innate and adaptive immune responses.

doi:10.1038/s41375-026-03160-5.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells are highly dependent on mitochondrial activity for survival, with this metabolic reliance driven in part by BCL-2, which is therapeutically targeted by venetoclax-based therapies. The regulation of mitochondrial dynamics in leukemic cells is therefore essential for maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis. However, the mechanisms that enable selective degradation of damaged mitochondria (mitophagy) are still poorly understood in AML. In this study, we sought to elucidate the role of PTEN-induced putative kinase 1 (PINK1), a key sensor of mitochondrial stress, in regulating mitophagy in leukemic cells. Our results identified PINK1 as a central modulator of mitophagy. Genetic depletion of PINK1 reduced both basal and stress-induced mitophagy, leading to mitochondria accumulation and functional impairment. Additionally, we discovered that PINK1 stabilization during mitochondrial stress is regulated by Prohibitin 2 (PHB2), and that depletion or inhibition of PHB2 mirrored the biological effects of PINK1 loss. Notably, both genetic depletion of PINK1 or PHB2, as well as pharmacological inhibition of PHB2, significantly increased AML cell sensitivity to venetoclax both in vitro and in vivo. Together, these findings highlight the potential of targeting the PHB2/PINK1 signalling pathway to improve the efficacy of venetoclax-based therapies in AML by disrupting the mitophagy process.

doi:10.1038/s41388-024-02996-4.abstract: Abstract Colorectal cancer (CRC) has a high degree of heterogeneity and identifying the genetic information of individual tumor cells could help enhance our understanding of tumor biology and uncover potential therapeutic targets for CRC. In this study, we identified LPCAT2+ tumor cell populations with less malignancy than LPCAT2- tumor cells in human and mouse CRC tissues using scRNA-seq. Combining in vitro and in vivo experiments, we found that LPCAT2 could inhibit the proliferation of CRC cells by inducing ferroptosis. Mechanistically, LPCAT2 arrested PRMT1 in cytoplasm of CRC cells via regulating acetylation of PRMT1 at the K145 site. In turn, PRMT1 enhanced SLC7A11 promoter activity. Thus, LPCAT2 attenuated the positive regulatory effect of PRMT1 on SLC7A11 promoter. Notably, SLC7A11 acts as a ferroptosis regulator. Furthermore, in LPCAT2 knockout mice (LPCAT2−/−) colon cancer model, we found that LPCAT2−/− mice exhibited more severe lesions, while PRMT1 or SLC7A11 inhibitors delayed the progression. Altogether, we elucidated that LPCAT2 suppresses SLC7A11 expression by inhibiting PRMT1 nuclear translocation, thereby inducing ferroptosis in CRC cells. Moreover, inhibitors of the PRMT1/SLC7A11 axis could delay tumor progression in CRC with low LPCAT2 expression, making it a potentially effective treatment for CRC.

doi:10.1038/s41388-026-04008-z.abstract: T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains (TIGIT) is a key inhibitory receptor on cytotoxic lymphocytes, yet the mechanisms governing its context-dependent upregulation in tumors remain poorly defined. Here, we identify tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα) signaling as an upstream driver of TIGIT expression. Integrated analyses of patient transcriptomic datasets revealed a consistent positive association between TNFα pathway activity and TIGIT expression across multiple cancer types, with strong concordance in melanoma and prognostic relevance in kidney renal clear cell carcinoma. Mechanistically, TNFα directly induced TIGIT expression in natural killer cells via TNFR2 signaling, increasing chromatin accessibility at distal TIGIT enhancers and promoting NF-κB and AP-1 recruitment together with BRD4 and P300. Functionally, combined anti-TNFα and anti-TIGIT treatment suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival more effectively than either monotherapy in murine melanoma and colon cancer models. These findings define a TNFα-TNFR2-enhancer axis controlling TIGIT expression and provide a mechanistic rationale for dual TNFα and TIGIT targeting in inflamed tumors.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02786-2.abstract: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is an interstitial lung disease that advances over time and is ultimately life-threatening. Despite advances in antifibrotic therapies, disease progression remains largely unavoidable, highlighting the necessity for advancing mechanistic research and identifying new therapeutic options. Bone morphogenetic protein receptor 2 (BMPR2) is a key receptor for BMP signaling and exerts potent antifibrotic role in lung fibrosis; however, the molecular mechanisms regulating BMPR2 protein stability in fibrotic lungs remain poorly understood. In this study, we identify that the E3 ubiquitin ligase neural precursor cell expressed developmentally downregulated protein 4-like (Nedd4L) as a critical regulator of BMPR2 stability in lung fibroblasts. BMPR2 levels are markedly reduced in lung fibroblasts derived from patients with IPF and in lung tissues from experimental lung fibrosis models. Mechanically, elevated lipid peroxidation in fibrotic lungs induces K48-linked ubiquitination of BMPR2, leading to its degradation and attenuation of BMPs-induced Smad1/5 phosphorylation. Notably, Nedd4L overexpression counteracts lipid peroxidation-induced BMPR2 degradation and promotes BMPs/BMPR2 signaling by shifting BMPR2 ubiquitination toward a stabilizing K63-linked polyubiquitination in lung fibroblasts. We further show that Nedd4L is regulated through threonine phosphorylated by Raf1 kinase in response to increased lipid peroxidation. In vivo, fibroblast-Nedd4L-deficient mice exacerbates experimental lung fibrosis, which is significantly alleviated by BMPR2 overexpression. Collectively, our findings reveal a previously unrecoganized regulatory mechanism of BMPR2 degradation in fibrotic lungs and indicate that stabilizing BMPR2 in lung fibroblasts may represent a promising approach for the treatment of lung fibrosis.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02840-z.abstract: Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), constituting a major family of cell-surface transmembrane receptors, are essential for intracellular tyrosine phosphorylation and signal transduction. RTK signaling is crucial for cellular fate regulation and tissue homeostasis, and its disruption is linked to numerous diseases. Herein, we present a comprehensive review of signaling pathways involving RTKs, with a focus on their signal transduction mechanisms and key components, along with their interactions with major signaling cascades such as G protein-coupled receptors, Wnt, and transforming growth factor β pathways. We also elucidate the multidimensional roles of RTKs in cancer development and progression, highlighting their key effects on cancer stem cell maintenance, tumor microenvironment modulation, and other factors. Furthermore, we systematically summarize the roles of RTKs in noncancerous diseases, including cardiovascular disorders, neurodegenerative diseases, metabolic syndrome, autoimmune conditions, and fibrotic disorders. We then examine current RTK-targeted therapeutics, including small-molecule inhibitors and monoclonal antibodies, for the treatment of various cancers. Finally, novel therapeutic strategies, along with the challenges associated with their development and application, are discussed. In summary, this review will enhance the understanding of the mechanistic aspects of RTK signaling in major disease pathways and provide a detailed overview of recent advancements in targeted therapeutic interventions.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02869-0.abstract: Diabetic foot infection (DFI) significantly increases the risks of hospitalization and amputation, with biofilm infections caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and carbapenem-resistant Escherichia coli (CREC) being key drivers of treatment failure. Here, we analyzed MRSA/CREC biofilm-infected ulcer tissues from patients using proteomics and metabolomics. Compared with nonhealing tissues, healed tissues exhibit activation of low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR)-mediated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) endocytosis and increased free fatty acid production; thus, we hypothesize a potential countermeasure against biofilms. However, the oxidative instability of free fatty acids limits their therapeutic use. Building on our findings demonstrating the potent anti-MRSA/CREC activity of rhein and its synergy with Ag⁺, we developed an injectable hydrogel for sustained codelivery of both agents. This formulation outperforms Ag⁺ monotherapy, accelerating wound closure in biofilm-infected diabetic wounds. Mechanistically, rhein binds to LDLR, upregulates its expression, and enhances the LDL-C endocytosis pathway in vascular endothelial cells to generate more free fatty acids. Among these, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) is identified as the most critical free fatty acid that promotes healing, as it inhibits biofilm formation and synergizes with Ag⁺ to exert antibacterial and pro-healing effects. In summary, this study identifies endogenous host lipid metabolites as "metabolic antibiotics" and establishes a synergistic therapeutic strategy that concurrently suppresses biofilm formation, inhibits planktonic bacteria, alleviates inflammation, and promotes tissue repair in drug-resistant biofilm-infected diabetic wounds.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02886-z.abstract: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder with a high unmet need, particularly for treatment-resistant tunnels. Integrated multiomics analysis revealed that HS tunnels are spatially organized, self-amplifying inflammatory circuits driven by synergistic IL-17/IL-36γ activation of a unique keratinocyte subset, which activates neutrophils and inflammatory fibroblasts. This mechanistic insight coupled with spatial coenrichment of IL-17A and IL-36R provided the rationale for HB0043, a bispecific antibody that leverages IL-36R binding to locally dual-block both cytokines. HB0043 outperformed IL-17A/IL-17F bispecific and parental antibodies in vitro. In a proof-of-concept trial (NCT06895499) involving severe, tunnel-dominant Hurley Stage III HS patients, HB0043 induced promising clinical responses. At week 16, patients demonstrated an 82.13% mean percentage reduction from baseline in total abscess and inflammatory nodule count (AN), while 100% and 80% achieved HiSCR50 and HiSCR75, respectively, alongside ultrasound-confirmed tunnel regression and no major short-term safety signals. Longitudinal plasma proteomics showed suppressed inflammation and restored metabolic homeostasis. By tracking these dynamic systemic alterations alongside local structural changes, our multiomics approach bridges the gap between focal tissue lesions and global systemic disease activity. These findings establish dual blockade of IL-17A and IL-36R as a potential therapeutic strategy, offering a targeted strategy for recalcitrant disease that effectively improves the anatomical therapeutic barriers of advanced hidradenitis suppurativa, thereby demonstrating that cross-pathway bispecific antibodies can dismantle complex inflammatory circuits to achieve structural tissue healing where traditional monotherapies consistently fail.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02905-z.abstract: Free radicals are highly reactive molecules that are ubiquitous in aerobic organisms. Among them, oxyradicals like superoxide (O2•-), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), and hydroxyl radical (OH•), collectively called reactive oxygen species (ROS), have drawn the most attention from researchers in the life sciences and biomedicine because these are the byproducts of aerobic metabolism that are responsible for the oxidative burden experienced by mammalian cells. However, it is now known this oxidative stress only occurs when cells are overwhelmed with ROS and that controlled bursts in free radical production orchestrate signaling pathways essential for organismal health. ROS like H2O2 is now a well-characterized second messenger that transmits signals through protein sulfur switches to activate cell stress coping strategies and induce pathways involved in proliferation, growth, and development. Additionally, defects in these redox systems have been found to be related to many diseases, which has led to the development of new therapeutic modalities to treat and prevent various disorders. In this Review, I will discuss the history of the Redox Biology and Medicine field and how these findings led to the discovery of the three known H2O2 signaling pathways that occur in cells; the floodgate, redox relay, and S-glutathionylation signaling mechanisms. Using this information and new findings generated with advanced molecular biology techniques that have quantified the cellular distance traveled by H2O2, I then propose that cells use these three redox signaling mechanisms to sense and transmit H2O2 signals over short and long cellular distances in mammalian cells.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02931-x.abstract: Pain is a multifaceted sensory and emotional experience that profoundly affects human health and quality of life. It functions as a double-edged sword: while acute pain serves as a protective warning signal, chronic pain compromises physiological and psychological well-being. Pain is now widely regarded as the "fifth vital sign," and given its rising prevalence and substantial global burden, chronic pain may also be considered a major chronic disease entity. Accordingly, elucidating the neural and molecular underpinnings of pain and developing effective analgesic strategies remain urgent priorities. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the molecular and neural circuit mechanisms that govern pain. At the molecular level, ion channels, diverse receptor systems, and intricate signaling pathways play central roles in the transduction and modulation of nociceptive signals. At the circuit level, pain processing involves ascending pathways, descending modulatory systems, and distributed brain regions that collectively encode the sensory and affective dimensions of pain. Building on these mechanistic insights, we discuss current therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions, as well as emerging approaches such as gene therapy, stem cell-based therapies and neuromodulation. Despite notable progress, several challenges remain, including the adverse effects associated with existing analgesics and an incomplete understanding of visceral pain mechanisms. Future research should prioritize the integration of multiomics approaches, advanced neural circuit mapping technologies, and artificial intelligence to refine mechanistic insights and enable the development of more precise and effective pain management strategies.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02952-6.abstract: Pulmonary nodules are highly prevalent in adult human populations, with a substantial proportion representing dormant cancerous lesions. We hypothesized that these pulmonary dormant cancers debilitate in growth owing to the lack of an angiogenic switch in tumors. In this study, we comprehensively investigated the hypothesis that specific pathological triggers can activate this angiogenic switch utilizing severe acute respiratory coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection-induced hypoxia as a primary physiological stimulus. Our findings provide compelling experimental evidence demonstrating that SARS-CoV-2 infection induces profound pulmonary hypoxia and severe tissue inflammation in animal models. This microenvironmental disruption markedly upregulates the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2) within lung tissues. The resulting hyperactivation of the downstream VEGF-VEGFR2 signaling pathway effectively drives robust pulmonary neovascularization, a phenomenon frequently documented in clinical observations of COVID-19 patients. Furthermore, employing an established experimental tumor model, we demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 infection directly accelerates tumor outgrowth via this specific VEGF angiogenesis-dependent cascade. Crucially, the targeted administration of a neutralizing antibody to block VEGF significantly suppressed tumor progression and outgrowth in SARS-CoV-2-infected, tumor-bearing animals. Our data show that the COVID-19-induced hypoxia-VEGF-angiogenesis axis serves as one of the mechanisms for initiating tumor outgrowth in pulmonary tissues.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02964-2.abstract: Acne vulgaris is a widespread chronic inflammatory skin condition particularly affecting the pilosebaceous unit, with its pathogenesis intricately linked to excessive sebum production, abnormal follicular keratinization, overcolonization by Cutibacterium acnes (C. acnes), and dysregulated host immune responses. Beyond its dermatological manifestations, the disorder is frequently associated with psychological comorbidities such as anxiety and depression, significantly impacting patients' quality of life. A genetic predisposition is evident, with associated polymorphisms involving pathways related to sebaceous gland activity, inflammatory regulation, and hormonal metabolism. Interactions among immune cells, including macrophages and dendritic cells, along with underlying molecular mechanisms, further contribute to its pathogenesis. Conventional acne treatments face challenges such as increasing antibiotic resistance and limited patient adherence. As a result, clinical research and practice are increasingly focusing on targeted, mechanism-based precision strategies. Recent advances in targeted biologics and vaccines directed against C. acnes have demonstrated promise in clinical studies, offering new avenues for acne management. This review provides a systematic overview of the epidemiology, risk factors, diagnostic classifications, and comorbidities associated with acne, with a particular focus on contemporary insights into its immunopathogenesis and molecular mechanisms. Additionally, it synthesizes current treatment modalities and explores emerging directions, such as acne vaccines and biologics, to serve as a reference for further mechanistic investigation and therapeutic advancement.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-02984-y.abstract: Definitive chemoradiotherapy followed by immunotherapy consolidation is the current standard of care for limited-stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC). We conducted a randomized phase II trial (ChiCTR2000032275) to evaluate a camrelizumab-based induction-consolidation strategy in previously untreated patients with LS-SCLC. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive induction camrelizumab plus etoposide-platinum followed by concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT) and camrelizumab consolidation (camrelizumab group), or induction chemotherapy followed by concurrent CRT alone (cCRT group). The primary endpoint was the 1‑year progression‑free survival (PFS) rate. Secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR), PFS, overall survival (OS), and safety. Between November 2020 and April 2024, 41 patients were enrolled. At a median follow‑up of 32.1 months (interquartile range [IQR]: 26.4-38.7), ORR was 100% in the camrelizumab group and 83.3% in the cCRT group. The 1‑year PFS rates were 65.5% with camrelizumab versus 47.4% with cCRT (P = 0.029). Median PFS was 24.0 months versus 11.8 months, and median OS was not reached versus 23.9 months (P = 0.042). Exploratory biomarker analyses indicated that patients with lower baseline systemic inflammatory indices, including neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio <2.8 and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio <207.0, and those with a decline in lactate dehydrogenase at week 12 after CRT, derived greater benefit from camrelizumab. The OS benefit was also more evident in patients with Ki-67 ≤80%. Toxicities in the camrelizumab group were manageable, with a low incidence of severe immune-related adverse events (4.8%), and radiation pneumonitis rates were comparable between groups. Taken together, induction camrelizumab combined with chemotherapy, followed by CRT and camrelizumab consolidation, significantly improved survival outcomes in LS-SCLC, with a manageable safety profile, warranting further validation for this aggressive malignancy.

doi:10.1038/s41392-026-03103-7.abstract: Pulmonary nodules are increasingly detected by thoracic imaging and low-dose computed tomography-based lung cancer screening, but most are benign, transient, or indolent. Clinically, the key task is to distinguish nodules that require timely cancer-directed evaluation from those that can be safely observed. This review summarizes the classification, disease spectrum, risk assessment, early diagnosis, biomarkers, signaling mechanisms, translational models, and management of pulmonary nodules. We first distinguish imaging phenotypes and disease entities, then differentiate the individual-level models used to select candidates for lung cancer screening from the nodule-level models and structured reporting systems used after nodule detection. Low-dose computed tomography remains the foundation of screening and surveillance approaches, whereas magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography, contrast-enhanced computed tomography, nonsurgical biopsy, surgical diagnosis, and local therapies play more selective roles depending on the probability of malignancy and patient fitness. Noninvasive biomarkers, including circulating cellular, nucleic acid, methylation, protein, autoantibody, extracellular vesicle, and metabolic analytes, are most likely to serve as adjuncts to imaging and clinical risk assessment rather than as stand-alone diagnostic tests. Artificial intelligence may support detection, workflow efficiency, malignancy risk reclassification, invasiveness assessment, and multimodal integration, but its value depends on external validation, calibration, implementation, and prospective evidence of management benefit. Mechanistic studies of adenocarcinoma spectrum subsolid nodules have implicated the involvement of early oncogenic signaling, genomic instability, immune escape, stromal and vascular remodeling, and adaptive survival pathways. Translational models can support mechanistic and procedural research, but do not replicate real-world nodule management in patients. Overall, care for pulmonary nodules should be risk-adapted, longitudinal, multidisciplinary, and patient-centered.

doi:10.1038/s41416-020-01074-2.abstract: Abstract Background Recurrent and/or metastatic squamous cell carcinoma of head and neck (R/M SCCHN) is a common cancer with high recurrence and mortality. Current treatments have low response rates (RRs). Methods Fifty-three patients with R/M SCCHN received continuous oral buparlisib. In parallel, patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) were established in mice to evaluate resistance mechanisms and efficacy of buparlisib/cetuximab combination. Baseline and on-treatment tumour genomes and transcriptomes were sequenced. Based on the integrated clinical and PDX data, 11 patients with progression under buparlisib monotherapy were treated with a combination of buparlisib and cetuximab. Results For buparlisib monotherapy, disease control rate (DCR) was 49%, RR was 3% and median progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were 63 and 143 days, respectively. For combination therapy, DCR was 91%, RR was 18% and median PFS and OS were 111 and 206 days, respectively. Four PDX models were originated from patients enrolled in the current clinical trial. While buparlisib alone did not inhibit tumour growth, combination therapy achieved tumour inhibition in three of seven PDXs. Genes associated with apoptosis and cell-cycle arrest were expressed at higher levels with combination treatment than with buparlisib or cetuximab alone. Conclusions The buparlisib/cetuximab combination has significant promise as a treatment strategy for R/M SCCHN. Clinical Trial Registration NCT01527877.

doi:10.1038/s41416-026-03632-6.abstract: The hypoxic microenvironment, a common feature of solid tumors, is critically involved in driving cancer malignancy. This research focuses on elucidating the function of high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), induced by such hypoxia, in the context of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). We first profiled HMGB1 expression patterns in clinical OSCC specimens and evaluated their potential associations with clinicopathological parameters. To functionally characterize HMGB1, we conducted in vitro experiments utilizing silencing strategies. The impact of chronic cyclic hypoxia and HMGB1 depletion on key cellular processes-including proliferation, pyroptosis, and cell cycle-was systematically examined in OSCC cells. Signaling activity along the HMGB1/NLRP3/Caspase-1 axis was determined by immunoblotting. Furthermore, in vivo relevance was substantiated through murine xenograft models and a 4-NQO-induced carcinogenesis protocol. Analysis of clinical samples revealed that HMGB1 is constitutively upregulated in OSCC tissues. This elevated expression demonstrated a positive relationship with both increased tumor dimensions and lymph node metastasis. Subsequent Kaplan-Meier survival curves indicated that heightened HMGB1 levels are a marker for unfavorable patient outcomes. Furthermore, in cell culture systems, hypoxia treatment significantly elevates HMGB1 expression levels in OSCC cells. Knockdown of HMGB1 expression inhibits hypoxia-induced NLRP3, cleaved-caspase-1, and HIF-1α expression. Hypoxia treatment markedly enhanced OSCC cell proliferation, induced pyroptosis, and alleviated G2/M phase arrest, while HMGB1 knockdown reversed the pro-tumor effects of hypoxia. In vivo experiments demonstrated that HMGB1 knockdown inhibited tumor growth, whereas NLRP3 or caspase-1 deficiency delayed oral cancer progression. Our findings suggested that HMGB1 contributes to the progression of OSCC and has prognostic value. Targeting the hypoxia-induced HMGB1/NLRP3/Caspase-1 signaling axis may offer a viable therapeutic strategy.

doi:10.1038/s41416-026-03641-5.abstract: The Geriatric Core Dataset (G-CODE) was developed to standardise geriatric assessment (GA) in older adults with cancer. This study aimed to develop and externally validate a mortality prediction score based on the G-CODE at 6-month (main endpoint), 12- and 24-month (secondary endpoints), in older patients with cancer. Data came from two prospective French cohorts of cancer patients aged ≥70 referred for GA: the Elderly Cancer Patients (ELCAPA) cohort (training set) and the Geriatric Oncology Marseille (GOM) cohort (validation set). G-CODE items were evaluated using multivariate Cox regression analyses, with Akaike information criterion selection. Discrimination was assessed using time-dependent area under the receiver operator curve (tAUC) for 6-, 12-, and 24-month mortality. We included 950 and 766 patients in the training and validation sets (mean ± sd age: 83 ± 6 years/81 ± 6 years; men: 55%/59%; 6-month mortality: 27%/22%). The final G-CODE model highlighted five strong predictors of 6-month mortality: not having a caregiver, weight loss, comorbidities, an impaired 4-instrumental activities of daily living score, and an impaired timed-up-and-go test. The tAUCs of the model, including the G-CODE, age, cancer type, metastases, and treatment, were 82%, 78% and 80%. The final G-CODE score (range: 0-17) accurately predicts 6-, 12-, and 24-month mortality. NCT02884375 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

doi:10.1038/s41422-020-00451-z.abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma (GBM) is an incurable and highly heterogeneous brain tumor, originating from human neural stem/progenitor cells (hNSCs/hNPCs) years ahead of diagnosis. Despite extensive efforts to characterize hNSCs and end-stage GBM at bulk and single-cell levels, the de novo gliomagenic path from hNSCs is largely unknown due to technical difficulties in early-stage sampling and preclinical modeling. Here, we established two highly penetrant hNSC-derived malignant glioma models, which resemble the histopathology and transcriptional heterogeneity of human GBM. Integrating time-series analyses of whole-exome sequencing, bulk and single-cell RNA-seq, we reconstructed gliomagenic trajectories, and identified a persistent NSC-like population at all stages of tumorigenesis. Through trajectory analyses and lineage tracing, we showed that tumor progression is primarily driven by multi-step transcriptional reprogramming and fate-switches in the NSC-like cells, which sequentially generate malignant heterogeneity and induce tumor phenotype transitions. We further uncovered stage-specific oncogenic cascades, and among the candidate genes we functionally validated C1QL1 as a new glioma-promoting factor. Importantly, the neurogenic-to-gliogenic switch in NSC-like cells marks an early stage characterized by a burst of oncogenic alterations, during which transient AP-1 inhibition is sufficient to inhibit gliomagenesis. Together, our results reveal previously undercharacterized molecular dynamics and fate choices driving de novo gliomagenesis from hNSCs, and provide a blueprint for potential early-stage treatment/diagnosis for GBM.

doi:10.1038/s41422-020-0332-7.abstract: Abstract The interplay between the commensal microbiota and the mammalian immune system development and function includes multifold interactions in homeostasis and disease. The microbiome plays critical roles in the training and development of major components of the host’s innate and adaptive immune system, while the immune system orchestrates the maintenance of key features of host-microbe symbiosis. In a genetically susceptible host, imbalances in microbiota-immunity interactions under defined environmental contexts are believed to contribute to the pathogenesis of a multitude of immune-mediated disorders. Here, we review features of microbiome-immunity crosstalk and their roles in health and disease, while providing examples of molecular mechanisms orchestrating these interactions in the intestine and extra-intestinal organs. We highlight aspects of the current knowledge, challenges and limitations in achieving causal understanding of host immune-microbiome interactions, as well as their impact on immune-mediated diseases, and discuss how these insights may translate towards future development of microbiome-targeted therapeutic interventions.

doi:10.1038/s41422-020-0354-1.abstract: Abstract Lung injury and fibrosis represent the most significant outcomes of severe and acute lung disorders, including COVID-19. However, there are still no effective drugs to treat lung injury and fibrosis. In this study, we report the generation of clinical-grade human embryonic stem cells (hESCs)-derived immunity- and matrix-regulatory cells (IMRCs) produced under good manufacturing practice requirements, that can treat lung injury and fibrosis in vivo. We generate IMRCs by sequentially differentiating hESCs with serum-free reagents. IMRCs possess a unique gene expression profile distinct from that of umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells (UCMSCs), such as higher expression levels of proliferative, immunomodulatory and anti-fibrotic genes. Moreover, intravenous delivery of IMRCs inhibits both pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis in mouse models of lung injury, and significantly improves the survival rate of the recipient mice in a dose-dependent manner, likely through paracrine regulatory mechanisms. IMRCs are superior to both primary UCMSCs and the FDA-approved drug pirfenidone, with an excellent efficacy and safety profile in mice and monkeys. In light of public health crises involving pneumonia, acute lung injury and acute respiratory distress syndrome, our findings suggest that IMRCs are ready for clinical trials on lung disorders.

doi:10.1038/s41422-020-0375-9.abstract: Abstract Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a highly heterogeneous disease, and molecular subtyping may result in improved diagnostic precision and targeted therapies. Our previous study classified TNBCs into four subtypes with putative therapeutic targets. Here, we conducted the FUTURE trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03805399), a phase Ib/II subtyping-based and genomic biomarker-guided umbrella trial, to evaluate the efficacy of these targets. Patients with refractory metastatic TNBC were enrolled and stratified by TNBC subtypes and genomic biomarkers, and assigned to one of these seven arms: (A) pyrotinib with capecitabine, (B) androgen receptor inhibitor with CDK4/6 inhibitor, (C) anti PD-1 with nab-paclitaxel, (D) PARP inhibitor included, (E) and (F) anti-VEGFR included, or (G) mTOR inhibitor with nab-paclitaxel. The primary end point was the objective response rate (ORR). We enrolled 69 refractory metastatic TNBC patients with a median of three previous lines of therapy (range, 1–8). Objective response was achieved in 20 (29.0%, 95% confidence interval (CI): 18.7%–41.2%) of the 69 intention-to-treat (ITT) patients. Our results showed that immunotherapy (arm C), in particular, achieved the highest ORR (52.6%, 95% CI: 28.9%–75.6%) in the ITT population. Arm E demonstrated favorable ORR (26.1%, 95% CI: 10.2%–48.4% in the ITT population) but with more high grade (≥ 3) adverse events. Somatic mutations of TOP2A and CD8 immunohistochemical score may have the potential to predict immunotherapy response in the immunomodulatory subtype of TNBC. In conclusion, the phase Ib/II FUTURE trial suggested a new concept for TNBC treatment, demonstrating the clinical benefit of subtyping-based targeted therapy for refractory metastatic TNBC.

doi:10.1038/s41422-021-00606-6.abstract: Abstract Cancer arises from a multitude of disorders resulting in loss of differentiation and a stem cell-like phenotype characterized by uncontrolled growth. Polycomb Group (PcG) proteins are members of multiprotein complexes that are highly conserved throughout evolution. Historically, they have been described as essential for maintaining epigenetic cellular memory by locking homeotic genes in a transcriptionally repressed state. What was initially thought to be a function restricted to a few target genes, subsequently turned out to be of much broader relevance, since the main role of PcG complexes is to ensure a dynamically choregraphed spatio-temporal regulation of their numerous target genes during development. Their ability to modify chromatin landscapes and refine the expression of master genes controlling major switches in cellular decisions under physiological conditions is often misregulated in tumors. Surprisingly, their functional implication in the initiation and progression of cancer may be either dependent on Polycomb complexes, or specific for a subunit that acts independently of other PcG members. In this review, we describe how misregulated Polycomb proteins play a pleiotropic role in cancer by altering a broad spectrum of biological processes such as the proliferation-differentiation balance, metabolism and the immune response, all of which are crucial in tumor progression. We also illustrate how interfering with PcG functions can provide a powerful strategy to counter tumor progression.

doi:10.1038/s41422-022-00679-x.abstract: Abstract Somatostatin receptors (SSTRs) play versatile roles in inhibiting the secretion of multiple hormones such as growth hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone, and thus are considered as targets for treating multiple tumors. Despite great progress made in therapeutic development against this diverse receptor family, drugs that target SSTRs still show limited efficacy with preferential binding affinity and conspicuous side-effects. Here, we report five structures of SSTR2 and SSTR4 in different states, including two crystal structures of SSTR2 in complex with a selective peptide antagonist and a non-peptide agonist, respectively, a cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of G i1 -bound SSTR2 in the presence of the endogenous ligand SST-14, as well as two cryo-EM structures of G i1 -bound SSTR4 in complex with SST-14 and a small-molecule agonist J-2156, respectively. By comparison of the SSTR structures in different states, molecular mechanisms of agonism and antagonism were illustrated. Together with computational and functional analyses, the key determinants responsible for ligand recognition and selectivity of different SSTR subtypes and multiform binding modes of peptide and non-peptide ligands were identified. Insights gained in this study will help uncover ligand selectivity of various SSTRs and accelerate the development of new molecules with better efficacy by targeting SSTRs.

doi:10.1038/s41422-025-01107-6.abstract: Abstract Pyroptosis is a type of programmed necrosis triggered by the detection of pathogens or endogenous danger signals in the cytosol. Pyroptotic cells exhibit a swollen, enlarged morphology and ultimately undergo lysis, releasing their cytosolic contents — such as proteins, metabolites, and nucleic acids — into the extracellular space. These molecules can function as danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), triggering inflammation when detected by neighboring cells. Mechanistically, pyroptosis is initiated by members of the gasdermin protein family, which were identified a decade ago as pore-forming executors of cell death. Mammalian gasdermins consist of a cytotoxic N-terminal domain, a flexible linker, and a C-terminal regulatory domain that binds to and inhibits the N-terminus. Proteolytic cleavage within the linker releases the N-terminal domain, enabling it to target various cellular membranes, including nuclear, mitochondrial, and plasma membranes, where it forms large transmembrane pores. Gasdermin pores in the plasma membrane disrupt the electrochemical gradient, leading to water influx and cell swelling. Their formation also activates the membrane protein ninjurin-1 (NINJ1), which oligomerizes to drive complete plasma membrane rupture and the release of large DAMPs. Since their discovery as pore-forming proteins, gasdermins have been linked to pyroptosis not only in host defense but also in various pathological conditions. This review explores the history of pyroptosis, recent insights into gasdermin activation, the cellular consequences of pore formation, and the physiological roles of pyroptosis.

doi:10.1038/s41422-025-01180-x.abstract: Abstract Lineage plasticity, the ability of cells to transition to an alternative phenotype as a means for adaptation, is an increasingly recognized mechanism of tumor evolution and a driver of resistance to anticancer therapies. The most extensively described clinical settings impacted by such molecular phenomena include neuroendocrine transformation in androgen receptor-dependent prostate adenocarcinoma, and adenocarcinoma-to-neuroendocrine and adenocarcinoma-to-squamous transdifferentiation in epidermal growth factor receptor-driven lung adenocarcinoma, affecting 10%–20% of patients treated with targeted therapy. Recent analyses of human tumor samples and in vivo models of histological transformation have led to insights into the biology of lineage plasticity, including biomarkers predictive of high risk of transformation. However, no clinically available therapies aimed to prevent or revert plasticity are currently available. In the present review, we will provide a biological and therapeutic overview of the current understanding of common and divergent molecular drivers of neuroendocrine and squamous transdifferentiation in tumors from different origins, including descriptive analysis of previously known and recently described molecular events associated with histological transformation, and propose evidence-based alternative models of transdifferentiation. A clear definition of the commonalities and differences of transforming tumors in different organs and to different histological fates will be important to translate molecular findings to the clinical setting.

doi:10.1038/s41422-025-01203-7.abstract: Abstract Mitophagy, an evolutionarily conserved quality-control process, selectively removes damaged mitochondria to maintain cellular homeostasis. Recent advances in our understanding of the molecular machinery underlying mitophagy — from receptors and stress-responsive triggers to lysosomal degradation — illustrate its key role in maintaining mitochondrial integrity and adapting mitochondrial function to ever-changing physiological demands. In this review, we outline the fundamental mechanisms of mitophagy and discuss how dysregulation of this pathway disrupts mitochondrial function and metabolic balance, driving a wide range of disorders, including neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, metabolic, and immune-related diseases, as well as cancer. We explore the dual role of mitophagy as both a disease driver and a therapeutic target, highlighting the efforts and challenges of translating mechanistic insights into precision therapies. Targeting mitophagy to restore mitochondrial homeostasis may be at the center of a large range of translational opportunities for improving human health.
