doi:10.1038/s41587-022-01567-w.abstract: Abstract Monoclonal antibodies (Abs) that recognize major histocompatability complex (MHC)-presented tumor antigens in a manner similar to T cell receptors (TCRs) have great potential as cancer immunotherapeutics. However, isolation of ‘TCR-mimic’ (TCRm) Abs is laborious because Abs have not evolved the structurally nuanced peptide–MHC restriction of αβ-TCRs. Here, we present a strategy for rapid isolation of highly peptide-specific and ‘MHC-restricted’ Abs by re-engineering preselected Abs that engage peptide–MHC in a manner structurally similar to that of conventional αβ-TCRs. We created structure-based libraries focused on the peptide-interacting residues of TCRm Ab complementarity-determining region (CDR) loops, and rapidly generated MHC-restricted Abs to both mouse and human tumor antigens that specifically killed target cells when formatted as IgG, bispecific T cell engager (BiTE) and chimeric antigen receptor-T (CAR-T). Crystallographic analysis of one selected pMHC-restricted Ab revealed highly peptide-specific recognition, validating the engineering strategy. This approach can yield tumor antigen-specific antibodies in several weeks, potentially enabling rapid clinical translation.

doi:10.1038/s41587-026-03310-1.abstract: Targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) offer a nonviral approach for in vivo cell engineering but efficient programming of natural killer (NK) cells remains underexplored. Here we develop NK cell-targeted LNPs (NtLNPs) using engineered biparatopic NK cell ligands to drive receptor-specific uptake and mRNA delivery. Lead NtLNPs achieve up to ~80% NK cell transfection with minimal off-target effects in mice. Systemic delivery of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) mRNA using NtLNPs generates CAR NK cells in vivo. CD19-targeted CAR NKs completely deplete circulating B cells in healthy mice and CD3-targeted CAR NKs eliminate nearly all autoreactive T cells in an autoimmune hepatitis model, highlighting a potential advantage over CAR T therapies for T cell-driven disease. In solid tumors, NtLNPs targeting the inhibitory checkpoint NKG2A enhance antitumor efficacy by relieving Qa-1b-mediated immunosuppression. Lastly, we optimized NtLNPs for in vivo engineering of human CAR NK cells, enabling regression of two humanized hematologic malignancy models and establishing NtLNPs as a modular immunotherapy system.

doi:10.1038/s41588-023-01640-3.abstract: Abstract Recent studies on pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (pAML) have revealed pediatric-specific driver alterations, many of which are underrepresented in the current classification schemas. To comprehensively define the genomic landscape of pAML, we systematically categorized 887 pAML into 23 mutually distinct molecular categories, including new major entities such as UBTF or BCL11B , covering 91.4% of the cohort. These molecular categories were associated with unique expression profiles and mutational patterns. For instance, molecular categories characterized by specific HOXA or HOXB expression signatures showed distinct mutation patterns of RAS pathway genes, FLT3 or WT1 , suggesting shared biological mechanisms. We show that molecular categories were strongly associated with clinical outcomes using two independent cohorts, leading to the establishment of a new prognostic framework for pAML based on these updated molecular categories and minimal residual disease. Together, this comprehensive diagnostic and prognostic framework forms the basis for future classification of pAML and treatment strategies.

doi:10.1038/s41588-025-02158-6.abstract: Abstract High-risk neuroblastoma, a leading cause of pediatric cancer mortality, exhibits substantial intratumoral heterogeneity, contributing to therapeutic resistance. To understand tumor microenvironment evolution during therapy, we longitudinally profiled 22 patients with high-risk neuroblastoma before and after induction chemotherapy using single-nucleus RNA and ATAC sequencing and whole-genome sequencing. This revealed profound shifts in tumor and immune cell subpopulations after therapy and identified enhancer-driven transcriptional regulators of neuroblastoma neoplastic states. Poor outcome correlated with proliferative and metabolically active neoplastic states, whereas more differentiated neuronal-like states predicted better prognosis. Proportions of mesenchymal neoplastic cells increased after therapy and a high proportion correlated with a poorer chemotherapy response. Macrophages significantly expanded towards pro-angiogenic, immunosuppressive and metabolic phenotypes. We identified paracrine signaling networks and validated the HB-EGF–ERBB4 axis between macrophage and neoplastic subsets, which promoted tumor growth through the induction of ERK signaling. These findings collectively reveal intrinsic and extrinsic regulators of therapy response in high-risk neuroblastoma.

doi:10.1038/s41588-025-02307-x.abstract: Abstract Aberrant DNA methylation has been described in nearly all human cancers, yet its interplay with genomic alterations during tumor evolution is poorly understood. To explore this, we performed reduced representation bisulfite sequencing on 217 tumor and matched normal regions from 59 patients with non-small cell lung cancer from the TRACERx study to deconvolve tumor methylation. We developed two metrics for integrative evolutionary analysis with DNA and RNA sequencing data. Intratumoral methylation distance quantifies intratumor DNA methylation heterogeneity. M R /M N classifies genes based on the rate of hypermethylation at regulatory (M R ) versus nonregulatory (M N ) CpGs to identify driver genes exhibiting recurrent functional hypermethylation. We identified DNA methylation-linked dosage compensation of essential genes co-amplified with neighboring oncogenes. We propose two complementary mechanisms that converge for copy number alteration-affected chromatin to undergo the epigenetic equivalent of an allosteric activity transition. Hypermethylated driver genes under positive selection may open avenues for therapeutic stratification of patients.

doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02779-5.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive cancer characterized by profound desmoplasia and cellular heterogeneity, which cannot be fully resolved using traditional bulk sequencing approaches. To understand how this heterogeneity contributes to PDAC biology, we analyzed a large cohort of primary tumors (n = 62) profiled using single-cell RNA sequencing (443,451 single cells), including a subset of 11 tumors with matched spatial transcriptomics (53,236 spots), to map clonal, transcriptional and spatial diversity. Moreover, our sample set includes a unique cohort of matched samples from six tumors collected before and after treatment with chemotherapy. Our analysis revealed notable intratumoral heterogeneity, with multiple genetically distinct neoplastic clones coexisting within individual tumors. We observed clone-specific ligand-receptor programs that are modulated by genomic dosage: amplifications of ligands or receptors enriched corresponding interactions, while deletions suppressed them, with genetically encoded differences supported by spatial transcriptomics and multiplex immunofluorescence. Phylogenetic integration identified focal 8q24 (MYC) amplification as recurrently associated with classical-to-basal transitions occurring within tumor lineages at a frequency above chance; these transitions were accompanied by coordinated depletion of immune-response programs. Functional perturbation experiments in murine and primary human models showed that MYC knockdown reactivates classical transcriptional programs and restores immune-response pathways, supporting a role for MYC in maintaining a basal, immune-depleted state. Spatial analyses further revealed dispersed clones enriched for epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition activity and immune suppression, correlating with metastatic potential and colonization of lymph node niches. These dispersed clones shifted toward a basal phenotype, contributing to disease progression. Our findings highlight the critical role of clonal diversity, transcriptional plasticity and tumor microenvironment interactions in shaping human PDAC biology. This work provides a detailed view of the molecular and spatial heterogeneity of PDAC and offers potential avenues for therapeutic intervention targeting clonal evolution and the mechanisms driving metastasis.

doi:10.1038/s41588-026-02782-w.abstract: Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) contributes to cancer genome instability by enabling high-copy oncogene amplification and genetic intratumoral heterogeneity. Micronuclei (MNs) are common in chromosomally unstable cancers, yet their role in ecDNA-driven tumors remains unclear. Here we investigate how ecDNA damage, mitotic segregation and MN formation are linked. We find that ecDNAs are a major source of MNs following their damage, particularly under replication stress. Replication stress promotes mitotic ecDNA clustering, asymmetric inheritance, mis-segregation into MNs and reduced transcriptional output. Single-MN sequencing reveals that multiple distinct ecDNA species coalesce within individual MNs. Cells inheriting ecDNA+ MNs display impaired proliferative capacity and are more likely to undergo cell death. In patients with MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma, higher frequencies of ecDNA+ MNs at diagnosis are associated with improved overall survival. Together, these findings identify ecDNA mis-segregation as a mechanism that limits tumor fitness, highlighting mitotic ecDNA retention as a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

doi:10.1038/s41590-024-01830-z.abstract: Abstract The lung is constantly exposed to the outside world and optimal adaptation of immune responses is crucial for efficient pathogen clearance. However, mechanisms that lead to lung-associated macrophages’ functional and developmental adaptation remain elusive. To reveal such mechanisms, we developed a reductionist model of environmental intranasal β-glucan exposure, allowing for the detailed interrogation of molecular mechanisms of pulmonary macrophage adaptation. Employing single-cell transcriptomics, high-dimensional imaging and flow cytometric characterization paired with in vivo and ex vivo challenge models, we reveal that pulmonary low-grade inflammation results in the development of apolipoprotein E (ApoE)-dependent monocyte-derived alveolar macrophages (ApoE + CD11b + AMs). ApoE + CD11b + AMs expressed high levels of CD11b, ApoE, Gpnmb and Ccl6, were glycolytic, highly phagocytic and produced large amounts of interleukin-6 upon restimulation. Functional differences were cell intrinsic, and myeloid cell-specific ApoE ablation inhibited Ly6c + monocyte to ApoE + CD11b + AM differentiation dependent on macrophage colony-stimulating factor secretion, promoting ApoE + CD11b + AM cell death and thus impeding ApoE + CD11b + AM maintenance. In vivo, β-glucan-elicited ApoE + CD11b + AMs limited the bacterial burden of Legionella pneumophilia after infection and improved the disease outcome in vivo and ex vivo in a murine lung fibrosis model. Collectively these data identify ApoE + CD11b + AMs generated upon environmental cues, under the control of ApoE signaling, as an essential determinant for lung adaptation enhancing tissue resilience.

doi:10.1038/s41590-026-02675-4.abstract: The regulatory mechanisms that maintain colonic immune homeostasis remain incompletely understood. Here we show that genetic deletion of Zbtb44, a previously uncharacterized member of the ZBTB transcription factor family, leads to spontaneous colitis and rectal prolapse. Zbtb44-/- T cells expressed increased IFN-γ, a pro-inflammatory cytokine strongly associated with human inflammatory bowel disease. Mechanistically, Zbtb44 undergoes SUMOylation, which facilitates its interaction with a conserved SUMO-interacting motif in T-bet, enabling binding to the IFN-γ promoter and enhancer to restrain chronic IFN-γ production. Together, these findings demonstrate that Zbtb44 is a key regulator of colonic inflammation, a role that could be exploited therapeutically.

doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04614-0.abstract: Menopause reshapes female physiology, yet current understanding is limited by small longitudinal cohorts that characterize it as a gradual transition. Large-scale biomedical datasets remain underutilized because the final menstrual period (FMP) age is rarely recorded. Here we present a computational framework, inspired by astronomy, that reconstructs FMP-anchored trajectories from cross-sectional data by removing the blurring caused by variation in FMP age across individuals. Applying this to two independent cohorts totaling 300 million laboratory tests revealed a step-like physiological cliff at the FMP including endocrine, skeletal, hepatic, renal and lipid systems. These discontinuities are absent in male individuals, are concordant across populations and appear markedly attenuated by menopausal hormone therapy. Dysregulation began more than a decade before FMP. These findings support a systemic, quantifiable view of menopause and provide a generalizable strategy for recovering hidden biological trajectories applicable to other transitions such as puberty or disease progression.

doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04680-4.abstract: One-third of the world's 70 million people with epilepsy have seizures uncontrolled by medication, and implantable devices are a promising treatment. These devices can detect impending seizures, missed medication and impaired cognition, but, like most medical devices, they cannot share this information with patients in real time. This is a missed opportunity for devices to learn from clinical events and teach patients how their behaviors affect their health. Here we present a device platform that converses with patients to help them manage their epilepsy. The inpatient prototype links scalp and intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) to a secure, large language model-based artificial intelligence (AI) that communicates bidirectionally through a smartphone app. The AI processes biomarkers of sleep, medication, cognition and seizure probability, notifies patients of clinical events and trends, records symptoms and responses, and uses their feedback to retrain its seizure detector, reducing false alarms. We validated this platform in 13 patients who are undergoing video-EEG monitoring for epilepsy (scalp, n = 11; intracranial, n = 2). In a pseudoprospective simulation, seizure detectors improved precision from patient feedback alone, without expert intervention. We propose this system as a scalable, safeguarded platform for medical devices that can rapidly adapt to patient and provider needs across epilepsy and other medical conditions.

doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04689-9.abstract: Cancer cachexia is a wasting syndrome with outsized impact on morbidity and mortality, yet its drivers and systemic consequences remain poorly defined. In this study, we repurposed longitudinal clinicogenomic data from 52,236 patients with cancer profiled by MSK-IMPACT (2010-2024) at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center to define episode-resolved trajectories of consensus-defined cachectic weight loss and linked these events to outcomes, serology and tumor genotypes. Cachectic episodes clustered near periods of disease progression and were associated with inferior outcomes in nearly all cancer types. Across diverse malignancies, cachectic weight loss episodes exhibited a consistent serologic signature characterized by lower albumin and hemoglobin and higher levels of liver enzymes. Numerous somatic tumor genotypes, including TP53 mutation across several diseases, were also associated with more frequent onset of cachectic episodes. Motivated by these observations, we developed a multivariate model to predict impending risk of cachectic weight loss in patients with lung, colorectal and prostate cancer, validated in an independent, external cohort from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (n = 5,785). Routine clinicogenomic data are, therefore, a scalable resource for discovery in cancer cachexia.

doi:10.1038/s41592-025-02797-x.abstract: Abstract Post-translational modifications (PTMs) are critical regulators of protein function, and their disruption is a key mechanism by which missense variants contribute to disease. Accurate PTM site prediction using deep learning can help identify PTM-altering variants, but progress has been limited by the lack of large, high-quality training datasets. Here, we introduce PTMAtlas, a curated compendium of 397,524 PTM sites generated through systematic reprocessing of 241 public mass-spectrometry datasets, and DeepMVP, a deep learning framework trained on PTMAtlas to predict PTM sites for phosphorylation, acetylation, methylation, sumoylation, ubiquitination and N-glycosylation. DeepMVP substantially outperforms existing tools across all six PTM types. Its application to predicting PTM-altering missense variants shows strong concordance with experimental results, validated using literature-curated variants and cancer proteogenomic datasets. Together, PTMAtlas and DeepMVP provide a robust platform for PTM research and a scalable framework for assessing the functional consequences of coding variants through the lens of PTMs.

doi:10.1038/s41592-026-03255-y.abstract: Using near-infrared photoswitchable photochromic genetically encoded probes, differential photoacoustic tomography (PAT) enables deep-tissue imaging with high resolution and sensitivity; however, current bacteriophytochrome-based probes are bulky multidomain proteins exceeding 55 kDa, which constrains their use for designing PAT molecular reporters. Here we engineer rsmiRFPnano, a compact cyanobacteriochrome-derived photoswitchable PAT probe. With a molecular weight below 19 kDa, rsmiRFPnano efficiently incorporates biliverdin, exhibits high extinction coefficients in both photochromic states and demonstrates robust performance in live cells. We established rsmiRFPnano-based reporters for NF-κB and AP-1 pathways, which display low basal activity and strong activation-dependent responses. These reporters effectively visualized acute inflammation using noninvasive PAT in vivo, further validated through cellular-level spatial omics mapping. We then created photoswitchable nanobody probes, rsNIR-Fbs, stabilized upon antigen binding and rapidly degraded otherwise, enabling selective photoacoustic immuno-imaging of intracellular antigens in vivo. Together, these results establish rsmiRFPnano as an ultracompact and versatile platform for molecular PAT.

doi:10.1038/s41698-017-0023-0.abstract: Abstract Reduction-oxidation factor 1-apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease (Ref-1/APE1) is a critical node in tumor cells, both as a redox regulator of transcription factor activation and as part of the DNA damage response. As a redox signaling protein, Ref-1/APE1 enhances the transcriptional activity of STAT3, HIF-1α, nuclear factor kappa B, and other transcription factors to promote growth, migration, and survival in tumor cells as well as inflammation and angiogenesis in the tumor microenvironment. Ref-1/APE1 is activated in a variety of cancers, including prostate, colon, pancreatic, ovarian, lung and leukemias, leading to increased aggressiveness. Transcription factors downstream of Ref-1/APE1 are key contributors to many cancers, and Ref-1/APE1 redox signaling inhibition slows growth and progression in a number of tumor types. Ref-1/APE1 inhibition is also highly effective when paired with other drugs, including standard-of-care therapies and therapies targeting pathways affected by Ref-1/APE1 redox signaling. Additionally, Ref-1/APE1 plays a role in a variety of other indications, such as retinopathy, inflammation, and neuropathy. In this review, we discuss the functional consequences of activation of the Ref-1/APE1 node in cancer and other diseases, as well as potential therapies targeting Ref-1/APE1 and related pathways in relevant diseases. APX3330, a novel oral anticancer agent and the first drug to target Ref-1/APE1 for cancer is entering clinical trials and will be explored in various cancers and other diseases bringing bench discoveries to the clinic.

doi:10.1038/s41698-021-00211-1.abstract: Abstract Neuroendocrine prostate cancer is an aggressive variant of prostate cancer that may arise de novo or develop from pre-existing prostate adenocarcinoma as a mechanism of treatment resistance. The combined loss of tumor suppressors RB1, TP53, and PTEN are frequent in NEPC but also present in a subset of prostate adenocarcinomas. Most clinical and preclinical studies support a trans-differentiation process, whereby NEPC arises clonally from a prostate adenocarcinoma precursor during the course of treatment resistance. Here we highlight a case of NEPC with significant intra-patient heterogeneity observed across metastases. We further demonstrate how single-cell genomic analysis of circulating tumor cells combined with a phenotypic evaluation of cellular diversity can be considered as a window into tumor heterogeneity in patients with advanced prostate cancer.

doi:10.1038/s41698-023-00407-7.abstract: Abstract Cyclin dependent kinases (CDKs) are serine/threonine kinases that are proposed as promising candidate targets for cancer treatment. These proteins complexed with cyclins play a critical role in cell cycle progression. Most CDKs demonstrate substantially higher expression in cancer tissues compared with normal tissues and, according to the TCGA database, correlate with survival rate in multiple cancer types. Deregulation of CDK1 has been shown to be closely associated with tumorigenesis. CDK1 activation plays a critical role in a wide range of cancer types; and CDK1 phosphorylation of its many substrates greatly influences their function in tumorigenesis. Enrichment of CDK1 interacting proteins with Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis was conducted to demonstrate that the associated proteins participate in multiple oncogenic pathways. This abundance of evidence clearly supports CDK1 as a promising target for cancer therapy. A number of small molecules targeting CDK1 or multiple CDKs have been developed and evaluated in preclinical studies. Notably, some of these small molecules have also been subjected to human clinical trials. This review evaluates the mechanisms and implications of targeting CDK1 in tumorigenesis and cancer therapy.

doi:10.1038/s41698-023-00494-6.abstract: Abstract Accurate prognosis for cancer patients can provide critical information for optimizing treatment plans and improving life quality. Combining omics data and demographic/clinical information can offer a more comprehensive view of cancer prognosis than using omics or clinical data alone and can also reveal the underlying disease mechanisms at the molecular level. In this study, we developed and validated a deep learning framework to extract information from high-dimensional gene expression and miRNA expression data and conduct prognosis prediction for breast cancer and ovarian-cancer patients using multiple independent multi-omics datasets. Our model achieved significantly better prognosis prediction than the current machine learning and deep learning approaches in various settings. Moreover, an interpretation method was applied to tackle the “black-box” nature of deep neural networks and we identified features (i.e., genes, miRNA, demographic/clinical variables) that were important to distinguish predicted high- and low-risk patients. The significance of the identified features was partially supported by previous studies.

doi:10.1038/s41698-024-00564-3.abstract: Abstract In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), classical cancer stem cells (CSC) markers were shared by normal stem cells, targeting which may hinder hepatic regeneration and cause liver failure. Additionally, the spatial structure of CSC still remained elusive. To address these limitations, we undertook a comprehensive study combining single-cell data (56,022 cells from 20 samples) and spatial data (38,191 spots from eight samples) to obtain CSC signature and uncover its spatial structure. Utilizing the CytoTRACE algorithm, we discretely identified CSC, which displayed upregulated proliferation pathways regulated by HIF1A. A CSC signature of 107 genes was then developed using Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA). Notably, HCC patients with high CSC levels exhibited an accumulation of SPP1+ macrophages (Macro_SPP1) expressing metalloproteinases (MMP9, MMP12, and MMP7) regulated by HIF1A, suggesting a hypoxic tumor region connecting Macro_SPP1 and CSC. Both CSC and Macro_SPP1 correlated with worse prognosis and undesirable immunotherapy response. Spatial analysis revealed the co-location of CSC and Macro_SPP1, with CD8 T cells excluded from the tumor region. The co-location area and non-tumor area of boundary exhibited a high level of hypoxia, with the HAVRC2 checkpoint highly expressed. Within the co-location area, the SPP1 signaling pathway was most active in cell-cell communication, with SPP1-CD44 and SPP1-ITGA/ITGB identified as the main ligand-receptor pairs. This study successfully constructed a CSC signature and demonstrated the co-location of CSC and Macro_SPP1 in a hypoxic region that exacerbates the tumor microenvironment in HCC.

doi:10.1038/s41698-024-00630-w.abstract: Abstract Anti-PD(L)-1 inhibition combined with platinum doublet chemotherapy (Chemo-IO) has become the most frequently used standard of care regimen in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The negative impact of antibiotics on clinical outcomes prior to anti-PD(L)-1 inhibition monotherapy (IO) has been demonstrated in multiple studies, but the impact of antibiotic exposure prior to initiation of Chemo-IO is controversial. We assessed antibiotic exposures at two time windows: within 60 days prior to therapy (-60 d window) and within 60 days prior to therapy and 42 days after therapy (-60 + 42d window) in 2028 patients with advanced NSCLC treated with Chemo-IO and IO monotherapy focusing on objective response rate (ORR: rate of partial response and complete response), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). We also assessed impact of antibiotic exposure in an independent cohort of 53 patients. Univariable and multivariable analyses were conducted along with a meta-analysis from similar studies. For the -60 d window, in the Chemo-IO group ( N = 769), 183 (24%) patients received antibiotics. Antibiotic exposure was associated with worse ORR (27% vs 40%, p = 0.001), shorter PFS (3.9 months vs. 5.9 months, hazard ratio [HR] 1.35, 95%CI 1.1,1.6, p = 0.0012), as well as shorter OS (10 months vs. 15 months, HR 1.50, 95%CI 1.2,1.8, p = 0.00014). After adjusting for known prognostic factors in NSCLC, antibiotic exposure was independently associated with worse PFS (HR 1.39, 95%CI 1.35,1.7, p = 0.002) and OS (HR 1.61, 95%CI 1.28,2.03, p < 0.001). Similar results were obtained in the -60 + 42d window, and also in an independent cohort. In a meta-analysis of patients with NSCLC treated with Chemo-IO ( N = 4) or IO monotherapy ( N = 13 studies) antibiotic exposure before treatment was associated with worse OS among all patients ( n = 11,351) (HR 1.93, 95% CI 1.52, 2.45) and Chemo-IO-treated patients ( n = 1201) (HR 1.54, 95% CI 1.28, 1.84). Thus, antibiotics exposure prior to Chemo-IO is common and associated with worse outcomes, even after adjusting for other factors. These results highlight the need to implement antibiotic stewardship in routine oncology practice.

doi:10.1038/s41698-025-01011-7.abstract: Abstract Immune-checkpoint targeting Drug Conjugates (IDCs) are a novel class of therapeutics that combine an immune checkpoint-targeting moiety, a cleavable linker, and a cytotoxic payload. By integrating features and functions of antibody-drug conjugates and immunotherapy, IDCs represent a promising strategy to remodel the tumor microenvironment and enhance antitumor efficacy. Several IDCs targeting checkpoints such as PD-L1, B7-H3, and B7-H4 are in early-phase clinical trials. This review summarizes available data on IDC efficacy and toxicity in human. Although current evidence is limited, ongoing phase III trials and biomarker studies will clarify their optimal clinical role, including potential for tumor-agnostic use.

doi:10.1038/s41698-026-01715-4.abstract: Abstract Radiotherapy (RT) transforms tumors into in situ vaccines that trigger antitumor immunity. However, the relevant pathways remain largely unelucidated, limiting clinical translation. Herein, we developed a hybrid dry-lab/wet-lab approach integrating systems-level immune phenotypes following homogenous or spatially fractionated RT (SFRT) with transcriptomic profiling of irradiated tumors. By combining feature extraction with machine-learning, including multilayer perceptron modeling, we ranked predictors of immune infiltration and patient survivability for each RT type. RT induced coordinated upregulation of viral RNA-binding proteins (OASes and RIG I-like receptors) along with endogenous retrovirus (ERV) RNAs predominately 400–800 bp long, which may serve as their ligands. During abscopal responses, OASes and ERV transcripts were co-induced and shared between irradiated and distant tumors. SFRT triggered earlier activation of OAS signaling versus homogenous RT. Our findings highlight ERVs as underappreciated contributors to RT-induced antitumor immunity and their interactions with intratumoral cytosolic sensors as potential novel biomarkers in precision radio-oncology.

doi:10.1038/s41698-026-01730-5.abstract: Abstract Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is an aggressive malignancy of children, adolescents, and young adults driven by the EWS::FLI1 fusion oncoprotein with few effective treatment options in the relapsed or refractory setting. We validate six transmembrane epithelial antigen of the prostate 1 (STEAP1) as a fusion-regulated and clinically actionable surface antigen with broad expression across a series of primary EwS tumors. Analysis of EWS::FLI1 perturbation in EwS models demonstrated regulation of STEAP1 transcript and protein expression by oncogenic EWS::FLI1. Second-generation STEAP1 CAR T cells induced complete tumor regression in orthotopic models and exhibited dose-dependent activity in disseminated disease without evidence of antigen escape. Armoring STEAP1 CAR T cells with IL-18 further potentiated antitumor efficacy, achieving complete responses without overt toxicity in approximately 80% of mice at a five-fold lower cell dose where unarmored STEAP1 CAR T cells were ineffective. Notably, adoptive transfer of autologous STEAP1 CAR T cells is currently being evaluated in a first-in-human phase I/II clinical trial in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (NCT06236139) and the compelling preclinical data presented here support clinical translation to relapsed/refractory EwS.

doi:10.1038/s41698-026-01733-2.abstract: Abstract Patients with multiple myeloma accumulate hundreds of clinical documents over years of sequential therapy, and every treatment decision depends on synthesis across that history. Whether large language model–based systems can match expert agreement on this task, and where they fail, has not been established. On longitudinal records of 811 patients treated over 25 years (44,962 documents and 1,334,677 laboratory values), an agentic reasoning system guided by an indexed clinical skill library was compared against single-pass retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), iterative RAG, iterative RAG augmented with the same skill library, and full-context input on 469 expert-adjudicated patient-question pairs, with an exploratory cross-dataset evaluation on MIMIC-IV. The skill-guided agent exceeded the ceiling at which iterative RAG (75.7%) and full-context input (75.8%) converged, reaching 80.1% concordance, with its advantage widening on the most complex tasks (+11.2 percentage points) and longest records. Providing the same skill library to iterative RAG matched the agent in aggregate (79.0%) and on shorter records, whereas the agent retained a significant advantage on the longest records (+10.3 percentage points in the top decile, p = 0.017) and a numerical, non-significant advantage on the most complex questions (+5.4 percentage points). The aggregate error rate (12.2%) was comparable to expert disagreement (13.6%), but a higher proportion of system errors were clinically significant (57.8 versus 18.8%).

doi:10.1038/s43018-021-00292-8.abstract: Abstract Anti-PD-1 treatment has shown unprecedented clinical success in the treatment of non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we performed temporal single-cell RNA and paired T-cell receptor sequencing on 47 tumor biopsies from 36 patients with NSCLC following PD-1-based therapies. We observed increased levels of precursor exhausted T (Texp) cells in responsive tumors after treatment, characterized by low expression of coinhibitory molecules and high expression of GZMK . By contrast, nonresponsive tumors failed to accumulate Texp cells. Our data suggested that Texp cells were unlikely to be derived from the reinvigoration of terminally exhausted cells; instead, they were accumulated by (1) local expansion and (2) replenishment by peripheral T cells with both new and pre-existing clonotypes, a phenomenon we named clonal revival. Our study provides insights into mechanisms underlying PD-1-based therapies, implicating clonal revival and expansion of Texp cells as steps to improve NSCLC treatment.

doi:10.1038/s43018-022-00356-3.abstract: Abstract Inferring single-cell compositions and their contributions to global gene expression changes from bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) datasets is a major challenge in oncology. Here we develop Bayesian cell proportion reconstruction inferred using statistical marginalization (BayesPrism), a Bayesian method to predict cellular composition and gene expression in individual cell types from bulk RNA-seq, using patient-derived, scRNA-seq as prior information. We conduct integrative analyses in primary glioblastoma, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and skin cutaneous melanoma to correlate cell type composition with clinical outcomes across tumor types, and explore spatial heterogeneity in malignant and nonmalignant cell states. We refine current cancer subtypes using gene expression annotation after exclusion of confounding nonmalignant cells. Finally, we identify genes whose expression in malignant cells correlates with macrophage infiltration, T cells, fibroblasts and endothelial cells across multiple tumor types. Our work introduces a new lens to accurately infer cellular composition and expression in large cohorts of bulk RNA-seq data.

doi:10.1038/s43018-022-00463-1.abstract: Abstract The pancreatic tumor microenvironment drives deregulated nutrient availability. Accordingly, pancreatic cancer cells require metabolic adaptations to survive and proliferate. Pancreatic cancer subtypes have been characterized by transcriptional and functional differences, with subtypes reported to exist within the same tumor. However, it remains unclear if this diversity extends to metabolic programming. Here, using metabolomic profiling and functional interrogation of metabolic dependencies, we identify two distinct metabolic subclasses among neoplastic populations within individual human and mouse tumors. Furthermore, these populations are poised for metabolic cross-talk, and in examining this, we find an unexpected role for asparagine supporting proliferation during limited respiration. Constitutive GCN2 activation permits ATF4 signaling in one subtype, driving excess asparagine production. Asparagine release provides resistance during impaired respiration, enabling symbiosis. Functionally, availability of exogenous asparagine during limited respiration indirectly supports maintenance of aspartate pools, a rate-limiting biosynthetic precursor. Conversely, depletion of extracellular asparagine with PEG–asparaginase sensitizes tumors to mitochondrial targeting with phenformin.

doi:10.1038/s43018-022-00470-2.abstract: Abstract Solid tumors are generally characterized by an acidic tumor microenvironment (TME) that favors cancer progression, therapy resistance and immune evasion. By single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis in individuals with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), we reveal solute carrier family 4 member 4 (SLC4A4) as the most abundant bicarbonate transporter, predominantly expressed by epithelial ductal cells. Functionally, SLC4A4 inhibition in PDAC cancer cells mitigates the acidosis of the TME due to bicarbonate accumulation in the extracellular space and a decrease in lactate production by cancer cells as the result of reduced glycolysis. In PDAC-bearing mice, genetic or pharmacological SLC4A4 targeting improves T cell-mediated immune response and breaches macrophage-mediated immunosuppression, thus inhibiting tumor growth and metastases. In addition, Slc4a4 targeting in combination with immune checkpoint blockade is able to overcome immunotherapy resistance and prolong survival. Overall, our data propose SLC4A4 as a therapeutic target to unleash an antitumor immune response in PDAC.

doi:10.1038/s43018-022-00475-x.abstract: Abstract Recent longitudinal studies of glioblastoma (GBM) have demonstrated a lack of apparent selection pressure for specific DNA mutations in recurrent disease. Single-cell lineage tracing has shown that GBM cells possess a high degree of plasticity. Together this suggests that phenotype switching, as opposed to genetic evolution, may be the escape mechanism that explains the failure of precision therapies to date. We profiled 86 primary-recurrent patient-matched paired GBM specimens with single-nucleus RNA, single-cell open-chromatin, DNA and spatial transcriptomic/proteomic assays. We found that recurrent GBMs are characterized by a shift to a mesenchymal phenotype. We show that the mesenchymal state is mediated by activator protein 1. Increased T-cell abundance at recurrence was prognostic and correlated with hypermutation status. We identified tumor-supportive networks of paracrine and autocrine signals between GBM cells, nonmalignant neuroglia and immune cells. We present cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic targets and a single-cell multiomics atlas of GBM under therapy.

doi:10.1038/s43018-023-00548-5.abstract: Abstract One key barrier to improving efficacy of personalized cancer immunotherapies that are dependent on the tumor antigenic landscape remains patient stratification. Although patients with CD3 + CD8 + T cell-inflamed tumors typically show better response to immune checkpoint inhibitors, it is still unknown whether the immunopeptidome repertoire presented in highly inflamed and noninflamed tumors is substantially different. We surveyed 61 tumor regions and adjacent nonmalignant lung tissues from 8 patients with lung cancer and performed deep antigen discovery combining immunopeptidomics, genomics, bulk and spatial transcriptomics, and explored the heterogeneous expression and presentation of tumor (neo)antigens. In the present study, we associated diverse immune cell populations with the immunopeptidome and found a relatively higher frequency of predicted neoantigens located within HLA-I presentation hotspots in CD3 + CD8 + T cell-excluded tumors. We associated such neoantigens with immune recognition, supporting their involvement in immune editing. This could have implications for the choice of combination therapies tailored to the patient’s mutanome and immune microenvironment.

doi:10.1038/s43018-023-00566-3.abstract: Abstract The immune-specialized environment of the healthy brain is tightly regulated to prevent excessive neuroinflammation. However, after cancer development, a tissue-specific conflict between brain-preserving immune suppression and tumor-directed immune activation may ensue. To interrogate potential roles of T cells in this process, we profiled these cells from individuals with primary or metastatic brain cancers via integrated analyses on the single-cell and bulk population levels. Our analysis revealed similarities and differences in T cell biology between individuals, with the most pronounced differences observed in a subgroup of individuals with brain metastasis, characterized by accumulation of CXCL13 -expressing CD39 + potentially tumor-reactive T (pTRT) cells. In this subgroup, high pTRT cell abundance was comparable to that in primary lung cancer, whereas all other brain tumors had low levels, similar to primary breast cancer. These findings indicate that T cell-mediated tumor reactivity can occur in certain brain metastases and may inform stratification for treatment with immunotherapy.

doi:10.1038/s43018-023-00576-1.abstract: Abstract Precision medicine is critically dependent on better methods for diagnosing and staging disease and predicting drug response. Histopathology using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained tissue (not genomics) remains the primary diagnostic method in cancer. Recently developed highly multiplexed tissue imaging methods promise to enhance research studies and clinical practice with precise, spatially resolved single-cell data. Here, we describe the ‘Orion’ platform for collecting H&E and high-plex immunofluorescence images from the same cells in a whole-slide format suitable for diagnosis. Using a retrospective cohort of 74 colorectal cancer resections, we show that immunofluorescence and H&E images provide human experts and machine learning algorithms with complementary information that can be used to generate interpretable, multiplexed image-based models predictive of progression-free survival. Combining models of immune infiltration and tumor-intrinsic features achieves a 10- to 20-fold discrimination between rapid and slow (or no) progression, demonstrating the ability of multimodal tissue imaging to generate high-performance biomarkers.

doi:10.1038/s43018-024-00781-6.abstract: Abstract Despite tremendous progress in precision oncology, adaptive resistance mechanisms limit the long-term effectiveness of molecularly targeted agents. Here we evaluated the pharmacological profile of MTX-531 that was computationally designed to selectively target two key resistance drivers, epidermal growth factor receptor and phosphatidylinositol 3-OH kinase (PI3K). MTX-531 exhibits low-nanomolar potency against both targets with a high degree of specificity predicted by cocrystal structural analyses. MTX-531 monotherapy uniformly resulted in tumor regressions of squamous head and neck patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. The combination of MTX-531 with mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase or KRAS-G12C inhibitors led to durable regressions of BRAF -mutant or KRAS -mutant colorectal cancer PDX models, resulting in striking increases in median survival. MTX-531 is exceptionally well tolerated in mice and uniquely does not lead to the hyperglycemia commonly seen with PI3K inhibitors. Here, we show that MTX-531 acts as a weak agonist of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ, an attribute that likely mitigates hyperglycemia induced by PI3K inhibition. This unique feature of MTX-531 confers a favorable therapeutic index not typically seen with PI3K inhibitors.

doi:10.1038/s43018-025-00976-5.abstract: Abstract DNA methylation-based classification of (brain) tumors has emerged as a powerful and indispensable diagnostic technique. Initial implementations used methylation microarrays for data generation, while most current classifiers rely on a fixed methylation feature space. This makes them incompatible with other platforms, especially different flavors of DNA sequencing. Here, we describe crossNN, a neural network-based machine learning framework that can accurately classify tumors using sparse methylomes obtained on different platforms and with different epigenome coverage and sequencing depth. It outperforms other deep and conventional machine learning models regarding accuracy and computational requirements while still being explainable. We use crossNN to train a pan-cancer classifier that can discriminate more than 170 tumor types across all organ sites. Validation in more than 5,000 tumors profiled on different platforms, including nanopore and targeted bisulfite sequencing, demonstrates its robustness and scalability with 99.1% and 97.8% precision for the brain tumor and pan-cancer models, respectively.

doi:10.1053/j.gastro.2026.09.025.abstract: Chronic pancreatitis (CP) is a progressive fibroinflammatory disease with rising global incidence and no curative therapy. Gut dysbiosis has been associated with CP, but its causal contribution to disease pathogenesis remains unclear. We intended to identify specific pathogenic microbial species that promote CP and to delineate the underlying pathogenic mechanisms. Multi-omics analyses were used to identify key microbial signatures in CP patients and mice. Novel pathogenic Escherichia coli strains were isolated and bioengineered for functional studies. In vitro and in vivo assays, along with macrophage-specific knockout mice, adenoviral tools, and pharmacological inhibitors, were employed to dissect host-microbe mechanistic pathways. Therapeutic intervention included administering a screened next-generation probiotic. Metagenomic sequencing identified HtpG-high-expressing E. coli (HHEC) enrichment as a dominant microbial signature in CP patients. Prevention of HHEC adherence and colonization alleviated CP, whereas recolonization with a new patient-derived HHEC strain PS718 exacerbated it. Mechanistically, E. coli-derived HtpG upregulated protein arginine methyltransferase 5 (PRMT5) in pancreatic macrophages. Pharmacological inhibition of PRMT5 or macrophage-specific deletion of PRMT5 mitigated pancreatic fibrosis and CP progression. PRMT5 methylated Krüppel-like factor 4 (KLF4) at residues R387/R389, stabilizing it, which promoted M2 polarization and pancreatic fibrosis. Therapeutic intervention with Akkermansia muciniphila, which is reduced in CP, suppressed HHEC colonization and ameliorated CP. These findings provide novel evidence for a pathogenic HHEC-HtpG-macrophage axis in CP, highlighting the potential of microbiota-targeted therapies for the condition.

doi:10.1053/j.gastro.2026.09.026.abstract: Excessive accumulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) derived from human intestinal myofibroblasts (HIMF) drives the significant clinical problem of intestinal fibrosis. Fibrosis is believed to progress even in the absence of intestinal inflammation. ECM-bound transglutaminase 2 (TG2) enzyme may exert direct pro-fibrotic effects. We investigated the role of TG2 in intestinal fibrosis. TG2 expression and activity in human intestinal tissue and HIMF from strictured Crohn's disease (CDs), and controls were measured. ECM accumulation by HIMF in presence or absence of TG2 inhibitors was determined. Putative TG2 signaling pathways discovered in HIMF using bulk RNA sequencing (bulk-RNAseq) and single cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) were functionally validated. Role of TG2 in vivo was confirmed using inducible global knockout of TGM2 (encoding TG2) in two experimental fibrosis models. TG activity was increased in CDs compared to controls, with up to 100% activity attributable to TG2. TG activity correlated with the degree of histopathologic tissue fibrosis. HIMF were the major source of TG2, with ≥95% of HIMF TG activity being derived from TG2. Tissue distribution of TG2 in myofibroblasts was confirmed by scRNAseq analysis. Selective inhibition of TG2 activity reduced fibronectin (FN), collagen (COL)I, III and VI accumulation by HIMF. Novel TG2 signaling pathways revealed by bulk-RNAseq, were functionally validated. Inducible TGM2 knockout prevented experimental fibrosis without affecting the degree of intestinal inflammation. TG2 may be involved in inflammation-independent progression of intestinal fibrosis.

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2518753.abstract: In eastern and southern Africa, approximately 1 million people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and receiving oral therapy do not have viral suppression because of adherence challenges. We conducted a phase 3b, open-label, randomized trial to compare long-acting injectable cabotegravir plus rilpivirine with oral dolutegravir-based therapy among adults with virally suppressed HIV type 1 (viral load, <200 copies per milliliter) and suboptimal adherence or care engagement. The participants were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive intramuscular injections of cabotegravir (600 mg) plus rilpivirine (900 mg) every 8 weeks, with the first two injection visits occurring 4 weeks apart, or to continue daily oral dolutegravir-based therapy; baseline drug-resistance testing was not performed. The primary end point was a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter at week 48; noninferiority was assessed with a margin of -10 percentage points. Confirmed virologic failure (two consecutive viral loads of ≥200 copies per milliliter) was a key secondary end point. A total of 540 participants were enrolled across seven sites in Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda; 537 were included in the primary analysis. At 48 weeks, 244 of 268 participants (91.0%) in the long-acting-therapy group had a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter, as compared with 240 of 269 participants (89.2%) in the oral-therapy group (risk difference, 1.9 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -3.1 to 6.9), which met the criterion for noninferiority. The results of a per-protocol analysis were consistent with those of the primary analysis. Confirmed virologic failure occurred in 5 participants (1.9%) in the long-acting-therapy group and in no participants in the oral-therapy group (risk difference, 1.9 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.3 to 3.5). Serious adverse events were reported in 11 of 271 participants (4.1%) who received long-acting therapy and in 8 of 269 participants (3.0%) who received oral therapy (risk difference, 1.1 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.1 to 4.2). Among persons with HIV in Africa who have adherence challenges, long-acting cabotegravir plus rilpivirine was noninferior to oral dolutegravir-based therapy for maintaining a viral load of less than 50 copies per milliliter. (Funded by Johnson & Johnson; IMPALA ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05546242; Pan African Clinical Trials Registry number, PACT202301600757432TMC278LAHTX3005.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2604435.abstract: Monoclonal antibodies targeting the interleukin-23 pathway are effective in treating inflammatory bowel disease. However, these therapies must be administered intravenously or by subcutaneous injection. We conducted a phase 2b, double-blind, randomized trial of oral icotrokinra, a peptide that blocks the interleukin-23 receptor, in adults with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis. Participants were assigned to receive icotrokinra at a once-daily dose of 400 mg, 200 mg, or 100 mg or placebo. The primary end point was clinical response at week 12. Secondary end points included clinical remission, remission of symptoms, and endoscopic improvement at week 12. A total of 252 participants underwent randomization: 63 were assigned to the 400-mg group, 62 to the 200-mg group, 64 to the 100-mg group, and 63 to the placebo group. All the doses of icotrokinra were superior to placebo with respect to a clinical response at week 12, which occurred in 63% of the participants in the 400-mg group, 58% in the 200-mg group, and 55% in the 100-mg group, as compared with 27% in the placebo group (P<0.001 for all comparisons with placebo). The percentage of participants with clinical remission at week 12 was also significantly higher in the 400-mg group than in the placebo group (30% vs. 11%, P = 0.006), as were the percentage of participants with symptomatic remission (46% vs. 19%, P<0.001) and the percentage of participants with endoscopic improvement (37% vs. 14%, P = 0.002). Clinical remission at week 12 occurred in 24% of the participants in the 200-mg group (P = 0.054 for the comparison with placebo); in accordance with the fixed-sequence testing procedure to account for multiple comparisons, no further formal testing of secondary end points was conducted. Through week 28, the percentage of participants with adverse events was 60% in the 400-mg group, 66% in the 200-mg group, 66% in the 100-mg group, and 62% in the placebo group. For serious adverse events, the percentages were 2%, 5%, 0%, and 10%, respectively. Among participants with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis, a clinical response at week 12 was significantly more common with once-daily oral icotrokinra at each of three tested doses than with placebo. (Funded by Johnson & Johnson; ANTHEM-UC ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06049017.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2606208.abstract: The outcome of Philadelphia-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph-positive ALL) has greatly improved with the use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors and immunotherapy. In this trial, we randomly assigned adult patients with Ph-positive ALL in a 2:1 ratio to receive ponatinib plus blinatumomab (intervention group) or imatinib plus chemotherapy (control group) as frontline treatment. A crossover to the intervention group was allowed for patients with persistence or reappearance of measurable residual disease in the control group. The primary end point was event-free survival. A total of 236 patients underwent randomization: 158 to the intervention group and 78 to the control group. The median age of the patients was 55 years (range, 24 to 82). At a median follow-up of 23.7 months, the estimated 24-month event-free survival was 86% in the intervention group and 67% in the control group (P<0.001). Survival with no measurable residual disease was 68% and 42%, respectively. At the end of induction, a complete hematologic response was observed in 94% of the patients in the intervention group and in 79% of those in the control group. After blinatumomab consolidation, a molecular response was observed in 71% and 49% of the patients, respectively. After crossover to the intervention group, 20 of 31 patients (64%) had a molecular response. Overall survival was 90% in the intervention group and 85% in the control group. The cumulative incidence of relapse was 5% and 13%, respectively. As of this report, only 19% of the patients in the intervention group had undergone hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation after having had a first complete hematologic response. In this phase 3 trial, a frontline chemotherapy-free targeted and immunotherapeutic approach was superior to the use of imatinib and chemotherapy. (Funded by Associazione Italiana per la Ricerca sul Cancro and others; GIMEMA ALL2820 ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT04722848.).

doi:10.1056/nejmoa2608397.abstract: The preferred method of renal-replacement therapy for acute kidney injury in critically ill patients remains uncertain. In this multicenter, open-label, noninferiority trial, we randomly assigned critically ill adults with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy to undergo intermittent hemodialysis or continuous renal-replacement therapy as the initial treatment. The primary outcome was a major adverse kidney event - defined as death, dependence on renal-replacement therapy, or a serum creatinine concentration more than 25% above the baseline value - by day 90. The trial was stopped early after sequential interim analyses showed a sustained signal of higher mortality with intermittent hemodialysis than with continuous renal-replacement therapy. A total of 554 patients underwent randomization, with 272 patients assigned to undergo intermittent hemodialysis and 282 to undergo continuous renal-replacement therapy; 535 patients (260 in the intermittent group and 275 in the continuous group) were included in the intention-to-treat population. A major adverse kidney event occurred by day 90 in 203 patients (78.1%) in the intermittent group and in 197 patients (71.6%) in the continuous group (adjusted absolute risk difference, 6.28 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -1.22 to 13.79). Death by day 90 occurred in 164 patients (63.1%) and in 147 patients (53.5%), respectively. Kaplan-Meier mortality estimates at day 90 were 63.3% and 53.6% (hazard ratio, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.04 to 1.63). The most common complication potentially related to acute kidney injury or renal-replacement therapy was hypotension, which occurred in 179 patients (68.8%) in the intermittent group and in 183 patients (66.5%) in the continuous group. Among critically ill patients with acute kidney injury who had indications for renal-replacement therapy, intermittent hemodialysis as the initial treatment approach was not shown to be noninferior to continuous renal-replacement therapy with respect to major adverse kidney events by day 90 and was associated with higher mortality. (Funded by the French Ministry of Health; ICRAKI ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT06032884.).

doi:10.1080/2162402x.2026.2740432.abstract: Membrane-associated proliferating cell nuclear antigen (mPCNA) is an attractive tumor-selective antigen for antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) development. We generated a chimeric IgG1 ADC, RC14-MMAE, to exploit three key properties of mPCNA that support its use as an efficient delivery platform. First, flow-cytometric and imaging analyses show abundant mPCNA surface expression on multiple tumor cell lines and in JIMT1 xenografts, providing accessible epitopes for binding. Second, comparative profiling against non-malignant counterparts and normal mouse tissues reveals minimal or undetectable mPCNA at the plasma membrane of healthy cells, indicating a sharp tumor-normal differential expected to limit off-tumor targeting and improve the therapeutic window. Third, live-cell internalization assays demonstrate that RC14 rapidly accumulates in LAMP1-positive lysosomes after engaging mPCNA, confirming efficient trafficking along the endolysosomal pathway required for protease-mediated cleavage of the valine-citrulline linker and release of monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE). Consistent with this target profile, RC14-MMAE exhibits potent antigen-dependent cytotoxicity in mPCNA-positive tumor models in NSG mice, favorable pharmacokinetics, sustained payload retention in serum, robust in vivo antitumor activity with limited overt toxicity, and a significantly increased fraction of F4/80⁺ tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells within dissociated tumors. These findings establish mPCNA as a functionally validated, tumor-selective internalizing target and support RC14-MMAE as a first-in-class mPCNA-directed ADC with broad translational potential.

doi:10.1080/2162402x.2026.2746847.abstract: Sex steroid exposure is a major risk factor for breast cancer initiation and progression through incompletely understood mechanisms. Novel therapeutics for prevention and treatment of estrogen-dependent breast cancer are needed. Cell-cell interactions within the microenvironment contribute to breast cancer progression through extracellular signaling. Here, extracellular proteins were sampled directly from live normal human breast tissue and breast cancers using microdialysis, and 1,101 proteins were quantified. Mechanistic studies were performed in cultured intact normal human breast tissue and mast cells. Findings were validated in vivo using ER+ breast cancer models in immunocompetent and immunocompromised mice and in a zebrafish xenograft model. We identified a breast tissue-specific extracellular protein signature comprising 150 proteins associated with local estradiol (E2) levels, of which several were linked to mast cell biology, including stem cell factor (SCF). Human ER+ breast tumors exhibited increased extracellular SCF levels and higher mast cell density, which was associated with poorer overall survival. In normal human breast tissue, E2 increased mast cell abundance and activity. In vitro, E2 rapidly activated mast cells, an effect blocked by desloratadine. In mouse breast cancer models, E2 increased and fulvestrant reduced mast cell density. In the zebrafish, mast cells promoted ER+ breast cancer growth, which was further enhanced by E2 and abrogated by desloratadine. Overall, our findings identify mast cells as estrogen-responsive stromal mediators and support targeting mast cell-dependent pathways as a potential strategy for the prevention and treatment of estrogen-dependent breast cancer.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkad027.abstract: Abstract Static biomarkers like programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) are insufficient to accurately predict response to immune checkpoint inhibition. Therefore, on-treatment biomarkers, which measure immediate therapy-associated changes, are currently shifting into the focus of immuno-oncology. A prime example of a simple predictive on-treatment biomarker is the early C-reactive protein (CRP) kinetics with its predictive CRP flare-response phenomenon. Here, we were able to confirm the predictive value of CRP flare-response kinetics in the pivotal phase III OAK trial (NCT02008227), which compared atezolizumab with docetaxel in patients with non-small cell lung cancer. Of note, CRP flare-response predicted favorable outcomes only in the immune checkpoint inhibition–treated subgroup, which suggests that it is an immunotherapy-specific phenomenon. In conclusion, we have for the first time validated the high predictive value of early CRP kinetics in a pivotal phase III trial, justifying the broad use of this cost-effective and easy-to-implement on-treatment biomarker to optimize therapy monitoring for patients with non-small cell lung cancer.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag106.abstract: Abstract This cross-sectional study examined patient-provider communication about colorectal cancer screening options using the 2024 Health Information National Trends Survey. The outcome measure was respondents’ report of being informed by a health care professional about multiple colorectal cancer screening tests. Covariates included race/ethnicity, income, education, number of health care visits, insurance, age, and sex. Uninsured participants had lower odds (adjusted OR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.46–0.93) of reporting colorectal cancer screening discussions than insured participants. Those who earned <$20,000 had lower odds (adjusted OR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.41–0.81) of reporting colorectal cancer screening discussions than those earning ≥$100,000. The predicted probability of a health care provider visit was lowest among respondents with no health care visits (adjusted probability, 33.3%; 95% CI, 25.3–41.2), compared with those in the other health care visit categories. Differences in colorectal cancer screening discussions were observed across groups. Further research should identify contributing factors.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag108.abstract: Breastfeeding reduces ovarian cancer risk, but the underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear. We examined the association between a previously reported metabolite-based breastfeeding score with incident epithelial ovarian cancer risk in case-control studies nested within the Nurses' Health Studies (NHS/NHSII, n = 436) and Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial (PLCO, n = 300) using conditional logistic regression to calculate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for each study and conducted a meta-analysis. We investigated 606 individual breastfeeding-metabolite associations among 9,904 mid-life parous women in NHS/NHSII and 663 one-year postpartum women in the Vitamin D Antenatal Asthma Reduction Trial (VDAART). Metabolites associated with breastfeeding at p ≤ 0.05 after multiple testing correction for number of effective tests (NEF) were then assessed for their associations with ovarian cancer. Metabolite set enrichment analysis using Normalized Enrichment Score (NES) identified metabolite classes associated with breastfeeding using false discovery rate (FDR) were used for multiple testing correction. The highest quartile of metabolite-based breastfeeding score was inversely associated with ovarian cancer risk (meta-analyzed odds ratio [OR]=0.62, 95%CI=0.39-0.99). Of the 14 individual metabolites associated with breastfeeding in NHS/NHSII and also measured in VDAART, similar direction of associations was observed for 11 metabolites. Phosphatidylcholines (PCs; NES=1.94; FDR=0.004) and phosphatidylethanolamines (PEs; NES=1.82; FDR=0.01) were positively enriched with increased breastfeeding duration. Ten metabolites including PCs and PEs were positively associated with breastfeeding and inversely associated with ovarian cancer. Our results suggest alterations of systemic metabolism, particularly among PC and PE pathways, provide insight into biological pathways underlying the inverse breastfeeding-ovarian cancer association.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag109.abstract: Redlining, introduced in 1933 by the Homeowners' Loan Corporation, created enduring structural inequities in housing, health care access, and neighborhood investment. These historical patterns may contribute to persistent disparities in breast cancer screening. This study examines how historical redlining, alongside contemporary socioeconomic factors, shapes screening disparities across the University of Kansas Cancer Center (KUCC) catchment area. We conducted a census tract-level spatial analysis across 123 counties (Kansas and western Missouri) by linking CDC PLACES breast cancer screening data with historical redlining maps. Explanatory variables included rurality, mammography facility availability, income inequality, gender pay gap, and uninsured rates. Logistic regression assessed overall associations, while geographically weighted binomial logistic regression evaluated spatial heterogeneity. Screening rates ranged from 56.9% to 84.5% across census tracts. Redlining was associated with lower screening odds in unadjusted models but was attenuated after accounting for socioeconomic and geographic factors. Rurality and income inequality were consistently associated with lower screening, whereas greater mammography facility availability was associated with higher screening rates. Spatial analyses revealed meaningful geographic variation, with localized negative associations of redlining and persistent, spatially varying effects of socioeconomic factors. Breast cancer screening disparities in this region reflect the combined influence of historical structural inequities and current socioeconomic conditions. Expanding access to mammography and implementing spatially targeted, equity-focused interventions may improve screening uptake and reduce disparities in underserved communities.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag110.abstract: COVID-19 has been associated with an increased thrombotic risk, potentially exacerbated in patients with active cancer. We conducted a retrospective cohort study including 119 cancer patients with COVID-19 and 214 matched pre-pandemic controls. Patients with COVID-19 had poorer performance status and were more frequently treated with palliative intent. After a median follow-up of 32.7 months, overall thrombotic event rates did not differ between groups. However, after adjustment for clinically relevant covariates and accounting for death as a competing event, COVID-19 status and palliative treatment intent remained independently associated with a higher cumulative incidence of thrombotic events. In conclusion, COVID-19 may increase thrombotic risk in patients with cancer and occurs more frequently in patients with poorer clinical status. These findings are exploratory and require confirmation in larger prospective studies.

doi:10.1093/jncics/pkag111.abstract: Abstract Background The incidence of gastro-entero-pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasms (GEP-NENs) has increased, alongside novel therapies and care models. Whether these advances translated into improved survival is unclear. Methods Population-based retrospective cohort study of GEP-NENs between 2000–2019. Overall survival (OS) was analyzed using time-to-event methods. Restricted cubic splines assessed non-linear associations between diagnosis year and hazards of death; multivariable Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, primary site, and metastatic status. Results Among 9,420 patients, 5-year OS was 75.8% overall, 88.8% for non-metastatic disease, and 57.0% for metastatic disease. Mortality risk declined in more recent years, with diagnoses in 2013–2019 associated with lower hazards of death (adjusted HR 0.91, 95%CI 0.83–0.99). Improvements were confined to non-metastatic disease and to pancreas, stomach, and rectal primaries. Conclusion OS has modestly improved over two decades, largely reflecting stage migration rather than clear therapeutic gains. Advances that meaningfully improve survival in advanced GEP-NENs are needed.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag077.abstract: Central nervous system (CNS) tumors pose a major global health challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where outcomes remain disproportionately poor. The global CONCORD-3 study (Lancet Oncology) highlighted stark disparities in five-year survival (2010-2014): from ∼15% in Thailand to 46% in Japan among adults, and from ∼ 80% in Denmark to < 40% in Brazil among children. Limited access to specialized pathology and molecular diagnostics in LMICs results in diagnostic uncertainty and restricted treatment options. DNA methylation-based tumor classification, has revolutionized CNS tumor diagnosis and got incorporated into the 2021 world health organization (WHO) CNS5 classification. However, its accessibility, feasibility, and performance in LMICs remain insufficiently explored. Importantly, several ethnic groups common in LMICs are underrepresented in current reference datasets. To address this, the Molecular Neuro-Pathology (MNP) Outreach Consortium was launched in Heidelberg, partnering with 11 countries-including nine LMICs from Asia, Africa, and South America. Early insights from Brazil, Jordan and Argentina, show methylation profiling changing diagnosis in up to 25% cases. Gains are greatest in pediatric and adolescents and young adults (AYA) populations. In addition, it reduced the designation of not otherwise specified (NOS) from 51.3% to 8.8% across 476 CNS tumours in Brazil.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag168.abstract: Pediatric brain tumors (PBTs) remain a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in children, underscoring the need for more effective therapeutic strategies. These tumors arise from disrupted neurodevelopmental programs and evolve within a developmentally constrained immune landscape that is tolerogenic, epigenetically plastic, and susceptible to tumor-mediated co-option. Increasing evidence indicates that, besides molecular heterogeneity, the tumor immune microenvironment critically influences clinical outcomes. Despite its therapeutic promise, immunotherapy has yet to demonstrate consistent clinical benefit in most PBTs, highlighting the need for rational multimodal strategies guided by deeper understanding of tumor-immune interactions in the developing brain. To provide a comprehensive perspective on fetal immune ontogeny and its tumor-driven dysregulation we used medulloblastoma, pediatric gliomas, atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors, and ependymoma as representative entities. Drawing on insights from developmental neurobiology, tumor immunology, and emerging multi-omic studies, we outline how PBTs exploit physiological immune maturation programs to establish immune evasion, sustain chronic inflammation, and promote therapy resistance. We further discuss emerging multimodal immunotherapeutic strategies and next-generation CAR T-cell approaches currently under clinical investigation. In addition, we highlight therapeutic avenues such as targeting tumor-associated myeloid populations and key inflammatory regulators that may offer promising opportunities for future clinical translation. We believe this Review will help address current limitations in preclinical models, improve patient stratification and guide rational design of therapeutic strategies.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag169.abstract: Sequential chemoradiotherapy remains a standard treatment option for patients with isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant gliomas. The results of the phase III INDIGO trial have led to the recent regulatory approval of vorasidenib, a brain-penetrant IDH1 and IDH2 inhibitor, indicated for patients with IDH1- or IDH2-mutant WHO grade 2 astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma after biopsy or resection. While IDH inhibitors represent a significant advancement for patients with IDH-mutant glioma, there is substantial controversy regarding which patients are most likely to derive benefit from IDH inhibition and how this strategy can be optimally integrated into clinical practice. Specifically, whether IDH inhibitors should be used prior to, in conjunction with or potentially in lieu of radiation-based treatment strategies are fundamental questions for the neuro-oncology community. Additionally, whether IDH inhibitors can be extrapolated to higher-grade disease settings or utilized in higher-risk patient populations remains unknown. These open questions provide an opportunity for the field of radiation oncology to develop pragmatic biomarker-based approaches to guide patient selection, to monitor treatment response and to identify optimal treatment strategy and timing/sequencing of treatment. Several candidate biomarkers have emerged for IDH-mutant glioma with unique potential to be rationally integrated into radiation oncology workflows to personalize care.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag255.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) invasion is clinically decisive but difficult to model systematically. Existing patient-derived xenograft (PDX) resources rarely couple reproducible in vivo invasion phenotypes with matched multi-omic profiles at scale, limiting mechanistic insight and phenotype-informed therapeutic hypotheses. We established the HGCC Phenobank, comprising 65 patient-derived GBM stem-like cultures with matched multi-omic profiling and orthotopic engraftment in 449 mice. Blinded histopathology quantified ten invasion traits per case. These phenotypes were integrated with RNA sequencing, DNA methylation, and mass-spectrometry-based proteomics. Multi-Omic Factor Analysis (MOFA) identified latent molecular programs. Phenotype-specific RNA signatures were matched to LINCS drug-perturbation profiles and validated in 3D gliomasphere and ex vivo brain-slice assays. Two dominant, reproducible invasion modes emerged across models: diffuse parenchymal infiltration and perivascular/condensed growth. Proneural cultures formed more aggressive tumors in immunodeficient mice, and mouse survival showed a modest correlation with patient survival in matched cases (Pearson r=0.1832, p=0.045). MOFA identified 15 latent factors; Factor 1, marked by ASCL1/OLIG1/OLIG2 programs across multiple molecular layers, was associated with increased tumor formation and diffuse invasion in mice. Higher Factor 1 scores were associated with significantly longer postoperative survival in both the matched patient cohort (p = 0.00018) and TCGA (p = 0.017), although Factor 1 was not associated with survival of the xenografted mice. Drug-signature matching separated mechanisms targeting diffuse versus perivascular invasion. Experimental validation confirmed phenotype-selective sensitivities, and inhibitors PIK-75 and buparlisib suppressed invasion dynamics across representative models in 3D and brain-slice assays. The HGCC Phenobank provides the first openly available PDX resource that systematically links GBM invasion phenotypes to multi-omic programs and therapeutic predictions. This framework enables reproducible model selection, mechanistic dissection of invasion modes, and phenotype-guided therapeutic discovery.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag255.title: A Multi-Omic Phenobank Reveals Axes of Glioblastoma Growth, Invasion, and Therapeutic Vulnerability.

doi:10.1093/neuonc/noag257.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across neuro-oncology domains to analyze complex, high-dimensional, multimodal data. Despite major advances in the biological understanding and classification of CNS tumors, clinical outcomes for many of them remain poor, reflecting intra- and inter-tumor heterogeneity and limitations of conventional reductionist approaches. AI offers a paradigm shift to capture this heterogeneity and provide quantitative, reproducible diagnostic, predictive, and prognostic insights. This article describes a joint effort across the Response Assessment in Neuro-Oncology (RANO) working groups to provide an overarching review of the AI use across six key domains of neuro-oncology: neuroimaging, neuropathology, laboratory medicine, neurosurgery, drug discovery, and clinical trials. Applications closest to clinical use include imaging segmentation and quantification, AI-assisted image reconstruction, DNA methylation-based classification, and workflow optimization. Radiogenomics, WSI-based molecular prediction, AI-guided surgical targeting, liquid biopsy interpretation, AI-guided drug discovery, digital twins, and in silico trials remain promising but require stronger prospective validation. Key challenges include limited availability of large diverse datasets, variability in data acquisition and reference standards, and limited external validation. This review provides a unifying framework for understanding the role of AI across neuro-oncology and highlights key considerations for its responsible implementation, emphasizing standardization, reproducibility, multi-institutional validation, and human oversight.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.ady1161.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder with no effective cure, characterized by the cerebral parenchymal and vascular accumulation of aggregated amyloid-β (Aβ) and hyperphosphorylated tau. Cerebrovascular and mitochondria dysfunction are early causal events in the progression of AD. Previous studies support that inhibiting carbonic anhydrases (CAs) may prevent mitochondrial and cerebrovascular dysfunction in AD models. Here, we selectively target the mitochondrial CA isoform CA-VB by pharmacological and genetic manipulation in human cerebral microvascular endothelial cells (hCMEC), and we confirm the protective effects of the CA-V inhibitor in AD mice. CA-V inhibition and CA-VB KO prevent Aβ induced mitochondria-mediated endothelial apoptosis, loss of barrier resistance, and hCMEC inflammatory activation. Strikingly, CA-V inhibition also mitigates caspase activation and endothelial cell activation in the brains of 3xTg AD mice, resulting in preserved memory function. Our results demonstrate that selective CA-V inhibition is an effective and promising strategy against AD-mediated cerebrovascular pathology, neuroinflammation and cognitive impairment.
