doi:10.1245/s10434-026-20419-4.abstract: Delayed diagnosis and treatment worsen survival in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Despite many potential causes, the influence of social determinants of health (SDoH) is understudied. We evaluated whether SDoH impact delays in diagnosis and treatment among patients who underwent resection for PDAC. Adults resected at a high-volume center were included (January 2016-November 2024). SDoH included insurance status, census-level income and education, rural-urban residence, and Area Deprivation Index. Primary endpoints were time from first imaging to histological diagnosis and time from first imaging to treatment initiation. Delay thresholds were derived using receiver operating characteristic analysis against overall survival. Uni- and multivariable logistic regression identified factors associated with delays, adjusting for demographic and clinical covariates, stratified by outpatient (OUP) versus emergency room (ER) presentation. Among 317 patients, the median age was 67 years, and 42.3% were female; 50.1% presented through ER. The median imaging-to-diagnosis interval was 11 days (interquartile [IQR] 3-27 days), and the median imaging-to-treatment interval was 40 days (IQR 27-59 days). In the OUP cohort, Medicare insurance was associated with delayed diagnosis compared with private insurance (OR 3.34 [95% CI 1.09-11.70]), whereas higher income was associated with up to 84% lower odds of delayed treatment. In the ER cohort, higher education was associated with reduced odds of delayed diagnosis (OR 0.27 [95% CI 0.07-0.88]) and delayed treatment (OR 0.33 [95% CI 0.11-0.91]). Post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) hospitalization predicted delays in the ER setting, whereas alarm symptoms reduced delays in both settings. SDoH are associated with diagnostic and treatment delays in resected PDAC. Targeted interventions may accelerate care and improve equity in outcomes.

doi:10.1245/s10434-026-20452-3.abstract: Lower socioeconomic status conveys a known survival disadvantage for patients with esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC). The potential role of the treating center volume in mitigating this disparity has not been described to date. Non-metastatic EAC patients were identified (NCDB 2012-2021). High- and low-risk zip code groups were derived from income and education quartiles. Center volume was delineated as "low" or "high," with an annual threshold of ≥ 10 esophagectomies. Standard chi-square modeling, multivariable Cox hazard regression models, and Kaplan-Meier survival analyses were used where appropriate. Of 7462 EAC patients, 38.2% (n = 2849) resided in high-risk zip code areas, and 87.1% were treated at low-volume centers. Clinical (p = 0.230) and pathologic (p = 0.992) staging distribution did not differ across zip codes. High-volume centers saw a slightly increased proportion of advanced disease (p = 0.001). Patients at high-volume centers experienced better survival (5-year overall survival [5yOS], 44.97%) than their low-volume counterparts (5yOS, 40.62%) (p < 0.001). Patients residing in high-risk zip code areas demonstrated worse 5yOS than their low-risk counterparts (38.20% vs 43.74%; p < 0.001). Evaluation of low-volume centers showed that the high-risk zip code group had shorter survival than their low-risk counterparts (36.80% vs 43.21%; p < 0.001). Interestingly, in high-volume centers, survival across zip code groups was notably comparable (45.69% vs 46.20%; p = 0.80). Center expertise may offer an avenue for mitigating sociodemographic survival disparities in esophageal cancer. As discussions regarding centralized oncologic care continue, particular attention should be paid to the impact of high-volume center referral on the treatment of patients with social risk factors.

doi:10.1245/s10434-026-20639-8.abstract: Primary breast angiosarcoma (PBA) is rare, and limited data exist because studies often combine primary and secondary angiosarcoma patients. For patients with PBA who received care at a comprehensive cancer center from 1991 to 2025 and underwent surgical resection, this retrospective study collected and analyzed clinicopathologic features, treatment patterns, and survival data. Among 176 patients, 138 met the inclusion criteria. The median age was 40 years (interquartile range [IQR], 32-49 years). Most of the tumors were high grade with a median size of 6.5 cm. Most of the patients underwent mastectomy (88%). Among the 50 patients (36%) who underwent axillary surgery, only 6 patients had nodal metastases. Multimodal treatment was performed for 121 patients (88%), including chemotherapy/surgery (n = 46, 38%), radiation therapy (RT)/surgery ( = 15, 12%), and chemotherapy/RT/surgery (n = 60, 50%). The median follow-up time was 3.7 years. The median overall survival (OS) was 6 years (IQR, 3.5-8.7 years), and the 5-year OS was 58%. Recurrence was experienced by 62% of the patients, with a median recurrence-free survival (RFS) of 3 years (IQR, 1.4-7.7 years). Most of the recurrences were distant (79%), with 14% of the patients experiencing local recurrence only. Tumor size larger than 5 cm and high-grade histology were independently associated with lower OS. When stratified by treatment modality, there was no statistical difference in OS (p = 0.475). Primary breast angiosarcoma arises in women with a median age of 40 years, and large, high-grade tumors are associated with worse survival outcomes. Distant recurrence is common, whereas nodal metastases and local failure are not. Most of the patients in this study received multimodal therapy without a clear impact of modality on OS. However, further collaborative studies may be required to assess the impact of modality on disease outcomes.

doi:10.1245/s10434-026-20711-3.abstract: Neoadjuvant therapy can improve the survival outcomes of patients with borderline resectable pancreatic cancer (BRPC). However, standard neoadjuvant regimens remain lacking. This study evaluated the clinical feasibility of tislelizumab plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel in the neoadjuvant setting for BRPC. In this prospective study, patients with BRPC preoperatively received three cycles of tislelizumab plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, and continued postoperatively. The primary endpoints were R0 resection rate and treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs). Exploratory objectives were resistance to this regimen. Of 30 enrolled patients, 80.0% (24/30) completed neoadjuvant therapy and underwent surgical resection. R0 resection was achieved in 80.0% (24/30) of the patients and in 100.00% (24/24) of those resected. The 12-month OS and RFS rates were 87.5% (95% CI 64.3-95.8%) and 82.8% (95% CI 60-95.8%), respectively, with median RFS of 28 months (95% CI 16.9-39.1). Most TRAEs were grade I-II, with no serious events. Quantitative proteomics combined with machine learning identified NT5DC2, FAM3D, CXCL5, and TMT1B as candidate biomarkers of resistance to this neoadjuvant regimen. In paired pre- and postoperative tissues from treatment-sensitive patients, CD8+ T-cell infiltration tended to increase and CD163+ M2-like macrophages were significantly upregulated after surgery. Neoadjuvant tislelizumab plus gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel is promising for improving the resection rate in BRPC, with a favorable safety profile. NT5DC2, FAM3D, CXCL5, and TMT1B may serve as candidate biomarkers of preoperative drug resistance, and tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) analysis further reveals immune microenvironment remodeling in postoperative tumors from treatment-sensitive patients. These findings warrant validation in larger-scale studies. Trial Registration Chinese Clinical Trial registry (ChiCTR2200063680).

doi:10.1245/s10434-026-20724-y.abstract: Reduced-port surgery has been developed to minimize abdominal wall trauma while maintaining the benefits of minimally invasive surgery. However, reduced-port robotic rectal surgery remains technically challenging due to interference of external arms. The modular design of the Hugo RAS system (Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN, USA) provides greater flexibility in arm positioning to minimize external arm interference without compromising instrument maneuverability1-4. In abdominoperineal resection (APR), the incision for a permanent colostomy is inevitable. We report the first case of completely robot-assisted APR performed using the Hugo RAS system through a planned stoma site. Three robotic trocars were inserted through the planned left lower-quadrant stoma site, and one arm through the right lower quadrant. We call this approach SIPORS, Single-Incision Plus One Robot-assisted Surgery. The procedure is presented in the accompanying video. As the first case, a 50-year-old woman with rectal cancer underwent APR after systemic chemotherapy. The console time was 167 min. The procedure was completed without significant robotic arm interference. The postoperative course was uneventful except for transient cystitis. The circumferential and distal resection margins were 3 and 35 mm, respectively. The mesorectal specimen was complete, 25 lymph nodes were harvested, and the pathological stage was pT3N2bM1. SIPORS using the Hugo RAS at a planned stoma site was technically feasible and achieved an oncologically acceptable resection in this patient. It may offer improved cosmesis, reduced postoperative pain, fewer wound complications, and a lower risk of trocar-site incisional hernia. Further experience is needed to confirm its reproducibility and clinical benefits.

doi:10.1245/s10434-026-20728-8.abstract: Staging laparoscopy (SL) is a minimally invasive approach for detecting occult metastases in patients with pancreatic cancer (PC) without signs of metastasis on imaging. This study aimed to identify the predictive factors for imaging-negative occult metastases. This prospective study enrolled 199 patients with histologically confirmed PC from three institutions between August 2021 and April 2023. All patients were scheduled for a treatment plan that included SL. The overall metastasis rate as detected using SL was 25.1%, which varied from 20.6% in patients with resectable PC (R-PC) to 33.8% in those with borderline resectable or locally advanced unresectable PC (BR/URLA-PC). In 152 patients who did not receive neoadjuvant therapy, BR/URLA status (odds ratio 3.261; 95% confidence interval 1.185-9.483, p = 0.022) and pancreatic body/tail lesions (odds ratio 2.653; 95% confidence interval 1.037-7.214, p = 0.042) were independent risk factors for occult metastatic lesions (M1). Among the 107 patients with R-PC, M1 disease was significantly associated with pancreatic body/tail lesions, tumor size, and elevated levels of tumor markers. In particular, elevated carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels were consistent across all patients with M1 pancreatic head cancer. In contrast, no statistical differences were observed for any of these factors in the 45 patients with BR/URLA-PC. Our findings support the importance of SL in patients with BR/UR PC. For R-PC, patients with pancreatic head lesions and normal tumor marker values may represent a very low-risk subgroup where selective omission of SL can be considered in resource-constrained settings.

doi:10.1245/s10434-026-20729-7.abstract: Data on robot-assisted minimally invasive esophagectomy (RAMIE) after neoadjuvant therapy, particularly after neoadjuvant immunochemoradiotherapy, remain scarce. This study compares the perioperative outcomes of RAMIE versus conventional minimally invasive esophagectomy (MIE) in patients with resectable esophageal cancer after neoadjuvant therapy. We conducted a dual-center, retrospective study of consecutive patients with esophageal cancer who underwent MIE after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy or neoadjuvant immunochemoradiotherapy between 2020 and 2025. Propensity score matching was applied based on preoperative variables. Perioperative outcomes were analyzed. After 1:1 propensity score matching, 137 patients were allocated to each group. The RAMIE group demonstrated a higher rate of left recurrent laryngeal nerve lymph node dissection (67.9% vs. 53.3%, p = 0.02) and yielded more lymph nodes in this station after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (mean 1.6 vs. 1.0, p = 0.02). However, RAMIE was associated with a higher overall incidence of postoperative complications (38.0% vs. 24.8%, p = 0.03). No significant differences were observed in operation time, pathological complete response rate, severe complications, length of stay, 30-day readmission, or 90-day mortality. In expert hands, RAMIE achieves perioperative safety comparable to that with MIE after neoadjuvant therapy and offers a superior ability to dissect critical lymph node stations. This technical advantage establishes RAMIE as a viable and promising surgical option, warranting further prospective investigation in randomized trials.

doi:10.1245/s10434-026-20736-8.abstract: Reliable biomarkers for predicting tumor aggressiveness and pathological upstaging in renal cell carcinoma (RCC) remain limited. DR-70, a biomarker reflecting circulating fibrin and fibrin degradation products, has been associated with tumor progression in several malignancies. This study aimed to investigate the association between preoperative serum DR-70 levels and pathological stage and nuclear grade in patients with localized RCC. This prospective single-center study included 69 patients who underwent partial or radical nephrectomy for localized RCC. Tumors were staged according to the TNM classification and graded using the World Health Organization/International Society of Urological Pathology system. Preoperative serum DR-70 levels were measured, and their associations with clinical stage, pathological stage, and nuclear grade were evaluated. Multivariate logistic regression analysis was performed to identify independent predictors of pathological upstaging (≥ pT3). Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis was used to assess the predictive performance of DR-70. The median serum DR-70 level was 0.84 U/mL. DR-70 levels were significantly higher in high-grade tumors than in low-grade tumors (1.32 vs. 0.78 U/mL, p = 0.001). No significant association was observed between DR-70 levels and clinical stage (p = 0.53), whereas a significant association was found with pathological stage (p = 0.023). Multivariate analysis identified serum DR-70 as an independent predictor of pathological upstaging (≥ pT3) (odds ratio 1.40; 95% confidence interval 1.09-1.81; p = 0.008). Receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated good predictive performance for high-grade disease (area under the curve 0.823) and pathological upstaging (area under the curve 0.774), with an optimal cutoff value of 1.02 U/mL. Serum DR-70 was associated with tumor aggressiveness and independently predicted pathological upstaging in patients with localized RCC. These findings suggest that DR-70 may serve as a complementary biomarker for preoperative risk stratification and may help identify patients at increased risk of aggressive pathological features. Larger multicenter studies are warranted to validate these findings.

doi:10.1245/s10434-026-20765-3.abstract: Conventional survival analyses cannot fully account for recurrence as an intermediate event that dynamically influences subsequent mortality. Multistate models (MSMs) enable explicit modeling of transitions between clinically relevant disease states; however, their application among patients undergoing resection for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) remains limited. An international multi-institutional database was queried to identify patients undergoing curative-intent hepatectomy for CRLM between 1998 and 2023. A four-state MSM was constructed comprising alive and recurrence-free, alive with recurrence, colorectal cancer (CRC)-related death, and non-CRC-related death. Transition probabilities and transition-specific prognostic factors were evaluated RESULTS: Among 3002 patients, 1624 (54.1%) developed recurrence and 911 (56.1%) died, predominantly from CRC-related causes (92.8%). The probability of recurrence decreased substantially the longer patients remained recurrence-free after surgery, whereas recurrence markedly worsened subsequent prognosis. High tumor burden score was independently associated with transition to recurrence (hazard ratio [HR] 1.06 per unit; 95% confidence interval 1.03-1.08; p < 0.001) but not post-recurrence mortality, suggesting that the adverse prognostic impact of tumor burden was mediated primarily through recurrence. Adjuvant chemotherapy reduced recurrence (HR 0.76; p = 0.005) and CRC-related death from the recurrence-free state (HR 0.39; p = 0.002). MSMs provide a dynamic framework to characterize disease evolution after CRLM resection and represent recurrence as a clinically meaningful time-dependent intermediate state rather than a simple binary endpoint. Recurrence was the dominant determinant of long-term prognosis, supporting the role of MSMs for individualized prognostication and surveillance after hepatectomy for CRLM.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1800218.abstract: Breast cancer remains a leading cause of cancer incidence and mortality among women worldwide, with ongoing challenges in early detection, accurate diagnosis, prognosis estimation, and treatment-response assessment. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, has rapidly advanced breast cancer research by enabling analysis of high-dimensional imaging, pathological, genomic, and clinical data. However, the rapid expansion of this literature has resulted in substantial fragmentation across clinical tasks, data modalities, algorithmic paradigms, and software ecosystems. This systematic review presents a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of AI-driven breast cancer research published recently. Using a multi-database, Scopus and Web of Science, as primary data sources, a systematic bibliometric framework integrating performance analysis, science mapping, and thematic evolution was employed. The analysis is guided by explicit research questions examining: (i) the evolution of AI applications across diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment-response prediction; (ii) the adoption of explainable AI and hyperparameter optimization practices; (iii) the datasets, software frameworks, and algorithms shaping the field; (iv) the role of mammography as a core modality; and (v) emerging research hotspots, including transformer-based architectures. Unlike prior bibliometric studies focused mainly on citation metrics, this work adopts a task-aware, methodologycentric perspective, offering actionable insights to support reproducible, interpretable, and clinically integrated AI systems for breast cancer care.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1804620.abstract: This comprehensive review explores advancements in the treatment of Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC), emphasizing the transformative impact of targeted therapies and immunotherapies. Given TNBC's aggressive nature and limited therapeutic options, this review provides an in-depth analysis of emerging strategies that aim to enhance patient outcomes. Within targeted therapies, we discuss molecular subtypes and evaluate the efficacy of PARP inhibitors, EGFR inhibitors, and PI3K inhibitors, integrating insights from clinical trials. The immunotherapy landscape is examined through immune checkpoint inhibitors, Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, and novel vaccine-based approaches. Combination strategies are assessed, focusing on clinical efficacy, safety, and resistance mechanisms. Additionally, we highlight emerging therapeutic innovations, including bispecific antibodies, advanced drug delivery systems, and personalized medicine approaches. Beyond treatment modalities, the review addresses key challenges such as therapy resistance, biomarker-driven treatment selection, and the integration of Artificial Intelligence in TNBC management. Future directions emphasize ongoing clinical trials and evolving therapeutic paradigms aimed at improving survival and quality of life for TNBC patients. As the field progresses, a multidisciplinary approach integrating precision oncology, innovative therapeutics, and patient-centered care will be critical. In conclusion, this review encapsulates current breakthroughs and envisions a future where targeted and immune-based interventions redefine TNBC treatment, offering new hope for patients and clinicians alike.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1849274.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the most common and lethal malignancies, whose prognostic prediction is particularly challenging. Histopathological biomarkers are critical for cancer prognosis assessment. Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have made it possible to automate the classification and detection of information from whole-slide pathology images using deep learning. This study aims to utilize AI deep learning to analyze histopathological slides of HCC patients for prognostic stratification, thereby assisting in the development of clinical treatment plans. The Otsu thresholding method was employed to automatically segment whole-slide images (WSIs) from two HCC datasets, The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and HCC slides from Ansteel General Hospital. The pathological features of WSIs, extracted by the pretrained CONCH model were utilized as model inputs. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and additional metrics. Then Attention Heatmap Visualization was employed to analyze interpretability. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov curve was utilized to stratify patients into distinct risk groups. Survival analysis was performed to evaluate differences in overall survival between distinct risk groups. Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses were used to identify key clinical indicators and pathological features as significant predictors. The riskRegression package generated calibration curves comparing predicted versus observed survival outcomes. Calibration curves were quantify the deviation between model-predicted probabilities and actual observed outcomes. A prognostic prediction model was developed using the CLAM self-attention framework based on TCGA dataset, whose generalization capability was verified by histologically stained slide data from a proprietary dataset. The results showed that the model could achieve better migration. Mortality rates demonstrated a progressive increase across ascending risk groups. The risk stratification system possesses potential clinical utility for guiding treatment selection. Forest plots generated demonstrated that the risk stratification system functions as an independent prognostic predictor for HCC. Calibration curve analysis confirmed the predictive accuracy of the model, and this finding from Decision Curve Analysis underscores its superior utility in guiding clinical decision-making. This study developed a prognostic prediction model, whose risk stratification could be an independent prognostic predictor for HCC and a guide for therapeutic decision-making.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1893907.abstract: Microsatellite-stable (MSS) colorectal cancer (CRC) accounts for approximately 85% of all CRC cases and exhibits limited responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), representing a major challenge in current cancer immunotherapy. At the tumor-cell intrinsic level, low tumor mutational burden (TMB), impaired neoantigen generation, aberrant activation of oncogenic pathways such as WNT/β-catenin signaling, and defects in interferon-γ signaling contribute to impaired immune recognition and immune escape. Within the TME, the accumulation of immunosuppressive populations, including regulatory T cells (Tregs), myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), together with extracellular matrix remodeling and chemokine dysregulation, establishes an immune-excluded microenvironment that restricts effective antitumor immune responses. Furthermore, metabolic alterations, including enhanced glycolysis, lactate accumulation, and amino acid metabolic reprogramming, impair immune cell function and promote immunosuppression. Epigenetic modifications, including DNA methylation, histone remodeling, and non-coding RNA regulation, further contribute to the silencing of immune-related genes and reinforcement of immune evasion. In addition, recent advances in single-cell sequencing and spatial transcriptomics have provided unprecedented insights into the cellular heterogeneity and spatial organization of MSS CRC immune ecosystems. This review summarizes current knowledge regarding the molecular and cellular mechanisms driving immune resistance in MSS CRC and discusses future therapeutic opportunities for transforming immunologically "cold" MSS tumors into responsive immune microenvironments.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1901172.abstract: Ovarian cancer typically spreads via peritoneal seeding, hematogenous, or lymphatic routes. Bile duct metastasis is extremely rare, and peribiliary metastasis manifesting as diffuse Glissonian sheath infiltration without a detectable mass lesion, to our knowledge, has not been well documented. A 42-year-old woman with stage IVB high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, previously treated with cytoreductive surgery and multiple lines of chemotherapy, presented with fatigue, anorexia, and mild jaundice. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) revealed bile duct wall thickening, peribiliary edema (Glissonian sheath edema), and diffuse inflammatory changes without a discrete mass. Autoimmune and infectious workups were negative. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with biopsy showed micropapillary clusters of atypical cells. Immunohistochemistry was positive for CK7, CK19, PAX-8, P16, and mutant-type p53; CEA focally positive; ER negative; Ki-67 high. This confirmed metastatic high-grade serous carcinoma of ovarian origin involving the common bile duct wall. Imaging (MRI/MRCP) suggested diffuse peribiliary involvement compatible with Glissonian sheath infiltration, although the small biopsy did not directly sample the intrahepatic sheath itself. We hypothesize that the radiological changes reflect peribiliary lymphatic spread, but this remains an inference based on imaging-pathology correlation rather than a histologically proven mechanism. Effective biliary drainage could not be achieved because the patient was unable to tolerate the nasobiliary drain. She was discharged against medical advice and died shortly thereafter, according to family report. In cancer patients with unexplained cholestasis, peribiliary metastasis should be considered even when no mass is seen on cross-sectional imaging. ERCP with biopsy and immunohistochemistry are essential for diagnosis.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1906977.abstract: Prion proteins (PrP) are primarily known for their role in neurodegenerative conditions like Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease, where the misfolded, pathogenic isoform PrPSc propagates by using the normal cellular prion protein, PrPc, as a template, leading to aggregation and neuronal death. PrPc is a widely expressed glycoprotein that, beyond its role in prion disease, has emerged in specific contexts as a modulator of several hallmark cancer processes, including proliferation, apoptosis resistance, cellular signaling, adhesion, survival, and motility. This paper explores current evidence on how PrPc, and its misprocessed isoform pro-PrP, contribute to tumor progression across multiple cancer types, using colorectal cancer (CRC) as a unifying disease model to integrate mechanisms that are otherwise dispersed across the literature. This review will examine PrPc's role in sustaining proliferative signaling, resisting apoptosis, promoting migration and metastasis through its interaction with filamin A (FLNa), and contributing to therapy resistance. The goal is to consider the extent to which these mechanisms converge specifically in CRC, and what this means for PrPc's potential as a diagnostic and therapeutic target.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1910817.abstract: This study aimed to compare the effects of various first-line systemic therapies on health-related quality of life (HR-QoL) in patients with unresectable advanced gastric cancer (GC), and to comprehensively integrate survival benefits and HR-QoL outcomes associated with different treatments. A systematic literature search was conducted in the MEDLINE, CENTRAL and Scopus databases for studies published from database inception to December 2025. Manual retrieval of reference lists and abstracts from major oncology conferences held between 2016 and 2025 was performed as supplementary screening. Eligible studies were phase III randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared immune checkpoint inhibitors or targeted agents with platinum-based chemotherapy as first-line regimens for advanced GC and reported data on HR-QoL deterioration. Time to deterioration (TTD) of HR-QoL domains was assessed using the EORTC QLQ-C30, EORTC QLQ-STO22 and EQ-5D questionnaires. The surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) was applied to rank all included treatments based on HR-QoL indicators. We further performed an exploratory composite analysis integrating overall-survival and HR-QoL outcomes via the minimum distance criterion. In total, 10 RCTs enrolling over 8000 patients and covering six HR-QoL domains met the inclusion criteria. SUCRA analyses indicated that trastuzumab and tislelizumab had the lowest probability of the deterioration of global health status, physical function, nausea/vomiting, appetite loss and pain. When HR-QoL was combined with overall survival (OS) via an exploratory minimum distance criterion composite analysis, trastuzumab and tislelizumab showed favorable comprehensive performance across most evaluated domains. This composite metric remains exploratory without established uncertainty estimates and should not serve as primary evidence for clinical decision-making. This network meta-analysis suggests that trastuzumab (for HER2-positive disease) and tislelizumab (for largely biomarker-unselected populations) deliver the balance between HR-QoL preservation and OS benefit within their respective biomarker-eligible patient subgroups among systemic treatment options for unresectable advanced GC. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD420261422326.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1913824.abstract: Modified FOLFIRINOX (mFFX) and gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (GnP) are both recommended as standard first-line regimens for unresectable pancreatic cancer (PC). However, direct head-to-head comparative evidence remains scarce, and prior studies have largely failed to distinguish mFFX from standard FOLFIRINOX (sFFX). We systematically compared mFFX with GnP to evaluate their efficacy and toxicities. We searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies comparing mFFX with GnP as first-line therapy for unresectable PC published between January 2013 and May 2026. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were assessed using hazard ratios (HRs). Objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) were evaluated using risk ratios (RRs). Events of toxicities were assessed using odds ratios (ORs). Five studies (three RCTs and two retrospective studies) involving 1204 patients (578 in the mFFX arm and 626 in the GnP arm) were included. Compared with GnP, mFFX was associated with a shorter OS (HR 1.26, 95% CI 1.09-1.45; P = 0.002) and PFS (HR 1.21, 95% CI 1.04-1.40; P = 0.01), along with a borderline lower DCR (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.81-1.00; P = 0.05; I2 = 62%), which was consistent across RCTs (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81-0.94; I2 = 0%) but not observed in retrospective studies (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.71-1.29; I2 = 87%), and ORR did not differ significantly between the two regimens. As for toxicity profiles, mFFX showed an elevated incidence of grade ≥3 diarrhea (OR 5.63) and anorexia (OR 4.44). By contrast, grade ≥3 neutropenia (OR 0.66) and white blood cell decrease (OR 0.49) occurred more frequently under GnP. GnP was associated with more favorable OS and PFS than mFFX, a borderline DCR advantage, and distinct toxicity profiles. Given the modest effect size and the limitations of this study, clinical decision-making should integrate patient age, performance status, and anticipated second-line therapy. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420251175959.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1916260.abstract: Glioblastoma remains one of the most treatment-resistant cancers, and temozolomide (TMZ) resistance is a central barrier to durable clinical response. Inhibition of exportin-1 (XPO1) by selinexor has emerged as a promising strategy to overcome resistance in solid tumors; however, its ability to sensitize TMZ-resistant GBM cells and the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. We evaluated selinexor and TMZ, alone and in combination, in three GBM cell lines with distinct TMZ sensitivity profiles (LN18, resistant; U87MG, moderate; LN229, sensitive), assessing viability, apoptosis, cell cycle distribution, MMR/survival gene expression, apoptotic protein levels, and long-term colony-forming capacity. Selinexor potently sensitized GBM cells to TMZ across all three lines, with the most clinically meaningful effects observed in the TMZ-resistant background. The combination produced synergistic growth inhibition and robust apoptotic induction that neither agent achieved independently, driven by convergent suppression of MCL1 and BIRC6, partial restoration of mismatch repair gene expression, and CHK1-mediated checkpoint activation. Combination treatment induced nuclear p53 accumulation, markedly reduced BCL-2, and increased PARP cleavage, and durably suppressed long-term proliferative capacity. These findings position selinexor as a mechanistically rational TMZ sensitizer in resistant GBM and support further preclinical and translational investigation of this combination strategy.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1917039.abstract: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are closely associated with the progression of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, the clinical value of CTC detection in patients receiving systemic therapy for advanced HCC remains to be fully elucidated. A total of 125 patients with advanced HCC who underwent systemic therapy were enrolled in this study. Five milliliters of peripheral blood were collected at five time points: before treatment initiation, and 1 month, 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year after treatment. CTCs were isolated and captured using the Isolation by Size of Epithelial Tumor Cells (ISET) method. Tumor response to systemic treatment was evaluated according to the modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (mRECIST). We further analyzed the correlation between dynamic changes in peripheral blood CTC levels and tumor response to systemic therapy. The overall objective response rate (ORR) and disease control rate (DCR) were 39.2% (49/125) and 82.4% (103/125), respectively. Dynamic monitoring of CTCs revealed that CTC levels remained persistently high and gradually increased in patients with progressive disease (PD). In patients with complete response (CR) or partial response (PR), CTC levels decreased progressively during treatment and stayed at low levels thereafter. For patients with stable disease (SD), CTC counts began to decline 3 months after treatment but remained higher than those in patients with CR or PR. Baseline CTC levels were negatively correlated with treatment efficacy: patients with higher baseline CTC counts exhibited poorer tumor responses. Patients with baseline CTC counts < 15, CTC counts < 13 at 1 month post-treatment, and CTC counts < 10 at 3 months post-treatment were more likely to achieve an objective tumor response and obtained better therapeutic outcomes. Additionally, these patients had significantly longer progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) compared with those who exceeded the above cut-off values. Peripheral blood CTC counts are correlated with tumor treatment response in patients with advanced HCC. Serial CTC detection serves as a valuable tool for evaluating the efficacy of systemic therapy in advanced HCC.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1919105.abstract: Cervical cancer is one of the most common malignancies of the female reproductive system worldwide, and its development is closely associated with persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV). γδ T cells, as key effector cells bridging innate and adaptive immunity, exert unique and complex regulatory functions in tumor immune surveillance. However, the distribution patterns, functional polarization states, and antitumor mechanisms of distinct γδ T-cell subsets within the cervical cancer microenvironment have not yet been systematically elucidated, and the impact of HPV infection on the functional remodeling of γδ T-cell subsets remains controversial. This review summarizes the distribution characteristics and functional polarization states of the major γδ T-cell subsets, including Vδ1, Vδ2, and Vδ3 T cells, in the cervical cancer microenvironment. We further discuss the molecular mechanisms through which these subsets participate in immune surveillance via T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling, NKG2D-mediated recognition, Fas/FasL signaling, and cytokine secretion, and examine the regulatory effects of HPV infection on γδ T-cell subset remodeling. In addition, recent preclinical advances in γδ T-cell subset-based adoptive immunotherapy and combination strategies involving immune checkpoint blockade in cervical cancer are reviewed. Overall, this review aims to provide a theoretical basis and new perspectives for optimizing immunotherapeutic targets and developing individualized treatment strategies for cervical cancer.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1920042.abstract: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is a common neurological complication of cancer treatment that worsens function and quality of life. Topical herbal medicines are increasingly used as localized interventions for neuropathic symptoms; however, their clinical efficacy remains uncertain. This systematic review evaluated the effectiveness of topical herbal formulations for CIPN in cancer populations. We systematically searched Scopus, MEDLINE (Ovid), CINAHL, and Cochrane CENTRAL for randomized controlled trials assessing the use of topical herbal formulations in adults with CIPN. Outcomes included validated measures of CIPN pain, overall severity, sensory function, and adverse events. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool implemented in RevMan 5.3, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Five trials involving 201 participants were included, with an overall moderate risk of bias due to limited blinding and underpowered sample sizes. In breast cancer patients, henna vs. standard care significantly improved the overall severity of oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy, as measured by the CIPN Assessment Tool (p < 0.001), with significant reductions in sensory and functional subdomain scores. In a mixed-cancer population, Costus sp. oil vs. placebo significantly reduced neuropathic pain intensity, as measured by the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) (p = 0.001), and improved Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy/Gynecologic Oncology Group - Neurotoxicity (FACT/GOG-Ntx) scores (p = 0.028). Trials evaluating ajwain cream, Citrullus colocynthis oil, and a multi-compound essential oil formulation did not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in CIPN severity, pain, or quality of life compared with placebo. None of the included studies incorporated quantitative sensory or functional testing. All interventions were well tolerated, with only mild localized skin reactions reported. Despite modest benefits from certain herbal treatments in reducing CIPN pain and sensory symptoms, current evidence is limited by small sample sizes, methodological heterogeneity, and the lack of objective outcome measures. Rigorous, adequately powered RCTs with objective CIPN measurements are needed.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1922633.abstract: At present, the prognostic value of serum uric acid (SUA) in Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) remains controversial, and relevant clinical evidence lacks systematic and comprehensive verification. This the first-ever meta-analysis comprehensively synthesized evidence across various regimens to systematically evaluate the association between serum uric acid (SUA) levels and survival outcomes in NPC patients. This meta-analysis was strictly performed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Eligible clinical studies focusing on the prognostic role of SUA in NPC were systematically retrieved from domestic and international electronic databases. All retrieved literatures were screened strictly based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The methodological quality of enrolled studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Literature screening, data extraction, and quality evaluation were independently conducted by two investigators, and any discrepancies were resolved by consensus or consultation with a third senior researcher. Key prognostic data including hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for Overall Survival (OS), Progression-Free Survival(PFS), and Distant Metastasis-Free Survival (DMFS) were extracted and pooled for quantitative analysis to evaluate the prognostic significance of SUA in NPC. The pooled results demonstrated that elevated SUA was significantly correlated with OS in NPC patients, with a combined HR of 0.245 (95% CI: 0.092-0.398). In contrast, no statistically significant associations were observed between SUA levels and PFS or DMFS. The pooled HR for PFS was 0.557 (95% CI: 0.070-1.044), and the pooled HR for DMFS was 0.715 (95% CI: 0.023-1.407). The 95% CI of both PFS and DMFS crossed the invalid value of 1, indicating no significant statistical difference. SUA level is an independent prognostic factor for OS in patients with NPC, and higher levels of uric acid may improve the overall survival of patients. No significant correlation was identified between SUA levels and PFS or DMFS in NPC patients. SUA may serve as a novel, convenient, and non-invasive biomarker for prognostic evaluation of NPC, may provide a reference for prognostic risk stratification and individualized management. Further large-sample, high-quality prospective cohort studies are warranted to validate the present findings. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261483250, identifier CRD420261483250.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1935795.abstract: Altered N-glycosylation plays a critical role in immune regulation, yet the spatial distribution of N-glycans within immune niches of immunologically "cold" tumors remain poorly defined. Here, we combine matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI) with highly multiplexed immunohistochemistry using photocleavable mass tags. This integrated workflow enables spatial mapping of N-glycosylation and immune markers within lymphoid aggregates (LAs) in prostate and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma tissues, two malignancies that respond poorly to immunotherapy. Given the role of N-glycosylation in immune regulation, spatially resolved N-glycan profiling may provide insight into molecular heterogeneity within lymphoid aggregates and their surrounding tumor microenvironment. To assess the relationship between N_glycosylation and immune markers, candidate LAs from tissue samples collected from patients with varying stages of prostate cancer, PCa (n=49) and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, PDAC (n=26) were identified via histological stains prior to enzymatic release of N-glycans and MALDI-MSI. MALDI-IHC was used to target immune cell markers and extracellular matrix proteins. In tissues with LAs, three N-glycan structural classes were identified when detectable: oligo-mannose, fucosylated tetra-antennary, and bisecting N-acetylglucosamine in fucosylated bi,- tri- and tetra- antennary structures, with some N-glycans common to both tumor types. LAs showed predominantly central CD20 and CD44 signal surrounded by CD3 signal localized along the tumor periphery. Our analysis revealed unique N-glycan patterns within and surrounding LAs, with variable profiles in distant regions, highlighting heterogeneity in LA-associated N-glycan profiles.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1939329.abstract: Acute leukemias require rapid subtype identification to guide timely treatment. Differentiation of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute monocytic leukemia (AMoL/M5), and acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL/M3) often relies on specialized tests that may not be immediately available. This study evaluated differentiation only among patients already confirmed to have one of these three diagnoses, rather than screening an unselected population with suspected acute leukemia. This multicenter retrospective study included 9,398 newly diagnosed, previously untreated patients with established APL/M3, AMoL/M5, or ALL between May 2019 and May 2025 at four tertiary hospitals in China. Relapse, remission, follow-up, and non-initial disease episodes were excluded. Twenty-four routine hematological parameters were evaluated. One center served as the development cohort with five-fold stratified cross-validation, while three independent centers were reserved for external validation. Ten machine-learning algorithms were compared. Performance was assessed using AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and F1 score. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) supported feature selection and interpretation. An 18-feature random forest model achieved a development-stage cross-validated AUC of 0.93 and external AUCs of 0.89, 0.87, and 0.90. Overall sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, accuracy, and F1 score were 0.78, 0.90, 0.81, 0.91, 0.81, and 0.79, respectively. SHAP identified leukocyte, erythrocyte, and platelet indices as the most important features. A Streamlit application was developed for clinical evaluation. Using a development-derived APL alert threshold of 0.0966, APL sensitivity was 99.02% in development and 96.32%-97.94% across external cohorts, with PPVs of 54.34% and 35.58%-84.25%, respectively. External validation showed center-specific calibration shifts, indicating that predicted probabilities should not be interpreted as universally calibrated absolute diagnostic probabilities. Among patients already confirmed to have APL/M3, AMoL/M5, or ALL, this explainable model enabled low-cost preliminary differentiation using routine hematological data. It may support subtype prioritization and confirmatory testing but cannot replace standard diagnostics, identify other diagnoses, or screen unselected patients. Prospective multinational and workflow-based validation is required before routine implementation.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1941311.abstract: Myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) are driven by constitutive cytokine-receptor signaling, yet the metabolic programs associated with driver genotype and inflammatory remodeling remain incompletely defined. Here we integrated a 60-case clinical MPN cohort, the GSE174060 Affymetrix Human Transcriptome Array 2.0 microarray dataset, immune deconvolution, exploratory feature prioritization, the GSE228995 mouse single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) dataset, human-sample validation, and functional perturbation assays to investigate whether cuproptosis-related metabolism is associated with total calreticulin (CALR) abundance and Janus kinase-signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT)-related inflammatory signaling. GSE174060 included 36 samples: 6 essential thrombocythemia (ET), 11 polycythemia vera (PV), 9 primary myelofibrosis (PMF), 4 secondary myelofibrosis (SMF), and 6 healthy control (HC) samples. Clinically, CALR-mutated cases were enriched for thrombocytosis and distinctive megakaryocytic abnormalities, while inflammatory and fibrotic features tracked with higher interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Microarray-based transcriptomic analyses identified an MPN-associated cuproptosis-related and immune-response program, and consensus clustering separated samples into exploratory transcriptomic clusters. Within this expression-derived partition, post hoc multi-algorithm feature prioritization recurrently retained FDX1 and CALR among genes associated with the Cluster 1-versus-Cluster 2 transcriptional contrast. Single-cell analyses localized Calr and Fdx1 across hematopoietic and immune populations and highlighted inferred JAK-STAT-associated communication potential. In human MPN samples, FDX1 and total CALR protein and mRNA levels were increased and accompanied by STAT5 phosphorylation and elevated inflammatory mediators. Functionally, FDX1 knockdown reduced total CALR abundance, STAT5 phosphorylation, cytokine release, sensitivity to copper-dependent cytotoxicity, and proliferation, whereas FDX1 overexpression showed the reciprocal pattern and was partly counteracted by ruxolitinib. These findings support an association between FDX1 perturbation, total CALR abundance, STAT5-associated signaling, and inflammatory output in MPN, but do not establish direct regulation of mutant CALR or mutant CALR-MPL signaling.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1945631.abstract: Ewing sarcoma tumors are defined by chromosomal translocations fusing EWSR1 to ETS family genes, most commonly FLI1. The resulting EWS::FLI1 fusion oncoprotein drives tumorigenesis while simultaneously generating unique metabolic and molecular dependencies that may be exploited for Ewing sarcoma-specific therapies. Through analysis of the Cancer Dependency Map (DepMap, Broad Institute), we identified that Ewing sarcoma cell lines exhibit selective sensitivity to loss of genes regulating selenium metabolism compared to other cancer lineages. Ewing sarcoma cells are similarly sensitive to knockout of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), a selenoprotein that suppresses ferroptosis, a form of regulated, iron-dependent cell death characterized by the lethal accumulation of lipid peroxides. Using pharmacological inhibitors and targeted degraders of GPX4, as well as genetic knockout approaches, we demonstrate that Ewing sarcoma cells are selectively vulnerable to GPX4 loss or inhibition. We further identify ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1) as a modulator of ferroptotic sensitivity in Ewing sarcoma, with FSP1 expression level serving as a determinant of the magnitude of ferroptotic response. Together, these findings establish ferroptosis as a targetable vulnerability in Ewing sarcoma, define GPX4 and FSP1 as key regulators of ferroptotic sensitivity in this disease, and provide a mechanistic rationale for therapeutic strategies targeting the ferroptosis defense axis in Ewing sarcoma tumors.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1959240.abstract: The process of chronic gastritis transforming into gastric cancer (GC) follows the classic Correa cascade, with persistent inflammation driving the stepwise transition from normal gastric mucosa through superficial gastritis, atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, dysplasia, and ultimately carcinoma. Among these stages, intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia occurring on an atrophic mucosal background are widely regarded as the most common gastric precancerous lesions (GPL) because of their pronounced carcinogenic risk. Chronic inflammation can induce epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), thereby accelerating gastric malignant progression. In the GPL stage, the inflammatory gastric microenvironment commonly induces partial EMT (pEMT); importantly, this state is partly reversible and may be amenable to intervention to slow disease progression. As lesions advance, epithelial cells more fully undergo EMT, acquiring greater motility, invasiveness, and metastatic capability, which increases susceptibility to malignant conversion. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key molecular regulators in the transition from chronic gastritis to GC through EMT modulation. This review comprehensively discusses inflammation-driven EMT activation and functionally classifies pro-EMT oncomiRNAs (e.g., miR-21, miR-155) and anti-EMT tumor-suppressive miRNAs (e.g., miR-200 family, let-7 family, miR-34a), delineating a complex crosstalk network among inflammation, miRNA, and EMT. We further evaluate miRNAs as non-invasive biomarkers for early detection and prognosis of GPL and discuss emerging therapeutic strategies targeting the miRNA-EMT axis, including nanoparticle- or exosome-based delivery systems, miRNA antagonists, and miRNA sponges. Nevertheless, clinical application of circulating miRNAs remains limited by insufficient assay standardization and validation, incomplete target specificity, off-target effects, suboptimal delivery efficiency, and a lack of large-scale clinical evidence. By integrating molecular mechanisms and transformation status of miRNA-EMT axis in GPL, this review provides new insights for precision prevention and targeted intervention in gastric carcinogenesis.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1960553.abstract: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are abundant and functionally diverse components of the lung tumor microenvironment (TME) and are associated with therapeutic response and resistance in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Durable responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and targeted therapies remain limited, with TAM-associated immune evasion and therapy-refractory microenvironments representing potentially relevant components of this resistance landscape. This narrative review prioritizes evidence from human NSCLC specimens and clinically annotated cohorts, especially from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics, while integrating relevant mechanistic evidence from NSCLC experimental systems, animal models, and related cancer contexts. Moving beyond the M1/M2 paradigm, we synthesize convergent findings to describe recurring, niche-resolved TAM programs. Across NSCLC, we highlight recurrent SPP1-associated, TREM2-associated, and C1q/LAM-like macrophage programs as a practical framework for integrating recurrent TAM states across spatial and treatment contexts. We propose an integrative framework in which TAM state dynamics are associated with, and may contribute to, therapy-refractory phenotypes during (i) ICI therapy through immune exclusion, (ii) oncogene-targeted therapy through macrophage-associated bypass signaling and survival plasticity, particularly in EGFR-TKI resistance, and (iii) post-radiochemotherapy microenvironmental remodeling, with potential implications for residual disease ecosystems that require further clinical validation, particularly with respect to recurrence and relapse. TAM program signatures and spatial organization provide a rationale for investigating biomarker-guided stratification and macrophage-directed combination strategies targeting state-niche axes. Future work should prioritize clinically validated, state- and niche-resolved multimodal biomarkers and prospective translational studies to support rational pairing with ICIs and targeted therapies.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1974418.abstract: Purpose Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) accounts for more than 75% of renal cell carcinomas and is characterized by high metastatic potential and resistance to therapy. Fibronectin 1 (FN1), a major extracellular matrix glycoprotein, is overexpressed in various cancers and promotes tumor progression; however, its precise molecular mechanisms in RCC remain unclear. Methods We analyzed the expression level of FN1 and its clinical relevance in ccRCC using TCGA database. Subsequently, FN1 was knocked down in ACHN cells, followed by functional assays, RNA sequencing, and Western blot validation. Furthermore, we integrated FN1-interacting proteins from the BioGRID and STRING databases and combined this information with differentially expressed genes to identify key downstream effectors of FN1. Results FN1 was significantly upregulated in ccRCC and strongly associated with lymph node metastasis, distant metastasis, and poor overall survival. FN1 knockdown markedly suppressed invasion of ACHN cells, induced transcriptomic alterations, and downregulated key oncogenes, including CSF2, SOX9, and LAMC2. Pathway analysis revealed significant inhibition of the PI3K–Akt signaling axis. Integrating FN1-interacting proteins with the DEGs identified YWHAZ—a known regulator of the PI3K–Akt pathway—as a critical downstream effector of FN1, whose expression was markedly reduced upon FN1 knockdown. Rescue experiments further showed that YWHAZ overexpression substantially restored FN1 knockdown-impaired invasion but only modestly and non-significantly affected Akt phosphorylation. Conclusion FN1 promotes invasion in RCC cells at least in part through YWHAZ-dependent mechanisms, with partial involvement of PI3K-Akt signaling and additional pathways likely contributing. These findings suggest that the FN1/YWHAZ axis may serve as a candidate prognostic marker and a potential target for future preclinical investigation in RCC.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1974418.title: FN1 promotes invasion of RCC via YWHAZ-associated signaling with partial involvement of the PI3K-Akt pathway

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1979150.abstract: FOXM1, a forkhead-box transcription factor, is consistently overexpressed in breast cancer, particularly in the basal-like and triple-negative subtypes, in which high expression predicts poor survival. We propose, as a falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established mechanism, that FOXM1 may function as a dosage-integrating rheostat, in which convergent genomic, transcriptional, epitranscriptomic, translational, and post-translational inputs would determine discrete output states involving mitotic fidelity, chromosomal instability, metabolic rewiring, immune evasion, and stem-like plasticity. We further hypothesized that therapies directed elsewhere in the network are frequently buffered by the persistence or reactivation of FOXM1-associated outputs, while noting that resistance to direct FOXM1 inhibition proceeds instead through reversal of that output, which bounds the hypothesis rather than supporting it. Accordingly, we classified FOXM1-directed strategies, including direct inhibitors, degraders, condensate disruptors, upstream suppressors, and targeted delivery platforms, by their mechanism of engagement rather than by their chemical class. Existing evidence remains largely correlative and bulk-derived: available perturbation studies are categorical rather than graded, no study has titrated FOXM1 through intermediate levels or measured its outputs bidirectionally, and the few single-cell, time-resolved datasets resolve one output at a time. We identified these gaps, specified the components of an isoform-, localisation- and activation-resolved FOXM1 activity metric that would define dose in measurable terms, and proposed experiments to test threshold-dependent activation, discrete single-cell states, and history-dependent switching, grounding the last of these in the material properties and physical ageing of FOXM1 condensates rather than in an equilibrium phase boundary alone in order to distinguish dosage-dependent state selection from regulatory hub behavior.

doi:10.3389/fonc.2026.1988923.abstract: Recurrence remains common after curative-intent liver resection or thermal ablation for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). These interventions transiently remodel the hepatic and treatment-bed immune microenvironment through overlapping but distinct processes, including tissue injury, vascular and coagulation activation, neutrophil recruitment, and, particularly during resection, hepatic ischemia-reperfusion. We organize the evidence using a peri-interventional two-component heuristic: chronic liver disease and tumor-associated inflammation may shape baseline susceptibility, whereas acute treatment injury may trigger intervention-specific neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) accumulation. Experimental studies across liver-intervention and cross-cancer models link NETs to impaired CD8+ T-cell immunity, tumor-cell retention, extracellular-matrix remodeling, and metabolic adaptation. Patient-linked evidence remains limited and largely associative; much of the mechanistic framework therefore relies on colorectal liver metastasis and cross-cancer models. Translational studies should distinguish monitoring, pharmacodynamic, prognostic, and predictive applications and prioritize serial MPO-DNA as the best-supported circulating peri-interventional candidate, with NE-DNA or H3Cit-based measures as supportive assays and spatial validation where feasible. Candidate preclinical approaches include limiting NET formation, degrading established NET structures, and disrupting NET-target-cell signaling. NET-checkpoint combinations remain preclinical hypotheses, particularly because current phase III adjuvant ICI studies have not established postoperative HCC benefit. Because NET and neutrophil functions are context dependent, prospective studies should define intervention-specific NET kinetics, immune correlates, target engagement, recurrence phenotype, and safety.

doi:10.3390/cancers18203293.abstract: Objective: Our objective was to characterize the molecular–pathologic profile and recurrence patterns of endometrial cancer with pelvic lymph node isolated tumor cells (ITCs). Methods: A single-center retrospective study of patients with endometrial cancer and ITCs was conducted. Patients with concurrent lymph nodes or distant metastasis were excluded. Cases were reviewed by a gynecologic pathologist, and electronic medical records were reviewed. Descriptive statistics were performed using R 4.4.2. Results: A total of 43 patients were included, with a median follow-up time of 33 months. The majority were endometrioid carcinoma (91%) and stage I (72%). In total, 28 (65%) were MMR-proficient and p53-wild-type (MMRp p53wt), nine (21%) were MMR-deficient (MMRd), six (14%) were p53-abnormal (p53abn), and none were POLE-mutated (POLEmut). Additionally, 27 (96%) MMRp p53wt cases showed a microcystic, elongated, and fragmented (MELF) pattern of invasion. Adjuvant therapy was indicated in 38 (88%) patients; 32 (74%) received therapy and six (14%) declined. Four (9.3%) patients recurred, with a recurrence rate of 33% (2/6) for p53abn, 11% (1/9) for MMRd, and 4% (1/28) for MMRp p53wt. All recurrences were to distant sites. In the MMRp p53wt group, 16 (57%) had external beam radiation (EBRT) +/− vaginal brachytherapy (VBT), three (11%) had chemotherapy +/− radiation, and nine (32%) had no adjuvant treatment or VBT alone. Conclusions: Molecular profile is prognostically relevant in endometrial carcinoma with ITCs. ITCs in MMRp p53wt endometrioid carcinoma present a low risk of disease recurrence. As the majority of our cohort received adjuvant therapy, future work may explore de-escalating treatment in low-risk ITC cases.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7004.abstract: Immunotherapies have recently changed the treatment landscape of multiple myeloma (MM). CAR T cells and T-cell–redirecting bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) yield impressive responses and extend survival in patients with relapsed/refractory MM. There are now 2 BCMA-directed CAR T-cell products and 4 BsAbs (3 targeting BCMA, 1 targeting GPRC5D) currently approved by the FDA for relapsed/refractory MM, in which they demonstrated considerable efficacy. These drugs are now being evaluated in early treatment settings, including as part of frontline regimens for newly diagnosed MM. Importantly, administration of CAR T-cell therapy and BsAbs necessitate careful attention to unique toxicities, including cytokine release syndrome, immune effector cell–associated neurotoxicity syndrome, cytopenias, and heightened infection risk. This review summarizes the current landscape of immunotherapy in MM, including perspectives on sequencing CAR T-cell therapy and BsAbs. It also discusses ongoing clinical trials evaluating immunotherapy in new combinations and treatment contexts. Immunotherapies have become a key component of the MM therapeutic armamentarium and are poised to assume an even larger role in the coming years.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7035.abstract: Background: Fatigue is a prevalent and debilitating symptom among patients with cancer. Physical activity (PA) may help reduce fatigue and improve quality of life (QoL). This study evaluated longitudinal associations between PA, fatigue, and QoL across the cancer care continuum. Methods: Data were analyzed from 1,718 participants in a prospective multicenter cohort. Self-reported PA was assessed at baseline and up to 24 months post-diagnosis using a questionnaire based on the International PA Questionnaire (IPAQ). Metabolic equivalent task (MET)–minutes per week were calculated for walking, moderate, vigorous, and total physical activity. Fatigue and QoL were measured using the EORTC Quality of Life Questionnaire-Core 30 (QLQ-C30). Mixed-effects models evaluated associations between PA and outcomes. Lagged fluctuation models examined temporal relationships, separating between-person and within-person effects. Results: PA levels increased steadily from diagnosis through 24 months, coinciding with reduced fatigue and improved QoL. Higher PA was consistently linked to better fatigue and QoL outcomes. Walking was associated with lower odds of severe fatigue at 6 months (odds ratio [OR], 0.78; 95% CI, 0.62–0.98; P =.031) and 12 months (OR, 0.74; 95% CI, 0.59–0.94; P =.014), with higher odds of better QoL at all follow-up points. Vigorous activity showed the strongest protective effect against fatigue at 24 months (OR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.45–0.94; P =.023). In patients with nonmetastatic disease, protective associations were observed across all activity types and time points. Lagged models indicated that higher average vigorous activity predicted lower future fatigue ( P <.001). Conclusions: Greater PA, particularly walking, was associated with lower fatigue and improved QoL, especially in patients with early-stage disease. The posttreatment period (approximately 1 year post-diagnosis) may represent an important window for behavioral intervention. Findings support stage- and recovery phase–specific guidance and highlight walking as a scalable, low-risk target for survivorship care.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7048.abstract: Background: Treatment for B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) lasts >2 years and can impact families. The Children’s Oncology Group multicenter therapeutic trial AALL0932 randomized patients with NCI standard-risk, average-risk B-ALL (NCI-SR AR B-ALL) to receive maintenance vincristine/dexamethasone every 4 or 12 weeks (VCR/DEX4 or VCR/DEX12, respectively). Embedded in AALL0932, this study aimed to (1) longitudinally measure adverse family outcomes overall, and (2) determine whether patients on the VCR/DEX4 regimen (vs VCR/DEX12) had fewer adverse family outcomes. Methods: Patients with NCI-SR AR B-ALL who were offered enrollment on the multicenter randomized-controlled therapeutic trial AALL0932 were aged ≥4 years with an English-speaking parent. Parent-reported surveys were administered at T1–T5 (approximately 2, 9, 18, 26, and 38 months after diagnosis, respectively; T5 was assessed only in boys) and assessed household changes since leukemia diagnosis, leukemia-related household expenses in the past 4 weeks, unhealthy family functioning (Family Assessment Device score >2), and parents’ perceived child vulnerability (Child Vulnerability Scale ≥10). Postrandomization outcomes at T3 and T4 were compared between treatment groups using generalized linear mixed models and multivariable logistic regression models, as appropriate, adjusting for race and ethnicity. Results: Among 555 participants with completed evaluations, 420 were randomized (mean [SD] age, 6.0 [1.6] years; 45.7% female). At T1, 56.2% of randomized participants reported household changes since diagnosis (81.2% by T4), 88.6% reported ≥$100 in leukemia-related household expenses in the past 4 weeks (61.5% at T4), 19.0% had unhealthy family functioning (23.9% at T4), and 55.8% perceived their child as vulnerable (62.5% at T4). In multivariable models, VCR/DEX4 (vs VCR/DEX12) had an increased likelihood of reporting ≥$100 in leukemia-related expenses in the past 4 weeks (odds ratio, 1.73; 95% CI, 1.03–2.91), but other outcomes were similar between treatment arms. Conclusions: B-ALL family burdens develop early. Reducing maintenance VCR/DEX frequency may decrease expenses but not other outcomes. Interventions are needed to support families early and throughout ALL therapy.

doi:10.6004/jnccn.2026.7070.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have changed the treatment landscape of pleural mesothelioma (PM) over the past decade. This review summarizes the history of immunotherapy in PM, covering studies of single-agent immunotherapy, combination checkpoint blockade, the integration of ICIs into frontline therapeutic strategies, and ICI-VEGF combinations. Also discussed are the emerging role of biomarkers in guiding first-line therapy selection for patients with PM and novel therapeutic approaches. Dual checkpoint blockade targeting PD-1 and CTLA-4 demonstrated clinical efficacy in early-phase studies and led to the pivotal phase III CheckMate 743 trial, which established nivolumab and ipilimumab as a standard first-line systemic therapy for PM, particularly in patients with nonepithelioid histology. Since that time, other combination therapy approaches have been explored. For example, chemoimmunotherapy studies have evaluated ICIs, including pembrolizumab and durvalumab, in combination with platinum chemotherapy, with pembrolizumab plus platinum-doublet chemotherapy expanding the approved frontline treatment options for PM. VEGF inhibition, validated in the phase III MAPS study, provided a biologic rationale for combining antiangiogenic agents with ICIs. This prompted investigation of bevacizumab in combination with atezolizumab and chemotherapy in the BEAT-meso study. Unfortunately, this combination did not provide meaningful benefit in this setting. Optimal patient selection and treatment sequencing remain undefined. Although robust data support the use of second-line immunotherapy after first-line chemotherapy, there is a paucity of evidence regarding the efficacy of chemotherapy following frontline ICI. Despite advancements in therapeutic options in PM, biomarker-driven treatment selection remains limited at this time. Future large clinical studies must incorporate validated and standardized biomarker subanalyses, including approaches such as circulating tumor DNA and multiomics, for biomarkers to become clinically relevant in this heterogeneous malignancy. Finally, novel therapeutic strategies, including bispecific antibodies, targeted therapies, perioperative immunotherapy, vaccines, and cellular therapies, are under active investigation and may further expand treatment options for patients with PM.
